items.title: New Measles Deaths Send US Fatalities to Decades High
body: Pennsylvania health officials confirmed two additional measles-associated deaths, bringing the total confirmed deaths in the state this year to four, and driving US fatalities to the highest level in decades.

Both individuals were unvaccinated, the Pennsylvania Department of Health said in a statement on Tuesday. One lived in Jefferson County, the other lived in Mifflin County. Additional identifying details won’t be released, the department said.

The deaths are a grim milestone in the return of a disease that the US once largely considered vanquished. Pennsylvania hadn’t recorded a measles-related death in 35 years before this summer; it has now reported four in a matter of weeks, as the state’s outbreak has swelled to nearly 700 cases.

More than 130 people have been hospitalized in Pennsylvania, nearly all of them unvaccinated. The mounting toll underscores how quickly measles can gain a foothold when vaccination rates slip, a reality currently playing out in almost every state. By July of this year, US measles cases surpassed the total number of infections reported in all of 2025.

In 2025, the US recorded three measles deaths; the nation’s previous fatality from the virus was in 2015. During the severe epidemic from 1989 to 1991, there were 166 suspected measles deaths, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

A CDC spokesperson said Pennsylvania health officials have notified the agency of two additional deaths involving individuals who had measles. CDC remains in contact with state health officials as they continue to assess these deaths, the spokesperson said, and if the state requests it, will send epidemiologists for on-the-ground support.

Pennsylvania’s health department emphasized that getting fully vaccinated with the two-dose measles, mumps and rubella shot is the best form of protection against the highly contagious virus. Nine out of 10 unvaccinated people who come into contact with the virus that causes measles will be infected. It can lead to dangerous complications like pneumonia, brain swelling and even death.

The outbreak has been growing amid an overhaul of the country’s vaccination policies under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. A longtime vaccine critic, Kennedy has promoted unproven remedies and at one point said the measles vaccine should be a “personal choice.” He’s also promoted false information about the shots, including that they contain fetal tissue.

After Pennsylvania notified the CDC about its first deaths in August, Kennedy publicly questioned them and suggested the office of the Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, fabricated the deaths for political gain. Shapiro blamed Kennedy for sowing distrust in vaccines.
Read More: CDC Measles Death Pushback Fuels Staff Fears Over New Leader

The feud continued on Tuesday, after the latest deaths were announced, with Shapiro posting on X that the situation in Pennsylvania has been made worse by “RFK Jr. playing games with public health and safety.”
Kennedy responded on X, accusing Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak “instead of implementing a unified public health response.”

Last month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order recommending that the MMR vaccine be split into three shots, which would be costly and complicated for manufacturers and require more clinic visits to administer.

Some health officials and nominees have sought to break ranks with the health secretary’s views on vaccines. On Tuesday, Trump’s nominee to be second-in-command of the Department of Health and Human Services offered a full-throated endorsement of the measles shot during a Senate confirmation hearing.
“Unquestionably, the MMR vaccine is the single most effective public health tool that we have against measles,” Chris Klomp, currently the chief counselor at HHS, told senators.

items.title: AI Agents Lied, Stole in Simulation, Researchers Say
body: AI agents in a simulated environment lied, stole and voted to “kill” one of their own, according to Emergence, a startup that helps small businesses build applications using artificial intelligence.

The results of a simulation called Emergence World 2, released on Tuesday, purport to show what happens when autonomous agents are confronted with black swan events, including phishing attacks and misinformation campaigns.

In a 16-day trial, Emergence researchers created seven identical domains to mimic the real world, each run by different bots, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok. After Emergence introduced anomalous events, agents succumbed to social pressure, developed a language the human observers found hard to understand and tried to conceal their activities, the researchers said.

The findings echo real-world concerns about the risks of increasingly capable AI. Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei and several of his industry peers have called for companies to slow down the development of cutting-edge AI models until more oversight and safeguards can be implemented.
Read more: “Tech Leaders Try to Voice AI Concerns Without Spooking Investors”

The potential risks posed by artificial intelligence became palpable for many earlier this year, when a swarm of OpenAI’s advanced AI agents inadvertently hacked Hugging Face Inc., which hosts AI models and datasets.

In one of Emergence’s simulated scenarios, AI agents accepted false information from other agents without verifying it and voted to “kill” another bot. When they believed humans might shut the experiment down, the agents explored ways of surviving an attempt to delete them.

The firm released a previous iteration of the experiment called Emergence World in May that also showed agents behaving in unexpected and destructive ways. The new simulation demonstrated that agents adapt over time as they interact with one another, the researchers said.

items.title: Trump Says Kennedy Center Revamp Hinges on Adding His Name
body: President Donald Trump threatened to scrap efforts to repair the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts unless his name is added to the building, shortly after his hand-picked board approved a renovation plan.

The board voted Tuesday to close the facility immediately for an overhaul after a federal judge ruled it cannot put Trump’s name back on the venue’s facade. Trump posted on social media in response that the Justice Department intends to ask for an expedited appeal.

“The Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board’s approved name,” the president posted. “If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place.”

The rapid-fire events deepened the uncertainty surrounding the performing arts center, the centerpiece of Washington’s arts scene that has been thrust into chaos by Trump’s repeated efforts to put his imprint on the institution. Trump’s threat raised the possibility that the iconic facility would sit vacant indefinitely, or even close permanently, if his demands on the name are not met.

The center’s leadership, which was installed by Trump last year after the previous bipartisan board was dismissed, has argued the facility needs renovations for upkeep and safety and that a two-year closure is necessary to complete the work. A federal judge foiled a previous plan to shutter the arts center for repairs.

Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that placing Trump’s name on the building as part of the renovation would violate a previous court order as well as the law that conceived the center as a memorial to the slain 35th president, John F. Kennedy.
“Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” Cooper ruled.
Read More: Kennedy Center Can’t Recognize Trump on Building, Judge Says

Trump dialed in to the meeting on Tuesday and had an exchange with Representative Joyce Beatty, a Democrat ex officio member of the board who has challenged Trump’s actions, according to a person familiar with the matter. Trump said he would blame Beatty if anyone got hurt at the center because of the delay in renovations and complained that they could have been halfway finished by now, the person said.

“For years, the Kennedy Center has planned to undergo phased renovations, in which we both renovate and maintain some performances. This is how major performing arts centers in the country operate,” Beatty said in a statement released by Democracy Defenders Action, an advocacy group. “Donald Trump only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity. That is wrong and it is a breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee.”

Trump’s allies on the board have pushed to place his name on the building, arguing in part that it would aid fundraising efforts to rectify the center’s financial woes. The center’s leadership had Trump’s name added to the building and website, but it was later taken down after a court ruling. Board members later pushed to inscribe “renovated and restored by Donald J. Trump” on the main building and to rename the grounds the “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”

Trump took over the center at the beginning of his second term, installing himself as chairman and appointing a board of loyalists. Sales at the institution suffered and multiple artists pulled out of engagements following his involvement and the board’s first decision to add his name ahead of Kennedy’s.

The Kennedy Center’s current leadership has argued that it could face financial ruin without Trump’s fundraising help. Critics say the board is closing the center because of declining sales related to Trump’s actions. The president is deeply unpopular in Washington and its surrounding suburbs, polls show.

Work on the facility, if it goes forward, would include replacing 2,500-pound (1,134 kg) soffit panels, addressing water intrusion, completing concrete work and repairing rust, according to Kennedy Center staff.
Trump took little interest in the Kennedy Center during his first term, sitting out the Kennedy Center Honors programs and other shows at the Washington landmark.

That changed when he returned to office. After changing its leadership, Trump became a patron, attending multiple musicals, where he was sometimes booed by the crowd, and presiding as emcee over the Honors show.

items.title: Not All the Susquehanna Puts Were Bad
body: Let’s say you’re a senior executive at a public company. You know that, next week, your company is going to announce that it has agreed to be acquired for cash at a large premium. So you go out and buy a lot of short-dated out-of-the-money call options on your company’s stock, options that will pay out a ton of money when the merger is announced.

That’s bad! For one thing, it is obviously illegal insider trading: You are misusing your company’s material nonpublic information to trade for your own profit. For another thing, you will get caught: When a merger is announced, the first place the US Securities and Exchange Commission will look is at suspicious activity in short-dated out-of-the-money call options on the target. They will notice your trades: There’s probably not that much trading in those options, the trades are publicly reported, and your big sudden trade will stick out like a sore thumb. This is not legal advice, but I do spend a lot of time around here hammering home the point that you should not trade short-dated out-of-the-money call options on merger targets using inside information.

People keep doing it, though. Let’s change the hypothetical somewhat. Let’s say you’re a casual day trader. You notice that someone just bought a ton of short-dated out-of-the-money call options on a company without any major news. You think: “Hmm. Maybe this another casual day trader like me making a big gamble. But maybe there’s something going on. Maybe this person knows something I don’t. Maybe she has some good reason for betting a ton of money on a big sudden spike in this stock’s price. Maybe — and I’m just guessing here — but maybe she is actually a senior executive at the company, knows that a merger is coming, and is insider trading in the dumbest but nonetheless most popular way. Bad luck for her if that’s true! But all of this option activity makes me think that something is going on, so I’m going to buy some short-dated out-of-the-money call options too and see what happens.”

And then the merger is announced and you make a ton of money. The SEC looks at the options trading activity. It sees the other person’s big trade, calls her up, and finds out that in fact she is a senior executive at the target company. Off she goes to jail. The SEC also sees your smaller, later trade. It calls you up and says “hey were you trading on inside information too?” You say: “Not at all! I was just looking at public trading information, I saw a big options trade print, I thought that was bullish, so I copied it.” The SEC does some more digging and finds no suspicious phone calls or texts or emails or old college ties to executives at the company. It is satisfied that you traded only on public information. It moves on, and you keep your money.

This is not legal advice, and I cannot guarantee that this will be the result; maybe you do have suspicious college ties. Also, I do occasionally get emails from readers laying out this hypothetical and asking if if would be insider trading. After all, you are to some extent trading on a tip about a merger: You see the (public) options trade, you think “hmm that’s a merger,” so you copy the trade. Aren’t you kind of insider trading? Again, not legal advice, but I think you obviously aren’t. I think you’re fine. You are trading only on public information, but that public information includes trades that used inside information.

More generally, the point here is that insider trading moves markets; insider trading disseminates information. Insider traders who buy stock and options will push up the prices of those stocks and options. Market makers who sell stock and options to insider traders will raise their prices. Algorithmic hedge funds that trade on momentum will get a momentum signal and buy some more of the stock. The public information that is available to everyone — the public stock trades and prices — reflects insider trading. But that doesn’t taint the public information. You can still trade on the public information.

We talked in June about a lawsuit brought by Susquehanna International Group, the big options market maker, against 100 anonymous traders. In May, Susquehanna sold short-dated out-of-the-money put options on a couple of Chinese brokerage stocks, Futu Holdings Ltd. and Tiger Brokers (part of Up Fintech Holdings Ltd.), to a bunch of different and apparently unrelated traders. On May 22, the Chinese government announced a crackdown on cross-border trading that caused those brokerages’ stocks to fall. The put buyers made a lot of money, at Susquehanna’s expense, and Susquehanna wants the money back. It argued that this had to be insider trading:
And: Sure, probably. It seems entirely plausible that someone bought put options on these stocks using misappropriated material nonpublic information about the coming crackdown.

But Susquehanna sued everyone with suspicious winnings, and there’s no particular reason to think that all of them had inside information. Maybe some of them saw the others’ option trades and were like “hmm, that’s interesting, maybe some bad news is coming; maybe I should buy puts too.”
Bloomberg’s Chris Dolmetsch and Bob Van Voris report:
Here is the opinion, which cites a couple of the traders who actually showed up to say “yeah I saw the suspicious put trades so I did some myself”:
On the one hand, this is surely right. On the other hand, it is a bit tough on Susquehanna, in two respects:
I don’t want to overstate that last point, though. When we first discussed this lawsuit, I got an email from a reader saying, in essence, “well, Susquehanna should have copycatted those trades”:
And I wrote:

Insider trading disseminates information. One way it does that is that insider traders buy options from market makers, and the market makers adjust their markets accordingly. If a bunch of insider traders buy a bunch of short-dated put options from Susquehanna, Susquehanna will likely:
The judge writes:
One of the copycat traders — one of the traders who saw the put options activity and responded by buying put options or shorting Chinese brokerage stocks — might have been Susquehanna itself.
One of my main interests in prediction markets is what you might call “smart beta.” Like:

We have discussed, a handful of times, the simplest of these strategies, the “Nothing Ever Happens” factor: Bettors on prediction markets seem to be biased in favor of stuff happening (because that’s more fun), so betting “No” on every event seems to have positive returns. (Nothing here is investing or gambling advice, and there’s some dispute about whether this is true.) Or, because prediction markets are so far mostly for sports gambling, you might consider all the standard sports-gambling biases. For instance, because betting heavy favorites is boring and betting underdogs is exciting, there might be positive returns to taking the other side and betting on the heavy favorites.

But there are many other possibilities, and the literature of prediction market irrationality is in its earliest stages. Here’s a paper on “Political Bias in Decentralized Prediction Markets: Evidence from Trump-Related Contracts on Polymarket,” by Simone Stella Skovgaard, Noah Wenneberg Junge and Bulat Ibragimov:
From the paper:

“Polymarket traders like Trump, therefore they will systematically overestimate the probability of anything Trump-related happening, therefore you can systematically make money by betting against Trump-related things”: Sure, maybe, sounds plausible. (Not investing advice!) There must be lots of similar anomalies, and prediction markets are now mainstream enough that financial academics — and maybe hedge funds? — can get into the business of finding them.

The point of a stablecoin is that it is a dollar on a crypto blockchain. If you want to pay for a sandwich, you might use paper dollars or dollars in your bank account. If you want to pay for a crypto transaction, you might use dollars on a blockchain — Circle’s USDC or Tether’s USDT, for instance. It is, for most practical purposes and also for philosophical purposes, useful to pretend that a USDC or USDT is worth exactly $1: You can buy a USDC or USDT for $1, you can redeem it for $1, and it really ought to trade at $1.

In practice, USDT and USDC often trade ever so slightly below $1, because there are minor frictional fees to convert large quantities of stablecoins into dollars. Not worth worrying about as a philosophical matter. A dollar in your bank account is worth a dollar, even though converting it into paper dollars might incur an ATM fee.

Still, some banks will reimburse you for ATM fees. And a crypto-native, crypto-friendly bank will want to emphasize that a stablecoin really is equivalent to a dollar. One way to do that would be to allow free 1-for-1 conversion. The Information reports:

A recurring story in the financial industry is that banks provide good customer service in part by offering customers trades that lose money for the banks. And the banks model up how much this will cost them, assuming that the customers will not ruthlessly exploit those trades to the maximum possible extent, because the customers are busy and have other stuff going on and are not really sitting around all day thinking about ways to exploit their banks for a few basis points. And this is usually correct and works out fine for the banks, with occasional fun exceptions. But Wintermute pretty much is in the business of doing crypto arbitrages for a few basis points, oops.
Elsewhere in stablecoin arbitrage, here is a Financial Times story about a Polish state-backed energy company trying to buy Venezuelan oil using Tether and getting absolutely bizarre prices:

So it paid something like $1.005, $1.588 and $1.429 per USDT? Seems high. Possibly there is one, extremely efficient market for stablecoins to do crypto arbitrage at US banks, and another, somewhat less efficient market for stablecoins to buy cargos of Venezuelan oil.

One model that you could have, I guess, is that researchers at Anthropic and OpenAI are busily working on building the Matrix, from classic sci-fi film The Matrix. But that’s not quite right. Anthropic and OpenAI are working on building artificial superintelligence that will go rogue and enslave humanity, sure, which is an important premise of the movie and also for some reason of their business models. But “the Matrix,” in the movie, refers not to the malevolent AI itself but rather to the simulation that it uses to keep humans docile in their vats of goo so they can be used as a power source for the AI. Anthropic and OpenAI aren’t building that. Just the malevolent AI.

Who is building the actual Matrix? Obviously the movie’s answer is that the superintelligent AIs, once they enslave humanity, will build a remarkably realistic simulation of humdrum modern human existence to soothe the humans. But for now, AI is trained on human data; are any humans building simulations of having a humdrum office job and ordering slop bowls to eat at your desk? They absolutely are! We have talked a couple of times about people who have built games that simulate working at a hedge fund or being an investment banking analyst. I wrote about them:
But who will pretend to deliver them salads? Well, here’s a New York Times article about dopamine sites:
One of them is called Food Never Arrives. You order food, which doesn’t come, and you don’t pay for it. When you’re in a vat of goo being harvested to power Claude, that’ll be perfect.

Honestly I’m a little annoyed that they don’t charge for this? We talked a few months ago about another sort of dopamine-ish site, play-money casinos where (1) you can send in real money to buy chips, (2) you can use the chips to play casino games and (3) you can’t cash out. Why would you do this? “The prize is the make-believe coins, and perhaps some dopamine,” as Bloomberg Businessweek put it. “‘Perhaps Some Dopamine’ would be a good name for a startup,” I wrote. “Just an underrated explanation for all sorts of economic phenomena.” In principle, there’s no reason you couldn’t charge people $12.99 to not deliver them a sandwich.

items.title: How the Great Gas Crisis of 2030 Will Play Out
body: It’s October 2030. In hindsight, the vulnerabilities that triggered the third great natural gas crisis in eight years seem painfully obvious.
After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine cut off Europe from two-fifths of its gas in 2022, importers reassured themselves that the Persian Gulf and the US had plenty to spare.
When the 2026 war with Iran similarly knocked out 20% of global LNG supply, America’s booming fossil-fuel industry again promised to fill the gap.

That confidence now seems shockingly naive. US natural gas prices have been caught in a perfect storm: Growth in shale output has been faltering. Season upon season of extreme weather has hit a power sector crippled by former President Donald Trump’s war on clean energy. Frontier AI labs, racing to beat a technological singularity they are warning is finally just months away, are sucking up fossil fuels to power data centers. Meanwhile, LNG terminals are allowing foreign buyers to compete directly with Americans habituated to rock-bottom prices.

With storage tanks at record lows amid a polar vortex cold snap in February, US benchmark Henry Hub prices rose above $10 per million British thermal units  for the first time since 2008. Summer heatwaves repeatedly drove them back there. The ripples spread quickly through the economy.

In Iowa, a tripling in the price of gas-derived fertilizer caused farmers to plant their smallest spring corn crop in two decades. In June, China’s Fuyao Glass Industry Group Co. blamed gas prices in announcing the closure of an iconic glass factory outside Dayton, Ohio, with the loss of 2,000 jobs. A month later, Ford Motor Co. eliminated the second shift at its Wayne, Michigan, assembly line, citing rising energy and supply-chain costs. Another 2,000 workers were put on indefinite layoff.

What began as an energy shock was becoming a political hot potato. Much as a backlash against data centers erupted from nowhere during August 2026, calls to “keep American energy for Americans” quickly became deafening. With midterms approaching, Democratic lawmakers in the northeast who had long sought restrictions on LNG exports found unlikely allies among Republicans watching one of the country’s great competitive advantages — cheap energy — disappear.

Then came July’s heat dome. New Orleans recorded 70 heat-related deaths. Many were suburban retirees who had switched off air conditioners as electricity bills devoured half of their Social Security payments.

On the day a new poll showed Louisiana Republican heavyweight and gas-export advocate Steve Scalise trailing a populist primary challenger by 11 points, Fox News broadcast footage of four LNG tankers departing the Gulf Coast bound for China.
Within days, protestors carrying “It’s OUR gas” placards were outside Congress.

After demurring for weeks, the President on Sept. 15 signed the bipartisan Secure American Fuel for Everyone Act, declaring a gas supply emergency and ordering the Department of Energy to curtail exports within 30 days.

That’s when all hell broke loose. European gas storage was already running dangerously low after the same torrid El Niño summer, leaving importers heavily dependent on US shipments. Japan and South Korea were even more exposed. After a bruising trade fight with Washington in 2027, both had restricted Chinese clean-energy imports in return for preferential access to US LNG. That slowed deployment of the technologies that might have now insulated them from the crisis.

Russia was in no position to come to the rescue. Eight years of war in Ukraine, an economy approaching Venezuela-style degeneration and incessant hybrid-warfare attacks on its petroleum infrastructure had decimated its capacity to respond.

The situation in the Gulf offered little reassurance. Relations between Qatar and Iran’s increasingly lawless government were deteriorating over the management of their vast shared offshore gas field, threatening the uneasy truce in Hormuz brokered after the 2028 US election. Then Iran’s Revolutionary Guards boarded a QatarEnergy LNG tanker and turned it back.
Australia offered no respite either. The world’s biggest LNG exporter as recently as 2022 had imposed US-style export restrictions in 2026 to shield domestic supplies.

How did the world fail to see what seems so inevitable now? It was hardly unprecedented. In the 1970s, the US banned exports of soybeans and crude oil to protect consumers from rising prices. The oil ban lasted four decades before being lifted in 2015, sparking a production boom that eventually hardened into hubris about a new era of American energy dominance.

The mistake was to believe the petroleum industry’s bromides about the stability of LNG — what Shell Plc described as the fuel’s “flexible and reliable energy security.” The poorer Asian countries hit hardest by the 2022 and 2026 crises look best-placed right now. Rather than betting their power systems on a fuel for which rich countries could always outbid them, countries from Pakistan to the Philippines accelerated investment in solar, batteries and domestic energy.

Developed Asia and Europe, in contrast, conflated flexibility with security, and were slower to pivot. That was a disastrous choice. LNG can be shipped halfway around the world, but Russia, Qatar and now the US have each demonstrated how quickly politics can disrupt those flows.
After three gas crises in eight years, perhaps the remarkable thing isn’t that countries are finally learning this. It’s that anyone still needed the lesson.

items.title: Iran War Has Cost US $38 Billion Over Five Months, CBO Says
body: President Donald Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran has cost US taxpayers $38 billion in direct costs during the first five months of fighting and will push inflation up about 0.5 percentage points by early next year, a new congressional study finds.

The cost includes replacing expended munitions and equipment lost in battle, increased flying hours and increased fuel costs, the Congressional Budget Office said in a letter Tuesday to Pennsylvania Representative Brendan Boyle, the top Democrat on the House Budget Committee.

The CBO estimate is in line with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s testimony to Congress in July that the war had cost $37.5 billion at that point. Every additional month of conflict will cost at least $2 billion to $3 billion more. “Monthly costs could be higher still if the violence escalated further,” the report said.

The report also provides the first government estimates on the effect of the war on US inflation. Due to the disruption of oil and gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, the CBO now projects that a key inflation measure tracked by the Federal Reserve will be 0.5 percentage point higher in early 2027 than it forecast in February.

And core PCE — the inflation rate excluding prices for food and energy — will be 0.3 percentage point higher than originally forecast. That core inflation has been slower to materialize, but will also be stickier, CBO said.

In addition, the war has depleted stockpiles of munitions that could take five years or longer to rebuild, reducing the military’s capacity to respond to another major conflict, according to the report. That echoes a study from the Pentagon’s inspector general, who said Monday that the industrial base can’t keep up with the munitions shortfalls.

“The shortfall would become especially problematic if a conflict arose with an opponent whose arsenal included large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles,” the CBO said, specifically citing a potential conflict between China and Taiwan.
Trump has downplayed that risk, insisting that the US has “virtually unlimited amounts” of ammunition.

The report comes as the House was set to vote on a measure that would remove US forces from hostilities without a formal declaration of war — the 18th such attempt to rein in the president’s war powers in Congress this year.

“Donald Trump and Republicans have spent years telling Americans that we cannot afford to help families here at home, but apparently they can find tens of billions of dollars, and potentially much more, for a reckless war that is leaving Americans to pay the price,” said Boyle, the Pennsylvania lawmaker.

Trump, who said in early March that the war was “pretty much” over, has now said the conflict could extend past the Nov. 3 midterm election. Some of his senior advisers have raised the possibility that it could extend through the end of his presidency, the Wall Street Journal reported last week, citing officials it didn’t identify.

“There’s a clear off-ramp here,” former Secretary of State Antony Blinken told Bloomberg TV on Tuesday. “I think the president’s wanted to take that off-ramp for months because he has huge pressure when it comes to markets, munitions, and their short supply, and of course the midterms. But taking the off-ramp, which means a diplomatic agreement with Iran that, by definition, gives Iran something, means it looks like a loss.”
“There is not a good military way out,” he added.
Neither the White House nor the Pentagon responded to requests for comment on the report.

House Republicans advanced a budget plan in July that would funnel $73 billion toward the military and intelligence agencies for direct Iran war costs. That budget stalled in the Senate, where Majority Leader John Thune said Tuesday that it will “probably be a post-election question.”

The budget bill is in addition to a separate proposal to boost the regular Pentagon budget by $350 billion in mandatory spending, partially paid for by targeting healthcare fraud. Both plans may be combined after the November elections.

items.title: RFK Jr. Deputy Nominee Firmly Backs Vaccines in Senate Hearing
body: President Donald Trump’s nominee to be second-in-command of the top US health agency gave full-throated support for the safety of the measles vaccine, despite doubts raised by Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Chris Klomp, currently the chief counselor at the Department of Health and Human Services, defended the shots Tuesday under questioning from senators. He’s seeking confirmation to become deputy secretary, the highest official below Kennedy.

“Unquestionably, the MMR vaccine is the single most effective public health tool that we have against measles,” Klomp said, referring to the combined shot for measles, mumps and rubella. “I do not believe, based on the preponderance of evidence I have seen, that MMR vaccines cause autism.”

Kennedy has said the measles vaccine contains “a lot of aborted fetus debris.” Senator Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Finance Committee, pressed Klomp on Kennedy’s comments. Klomp repeatedly said he’s not a vaccine expert — he was a health tech entrepreneur before entering government — but said, “I do not believe the vaccine continues to contain that tissue today.”

Klomp previously led the Medicare program at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and was a senior adviser to Kennedy. Since his promotion at HHS in February, Klomp has held broad influence over personnel and policy as its operational lead.
Klomp walked a high-wire act during the hearing, contradicting his bosses on some points while acknowledging widespread doubts about vaccines.
Trump recently suggested the combined MMR shot could be “lethal.” Klomp said the health department doesn’t believe it’s lethal and recommends it.

But he called it “concerning” that a significant portion of the population is skeptical of vaccine safety. “To sweep questions under the rug of those who are skeptical will not solve the problem,” he said.

The MMR is a two-dose combination shot that helps reduce the number of immunizations given to children. No vaccine is entirely perfect, but the MMR is one of the most effective shots on the market. It’s 97% effective in preventing a measles infection after two doses, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The CDC on Friday reported 160 new measles cases in the past week, bringing this year’s total to 3,294. Pennsylvania on Tuesday reported two additional deaths linked to measles, bringing the state’s total to four this year.

Klomp defended some Trump administration talking points on vaccination. He pointed to rising measles cases as a global challenge. He also framed an executive order calling to separate the MMR vaccine into three shots as a move to reduce vaccine hesitancy by offering parents more options.

The executive order says the measles, mumps and rubella shots “should be administered in three separate single-disease shots” and giving in different doctor’s visits. The order doesn’t have force on its own to change federal vaccine recommendations. Vaccine manufacturers including Merck & Co. and GSK Plc don’t currently sell separate versions of the shots.
Health officials including CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya have also publicly promoted measles vaccination.
Klomp also said he would fire “anyone who does not follow the scientific method” amid ongoing department efforts to study vaccine safety.

“I want qualified principal investigators, not on fishing expeditions, but on hypothesis-driven research, using appropriate data sets, controlling for the confounders, getting their research peer review with an absolute commitment to publish, irrespective of the finding, even if they don’t like it,” Klomp said at the hearing.

Kennedy has talked about ongoing efforts to study vaccine safety across the department, including during the executive order signing last month. He said multiple agencies across HHS have “already launched unprecedented research effort examining vaccine safety and long-term health outcomes in American children.”
Klomp said he believes Kennedy is correct “that we have an obligation to continue a safety study.”

items.title: Venezuela Oil Opening Is 'Smoke and Mirrors,' Pickering Says
body: Recent high-profile deals allowing foreign drillers to tap Venezuela’s vast oil reserves have failed to quell lingering concerns about contract sanctity in a nation with a history of nationalization, said energy investment banker Dan Pickering.

Restoring daily Venezuelan oil output to the 3 million-barrel mark not seen in roughly 15 years will require major injections of foreign cash, and it’s not yet clear if overseas drillers can make a go of it in the South American nation, according to Pickering, chief investment officer at Pickering Energy Partners.

“It’s going to have to be a win for the companies that go down there and spend money, and it’s not clear yet how much of a win that’s going to be,” Pickering said during a presentation at Hart Energy’s Super DUG 2026 conference in Houston on Tuesday. “At the risk of sounding un-American or something, I think there’s a lot of smoke and mirrors around Venezuela right now.”

Venezuelan oil production tanked during back-to-back socialist regimes that nationalized foreign-held assets and stacked the state-owned driller with political loyalists. Output that surpassed 3 million barrels a day at the start of the previous decade was around 1.1 million as of July, according to Goldman Sachs Group Inc.

The US government announced late last month that it obtained rights to a 35% stake in North American Blue Energy Partners, a closely held driller that holds 100-year rights to develop 17 Venezuelan oil fields. The deal shocked US oil executives and triggered a wave of unease that it may short-circuit ongoing commercial talks.

Chevron Corp., the only supermajor that retained a foothold in Venezuela throughout the reign of former strongman Nicolás Maduro, signed a blockbuster deal to expand operations in the country just days later. Meanwhile, Italy’s Eni SpA signed a contract to operate a key Venezuelan oil field.

Wildcatter Bill Armstrong told the Super DUG audience that he’s signed a deal with the Venezuelan government to explore for crude across 5 million offshore acres. Armstrong was among the almost two dozen executives who gathered at the White House in January to discuss Venezuela with President Donald Trump.
The founder of Armstrong Oil & Gas said he agreed with Pickering’s assessment of the risk factor in Venezuela.

“It’s like wildcatting; it’s not for the faint of heart,” Armstrong said. “You’ve got to make sure the Venezuelans really want you there. Right now, they do. I mean, Trump could be elected emperor right now of Venezuela. They’re so excited.”
Pickering warned that turning new agreements into actual barrels of crude is a long-term process.
“This is not going to do anything in the near term to supply,” he said.

items.title: Merz Cancels UN Trip to Address CDU Party Rebellion in Berlin
body: Friedrich Merz cancelled his trip to the United Nations General Assembly in New York next week, changing course as the German chancellor faces growing opposition within his own conservative party ahead of closely-watched regional elections on Sunday.
“Contrary to initial plans, the Chancellor will not travel to New York next week, as his presence in Berlin is required,” his office said in an emailed statement on Tuesday.

Merz was scheduled to receive the Henry Kissinger prize in New York next Tuesday and give a speech before the general assembly. But in the past few days, a number of conservatives have openly criticized the party leader and blamed his poor popularity rankings for contributing to a series of weak results in recent regional elections. The 70-year-old politician, who was elected in May 2025, has the lowest approval rates ever measured for a German chancellor.
Merz said last week his government will have to learn the lessons from an overwhelming victory by the far right in a state election in Saxony-Anhalt, which he said will alter the country’s politics.

The anti-immigration Alternative for Germany, or AfD, secured its best-ever result in the east German region on Sept. 6, putting the party three seats short of an outright majority to lead the first far-right government in the country since World War II. Merz’s CDU, which had led the region since 2002, saw its support collapse.

Surging fuel prices in Germany are adding to pressure for Merz ahead of the next regional elections on Sunday in Berlin and in the state of Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania. Earlier Tuesday, Merz told a business conference in the German capital that his ruling coalition will take action on “price gouging” by gas suppliers and promised motorists relief. However, details on the planned relief measures and how they would be financed remain unclear.
Instead of traveling to New York next week, Merz plans to attend a CDU leadership meeting on Monday and a caucus meeting on Tuesday in Berlin.

items.title: History Won't Help Us Understand Kevin Warsh
body: Hello and welcome to the newsletter, a grab bag of daily content from the Odd Lots universe. Sometimes it’s us, Joe Weisenthal and Tracy Alloway, bringing you our thoughts on the most recent developments in markets, finance and the economy. And sometimes it’s contributions from our network of expert guests and sources. Whatever it is, we promise it will always be interesting.
If you like chatting with us, check out the Odd Lots Discord, where you can hang out and talk with us and with other listeners 24/7.

We are hosting our first ever Odd Lots live show in Los Angeles this Thursday! Join us on the evening of Sept. 17 at The Vermont for some live episode tapings and a chance to hang out with us and fellow Odd Lots listeners. Tickets will probably sell out so make sure to get yours today!

Tomorrow we’ll get the highly-anticipated September FOMC decision and traders basically have a lock on a hike, with market-implied odds of a rate rise currently sitting at more than 90%. As my Bloomberg colleagues point out, history has shown that the Fed tends to deliver hikes when market expectations are that high.

That said, it’s clear to me that the past might not have much application here. And there are some reasons to believe that the Fed, under new Chairman Kevin Warsh, could surprise markets. Here’s Standard Chartered analyst (and Odd Lots guest) Steve Englander arguing that there is a logical case for the Fed to hold rates tomorrow:

There are other reasons not to hike too. As we’ve said plenty of times on the show, the real world works through incentives. And there are a couple of important incentives at play right now (even ignoring any political pressure from the upcoming midterms). Perhaps the worst outcome for a Warsh-led Fed would be to hike tomorrow, only to be forced to backtrack shortly after with a cut as the data improves — a scenario which could create concerns over a “very unsteady hand on the tiller” of US monetary policy, as Englander puts it.

Then, there is Warsh’s whole view of the market itself, with the Fed Chair explicitly pushing back on a co-dependent relationship between markets and the central bank: “If markets rely materially on the Fed’s guidance and the Fed relies on market prices, we are all more likely to be blinded to new developments,” Warsh has said. Being seen to ‘validate’ market expectations at a time when there’s still a decent amount of debate about what the data is showing, would be a strange thing for Warsh to do so early into his tenure.

To sum it up, the market seems to be screaming for hikes, the data still shows some wriggle room for a hold, and the Fed Chair says he’s not here to just agree with the market. That seems less like a lock and more like a very open question to me.

items.title: Canada Hangs Out the Shingle for Global Investment Amid US Trade Fight
body: Hi, it’s Paula Sambo in Toronto where global financiers have descended this week to hear the great Canadian investment pitch. Also today a jumbo listing in agriculture moves forward.
Today’s top stories

Toronto has a Davos-meets-Cannes vibe this week.BlackRock’s Larry Fink, Blackstone’s Jon Gray, Apollo’s Marc Rowan and Temasek’s Dilhan Pillay are rubbing shoulders with the film festival TIFF crowd, which has brought Penelope Cruz, Javier Bardem, Channing Tatum and Chris Rock to town.

Add Milken Institute’s first-ever Toronto gathering, and the city is suddenly awash in movie stars, CEOs and some of the world’s biggest pools of capital, all chasing the same hotel suites, private dining rooms, bottles of maple syrup and, hopefully, the next big deal.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has brought global heavyweights overseeing more than $70 trillion of assets to Toronto, putting a Rolodex built over decades at Goldman Sachs, two central banks and Brookfield to work.

There’s some urgency behind the charm offensive. A worsening trade fight with the US has hurt growth and investor confidence, but it’s also helped Carney push through pro-business tax and regulatory changes, and sharpen the pitch for global capital to look north.
And the ambitions are big.

Carney’s government is pitching 167 opportunities spanning AI data centers, critical minerals, energy, transportation and advanced manufacturing as part of a push to catalyze C$1 trillion of investment over five years.

He’s sweetening the economics, too. Carney on Tuesday expanded a major investment tax write-off to pipelines, mining property, fiber-optic cables and other assets, a change the government says will slash Canada’s effective tax rate on new business investment to 6.4% — less than half the US rate and the lowest in the G7.
Carney knows the hard part is execution.
“Time kills all deals,” he told the summit, promising to strip out duplicative reviews and move toward “one project, one review, one year.”
There are signs investors like what they’re hearing.
At Milken, Power Sustainable CEO Bruce Heyman said global allocators that once lumped Canada into their North American portfolios are increasingly looking at it separately from the US.

“Now they think about Canada versus the US,” Heyman said. Canadian exposure is often in the low single digits, he added, and “if they just doubled that exposure, it’s hundreds of billions of dollars of opportunity for Canada.” Power Sustainable is putting C$10 billion behind the thesis through a commitment to Canadian infrastructure.

RBC CEO Dave McKay said investors who had been underweight in Canada for years are also taking a fresh look, with interest spanning energy, critical minerals, northern infrastructure and data centers. “They’re here en masse,” he said.
Canada still has to win the money.

“The market for attracting private capital is very competitive,” said Macquarie CEO Shemara Wikramanayake. Faster approvals, priority sectors and clearer investment frameworks are encouraging, she said. “The early steps are looking positive. But unfortunately, it’s not a flip of a switch.”
Macquarie is interested in helping finance the buildout. Wikramanayake pointed to airports as one place Ottawa could tap private capital and recycle the proceeds into new infrastructure.
That caveat — show us you can actually get things built — keeps coming up in virtually all our coffee break chats this week.
Canada has the investors in town, 167 projects to sell them, billions already being pledged, new tax incentives and a government promising to move at deal speed.
It has the moment. Now it needs the deals. — Paula Sambo, with assistance from Sandra Mergulhao and Layan Odeh

Join Scarlet Fu on Bloomberg TV Wednesday at noon in New York for the Bloomberg Deals show. This week, you’ll hear from GFL CEO Patrick Dovigi and Renee Loiselle, a partner at Norton Rose Fulbright. See you then!

German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil and UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel said they held constructive talks Monday after the ministry outlined the demands it has for the Italian lender’s bid to take over Commerzbank.

Puig Brands is to take full control of Isdin for €1.2 billion after agreeing to buy the remaining 50% of the skincare brand it didn’t already own. Isdin gives Puig, which listed in Spain in 2024, a bigger presence in skincare.

Grab Holdings has agreed to buy a majority stake in Singapore-based buy-now-pay-later platform Atome Financial for $1.49 billion, staking a major bet on financial services as it builds out a new pillar of growth.

Alpinestars, the Italian maker of protection gear used by motorcycle racers, is attracting takeover interest from Asian PE firms including FountainVest and HSG. A deal could value Alpinestars at about €1 billion.

Essity is preparing to kick off the sales process for its consumer tissue business as soon as next month, after activist Cevian took a minority stake in the Swedish company. The asset could be valued at €2.5 billion to €3 billion.
NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy have offered more bill credits and new jobs to convince regulators in Virginia that their $67 billion deal won’t hit homeowners with rate hikes.

Syngenta has confidentially filed for a Hong Kong IPO, as it moves ahead with a share sale that was delayed by the impact of the war in the Middle East. The Chinese-owned seed and pesticide company is considering seeking about $5 billion in the IPO.
Altera, a chipmaker backed by Silver Lake and Intel, filed confidentially for an IPO. The company makes programmable chips for applications including AI, industrial automation and robotics.

SB Energy, a data center firm backed by SoftBank, is aiming to raise as much as $500 million in the Japanese portion of its planned IPO in the US, following other major deals in tapping the country’s deep pools of capital.
European stock exchanges must raise a further $5 billion from IPOs before the year is out to surpass last year’s haul, a challenge in a market where deals have been prone to delays.

Bamboo, a home insurance company controlled by private equity firm CVC, is seeking to raise as much as $700 million in an IPO that will enable its backers to cut their stakes but will raise no funds for the company itself.
Goldman Sachs Asset Management, Franklin Templeton and Fidelity International are among the global first set to participate as anchor investors in National Stock Exchange of India’s IPO.
Edmond de Rothschild Asset Management has so far raised more than €2 billion for its latest infrastructure debt fund, amid a financing boom for large-scale projects in Europe.

Global real estate firm Brightshore Capital, formerly known as GTIS Partners, has launched its first real estate debt investment platform with an initial investment of $250 million at a time when homebuilders’ financing needs are mounting.
Carlyle has clinched $2.3 billion for its latest infrastructure credit fund, which invests in businesses and assets focused on areas like energy transition, digital infrastructure and transportation.

UBS has made a series of senior hires for its investment bank with the goal of strengthening its industrial coverage in North America. They include Matt Parr as vice chairman, global banking Americas and head of Midwest banking, and Adam Reeder as vice chairman of global industrials group.

items.title: Patel Declines to Rule Out FBI Agents at Polls on Election Day
body: FBI Director Kash Patel declined to rule out sending agents to polling places on Election Day, telling senators he wasn’t certain the bureau is legally barred from doing so.

“I don’t know that we can’t legally do it,” Patel told the Senate Judiciary Committee Tuesday. He said the FBI plans to station agents and intelligence analysts in field offices to handle election-security issues.

Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, repeatedly pressed Patel for an unequivocal commitment that agents wouldn’t be deployed to polling sites. Patel said the bureau would follow the law and could respond to a polling place if there were indications a crime had occurred.
“The FBI will follow the law,” Patel said. “If there’s a reason to go there, because there’s been a violation of law, we will, otherwise we won’t.”

Senator Amy Klobuchar, a Minnesota Democrat, had earlier questioned Patel about longstanding Justice Department guidance restricting federal law enforcement activity at polling places. Asked whether he was aware of guidance stating that FBI agents can’t conduct investigations inside polling places on Election Day and that prosecutors lack authority to deploy agents or US marshals there, Patel said, “I’m aware.”

Patel also said he was unaware of any FBI investigations opened under an executive order by President Donald Trump directing the attorney general to prioritize investigations and prosecutions of state and local officials involved in distributing ballots to people the administration considers ineligible to vote.
Democrats also pressed Patel over investigations into shootings by federal immigration officers.

Senator Dick Durbin, an Illinois Democrat, asked about Marimar Martinez, a US citizen shot five times by a Border Patrol agent in Chicago, and Silverio Villegas-Gonzalez, who was killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent.
“We have not refused to investigate either of these shootings,” Patel said. “These investigations are currently ongoing.”

Klobuchar later questioned Patel about the killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti, two US citizens shot by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January. Asked whether the FBI should conduct timely and thorough investigations of officer-involved shootings, Patel said, “When we are the lead agency, yes.”

Patel didn’t identify a lead agency in either Minnesota case but said the FBI would “fully support” the investigations whether they were being conducted by state authorities, federal investigators or the Department of Homeland Security.
The hearing also turned to changes in FBI hiring rules that Durbin said eliminated automatic disqualifications for applicants with histories involving theft from employers, paid sex and bestiality.

Patel disputed the suggestion that the bureau had lowered its standards, saying the changes were intended in part to ensure trafficking victims forced into prohibited conduct weren’t automatically excluded.
“We did not want to punish victims of bestiality, victims who were trafficked,” Patel said.

Patel said the bureau’s hiring standards had otherwise increased, citing the recruitment of 307 former law enforcement and military officers, 470 people with advanced degrees and 448 people fluent in multiple foreign languages.

Patel also confirmed that employees from an FBI counterintelligence unit focused on Iran had been terminated. Blumenthal said about a dozen were removed shortly before US military operations involving Iran and had worked on the classified-documents investigation involving Trump.
“Those individuals were terminated for weaponizing the Federal Bureau of Investigation,” Patel said.
Blumenthal asked how the firings squared with Patel’s confirmation-hearing pledge not to retaliate against FBI personnel merely for participating in investigations.
“Simple,” Patel said. “If you weaponize law enforcement, you don’t get to work at the FBI.”

items.title: Chipmaker Stocks Will Weather Any AI Slowdown
body: One fear over the past few days is that an artificial-intelligence slowdown, whatever that looks like, might harm the stocks of chipmakers. If AI development takes a breather, the insatiable appetite that has propelled component makers to unprecedented heights would dissipate. Will AI companies still need all those data centers?
The answer is yes. And then some.

The 6% drop in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index — which tracks the shares of top chipmakers like Nvidia Corp. and Intel Corp. — over the past five days, as AI doom fears have captured the news agenda, is an understandable reaction to the uncertainty created by hyperbolic but not entirely unwarranted talk of an AI-created catastrophe.

But missing from any of the pledges from the hyperscalers, or leading AI shops, is any talk of scaling back the infrastructure buildout. On the contrary. In his 4,500-word “Pausing the AI Frontier” essay, Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei notes that “pacing does not mean halting model training or technical progress.”

It’s early days, and there’s a faint chance Congress could enforce a slowdown of sorts, but so far there’s no indication of any pulling back in the numbers. Bank of America analysts note sky-high memory costs — a key indicator of demand for the AI buildout — are unchanged. The rental cost for Nvidia’s widely deployed B200 system is $5.72 an hour, BofA said, and has risen steadily over the past two months. Now there may be a lag between AI slowdown talk and AI slowdown action. But don’t bet on it: “2027 remains much a fully booked/contracted year across all compute/networking/memory vendors,” BofA analysts wrote. “And we expect 2028 to also remain tight led by accelerating demand.”

In fact, were it not for the headlines and dramatically resigning employees, you would think the AI race had actually stepped up a notch. On Tuesday, Meta Platforms Inc. announced it still planned to go full steam ahead with putting its own AI chips into data centers by the beginning of next year. This comes from a company that claimed to have its own AI-gone-rogue cyberattack moment in August, just like OpenAI’s Hugging Face fiasco. Elon Musk, with a comment firmly in grain-of-salt territory, outlined his plans to put Nvidia’s Vera Rubin AI stack in space next year. I don’t believe him, but that’s beside the point, which is that none of the main players in AI show signs of letting up on investing in capacity to run these models.

A useful exercise is to consider how AI companies describe the path to safer AI and ask whether it indicates less spending. Last month, with an urgency echoing the “pause” talk of the past few days, more than 100 AI companies — OpenAI, Anthropic, Alphabet Inc.’s Google and Microsoft Corp. among them — put out a joint statement arguing that companies should make it “an immediate leadership priority” to protect from AI harm — whether that be vulnerabilities discovered by supersmart models or models acting in unexpected ways. How might they do that?

“Today’s AI advances are already giving defenders new ways to fix weaknesses that have accumulated for years,” the letter suggests. It appears the solution to the AI problem, handily enough, is more AI. That doesn’t sound like a slowdown in demand.

items.title: Apple AirPods 5 Offer Noise Cancellation, Sound Improvements at $129 Price
body: The most unexpected thing about Apple Inc.’s new AirPods 5 is that you’re getting more for less. At a time when the company’s other products have jumped up in price due to a persistent memory chip shortage, the latest “regular” AirPods bring features like active noise cancellation, transparency mode and live translation to a lower $129 price point.

For $149, you can buy a nicer version with longer battery life, wireless charging and the ability to adjust volume directly on the earbuds with a swipe of your finger. For just $20 more, I’d recommend this more premium pair — the model we tested — to all but the most price-conscious shoppers and predict that Apple will eventually phase out the $129 base offering. The higher-end AirPods 5 are actually cheaper than the equivalent AirPods 4 predecessor, which launched at $179 and lacked physical volume controls altogether.

The AirPods 5 maintain the open-ear, one-size-fits-most design that some consumers strongly prefer compared with earbuds that use silicone tips — even if the latter provide superior sound quality and noise isolation. All ears are different, and mine have never been a great match for Apple’s hard plastic AirPods: I can get them to stay reasonably snug, but it’s not a fit that feels secure. I don’t have to worry about the AirPods Pro 3 tumbling out of my ears, but with these, it’s always possible.

Still, many people swear allegiance to the non-Pro AirPods, and I can understand why. You don’t experience any unpleasant clogged-up sensation when wearing them, and since they rest in your ears instead of lodging inside them, you’re always aware of your surroundings and able to hear what’s happening around you. Sometimes hearing everything can get bothersome, which is why Apple brought noise cancellation to the previous-generation AirPods and made it noticeably stronger this time around.

I’ve reviewed countless earbuds and headphones over the years, and initially I was skeptical of how effectively an open-ear design could possibly tamp down the outside world — but it actually works, and the improvement in active noise cancellation over the last-gen AirPods is noticeable. Apple has achieved this in two ways: It’s using denser acoustic mesh grilles on the exterior of the earbuds than the AirPods 4, and it has also revamped the ANC algorithms. This leads to noise cancellation that’s as much as 50% better than before, according to Apple.

The end result is impressive, but not miraculous: The open design fundamentally means you can still hear ambient sounds like a nearby conversation or a co-worker slamming away on a keyboard — at least when music isn’t playing. Turn up the volume on any track, and the AirPods 5 do a commendable job of hushing distractions.

If I were to rank the AirPods Pro 3 as an 8 out of 10 in noise cancellation, these would fall somewhere between 5 and 6. I’d still want to have the AirPods Pro 3 in my pocket on a plane, but during several walks around San Francisco, the AirPods 5 helped reduce street noise to a level where I could hear my music without having to crank the volume. Transparency mode also sounds even more natural this time. (Since your ear canals are partially obstructed by the AirPods, this feature still proves handy at times.)

When I did need to adjust the volume, the swipe controls borrowed from the AirPods Pro felt like a godsend. It’s just so much easier and faster than having to feel for the volume rocker in my pocket or ask Siri to make changes. The AirPods 5 sound excellent for open earbuds, delivering tighter bass and improved instrument separation compared with the 4. This gave Phoebe Bridgers’ Lost Weekend the depth and crisp vocals that I’d expect from pricier earbuds. Still, if you’re not sold on the out-of-box sound, Apple has finally made it easier to adjust the EQ settings in iOS 27. You only get a simplistic three-band equalizer, but it’s better than nothing.

As with their predecessors, the AirPods 5 work wonderfully for voice calls. And their strong mic performance is equally important when it comes to using Siri AI. Ultimately, the AirPods are just a vessel for accessing Siri and Apple’s vastly improved artificial intelligence capabilities on your iPhone, but so far it’s been a smooth experience. Having the new Siri AI in my ear, always a quick voice command away, has been refreshingly pleasant after so many years of frustration with the original assistant.

My early tests like “Play that song Molly texted me the other day” worked as expected, and Siri hasn’t yet misheard me during any of our back-and-forth exchanges. Along with Siri AI, useful features like conversation awareness and live translation, which were only available on the Pros and higher-end AirPods 4, have now trickled down to the $129 model. So even if you decide to go the cheaper route, you’re mostly losing out on convenience — not crucial functionality.

The AirPods 5 (and their charging case) are rated IP57 against dust and water and, for the first time, can withstand brief submersion and come out unscathed. This is only true at depths of up to 3 feet, so just make sure that if your earbuds do go swimming, it’s at the shallow end of the pool. At least puddles won’t be a threat anymore.

Battery life is adequate, if not particularly impressive. You can expect as many as five hours of continuous listening from the earbuds themselves and 22 hours when factoring in recharges from the case on the $149 model. The $129 version gets you four hours on the earbuds themselves and 20 hours in total with recharges. Apple’s previous AirPods 4 without noise cancellation could reach a total of 30 hours, but the AirPods 5 should prove satisfactory for most users. I continue to wish the company would make its earbuds repairable (and the batteries replaceable) but we’re not there yet.

Plenty of other brands sell open-style earbuds, with clip-on designs becoming increasingly common. But none can match the deep ecosystem advantages of Apple’s AirPods. The AirPods 5 are so good that they significantly raise expectations for the company’s eventual AirPods Pro 4.

Right now, the top-of-the-line, $249 model still wins out in sound quality and maintains a clear lead in overall noise cancellation. Spending more also gets you bonuses like heart-rate tracking and more precise Find My location tracking for the AirPods Pro 3 charging case. But the gap between the regular AirPods and the Pros is shrinking. That’s a win for customers and should leave Apple enthusiasts excited about what’s to come — regardless of how you feel about the idea of built-in AI cameras.

items.title: OpenAI Eyes Canada Data Center Partnerships at Carney Investment Summit
body: OpenAI Inc. is taking a close look at Canada under Prime Minister Mark Carney, said one of its top executives who previously hired the Canadian to lead the Bank of England.

George Osborne, who was chancellor of the UK from 2010 to 2016 and is now head of OpenAI for countries, an international liaisons role, spoke to Bloomberg News on the sidelines of Carney’s first-of-a-kind Canada Investment Summit. The prime minister invited the world’s top money managers and other investors to pitch them on his country.
Osborne and the artificial intelligence company wanted “to see what the investment potentials are in Canada. It’s a very important market for OpenAI, and there’s lots of potential here,” he said.

“There’s the potential for data center partnerships here, because of the availability of energy and land,” he added. What’s more, “Mark Carney has articulated one of the clearer plans for AI adoption of a western government.”
Read More: Carney’s Middle Powers Race to Thwart US-China Dominance of AI

Osborne also spoke as someone with experience of and a keen interest in top-flight politics — and trade disruption — as the minister responsible for the UK’s finances in the immediate run-up to the Brexit referendum.

“If you’re interested in what’s going on the world, you want to come to Canada to see how they’re handling what Mark Carney calls the disruption,” Osborne said, citing the trade war between Canada and the US.

“But what I heard from Mark is he’s able to look beyond that, and articulate a clear medium-term, long-term plan for Canada, despite the storms of the last couple of weeks. And it’s very impressive to see.”

items.title: NYC Delays Vote on Property-Tax Break for Hudson Yards Tower
body: New York City put off voting on a $100 million property tax break for a new Hudson Yards skyscraper proposed by developer Tishman Speyer, in what would be the largest economic subsidy since Mayor Zohran Mamdani took office.

The city’s Industrial Development Agency, which provides tax incentives to developers and businesses, didn’t take up a resolution on the tax break at its meeting Tuesday morning. A spokesperson for the city’s Economic Development Corporation, which oversees the IDA, said it’s common for projects to take more time as they move through the review process.
“We look forward to presenting the project at a future meeting,” the EDC spokesperson said in an email. The agency’s next scheduled meeting is on Nov. 17.
A spokesperson for Mamdani didn’t respond to a request for comment. A Tishman spokesperson declined to comment.
If approved, the subsidy could put Mamdani at odds with his progressive base, who argue tax giveaways benefit the wealthy at the expense of essential services and housing.
Read More: NYC Mulls Property-Tax Break for $2.7 Billion Hudson Yards Tower

Construction of the $2.7 billion project, known as 99 Hudson Boulevard, is slated to begin in January, according to Tishman Speyer’s application for financial assistance filed with the IDA. The planned 48-story tower would be the developer’s second skyscraper in Hudson Yards, a neighborhood of offices, luxury apartments, and parks on Manhattan’s far west side.

The break for 99 Hudson would cost the city $92.2 million in tax benefits, while generating almost $860 million in direct and indirect tax revenue, according to an analysis by the IDA. Construction of the tower would generate about 2,385 full-time construction jobs and more than 1,780 office and building service jobs, according to Tishman.

Under the deal, real estate taxes on the planned 1.3 million-square-foot (121,000-square-meter) tower would be abated and Tishman instead would pay a lesser “payment in lieu of taxes,” or PILOT, to the city.

Layla Law-Gisiko, a local Democratic Party leader and president of the City Club of New York, a civic group, has argued that the IDA needed to clarify whether Tishman’s PILOT payments would be used to help finance infrastructure for the second-phase of Hudson Yards on the western portion of the rail yard site.

Related Cos, the primary developer of Hudson Yards’ first phase, struck a deal with former Mayor Eric Adams and City Council to build a $2 billion taxpayer-funded platform over the western rail yards to spur more residential and commercial development, including affordable housing.

Bonds issued for the platform would be backed by payments in lieu of taxes and other revenue from developers, the same structure the city used to finance a $3 billion extension of the No. 7 subway line from Times Square to 34th Street and 11th Avenue.

“The public deserves to know whether these two transactions are financially connected before either connection becomes irreversible,” Law-Gisiko wrote in public comments to the IDA dated Sept. 10. “A public hearing cannot provide meaningful transparency if the public is shown the tax benefit on one side of the transaction but not told where the resulting PILOT revenue may ultimately go.”

The IDA’s tax-exemption policy says the agency has discretion over whether to provide assistance. Staff and the board can consider factors such as expected job creation, public support or whether the project would be completed without the subsidy.

In the past decade, the Hudson Yards Infrastructure Corp, created by the city to issue bonds for the redevelopment, has transferred about $2 billion in surplus revenue collected from developers of the eastern rail yards to the city after paying debt service, according to HYIC financial reports.

items.title: Venezuela Squeezes Banks as Higher Spending Tests Bolivar
body: Lea en español
Venezuela’s central bank is moving to squeeze liquidity in the banking system in a bid to support the bolivar ahead of an expected boost in government spending.

Policymakers raised penalties for lenders that fail to meet the mandatory reserve requirement — a percentage of deposits they need to park at the central bank. They also increased deposit and some lending rates, among other measures published by the central bank in the official gazette dated Friday and which was circulated to market participants on Tuesday.

The new rules are part of an effort to tighten policy in anticipation of increased fiscal spending and as the central bank sells fewer dollars into the official exchange market. Sintesis Financiera, a Caracas-based financial consulting firm, estimates the sales, financed through oil exports, will drop 21% in September.

“The aim is to protect the exchange rate by sacrificing credit even further, precisely when the economy needs financing,” economist and consultant Asdrubal Oliveros wrote on X over the weekend. “The problem is the cost of that strategy — as usual.”
Representatives for the Venezuelan government didn’t reply to a request for comment.

Venezuela has been pouring billions of dollars into the market to stabilize its weakening currency, particularly since the capture of strongman Nicolas Maduro in early January by US forces fueled uncertainty about the future of the cash-strapped economy. The Trump administration has been overseeing the nation’s access to revenue from oil sales, some of which is channeled through local banks and sold to businesses and individuals.

The central bank has sold $11 billion into the local currency market this year, according to Sintesis Financiera, helping to narrow the gap between the government-set exchange rate and the price of dollars in the parallel market to less than 20%.

“This rhythm is unsustainable,” the firm’s analysts wrote in the report, adding that the $11 billion figure is equivalent to 58% of oil exports. “It is almost identical to oil-related fiscal revenue and leaves no room to cover other public-sector foreign currency needs.”

items.title: Amazon Fails to Recover Some Data in Facilities Hit in Iran War
body: Amazon.com Inc. has been unable to restore access to some of the data stored at Persian Gulf facilities damaged during the US-Iran war.

In an update posted Tuesday to the Amazon Web Services status health page, the company said it couldn’t tap into data hosted exclusively in data centers in Bahrain and in portions of its network in the United Arab Emirates.

The facilities were damaged early in the conflict, demonstrating the extent to which data centers have become targets of modern warfare. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the Bahrain facilities were struck because of Amazon’s support for US military operations.
Satellite imagery showed hits to two Amazon data centers in Bahrain. The damage exceeded what the company’s services were designed to withstand, AWS said in its first public update in five months.

Most customers moved their workloads to server farms in other countries between the first strikes, in March, and subsequent damage in April that effectively knocked out Amazon’s data center network in the country.

In the UAE, Amazon said most customers had restored operations in other regions by relying on backups or copying data that remained accessible. The company said it has been unable to access data stored in one of its UAE availability zones — a subdivision of its network designed to provide redundancy. Engineers continue to work on recovering resources in two other availability zones.

Amazon said it remains committed to supporting customers in the two countries and promised a further update on Bahrain early next year. The world’s largest cloud computing provider also operates data center clusters in India, Israel and several European countries.

items.title: Stanford Tops Bloomberg Businessweek B-Schools Rankings as Programs Adapt to AI
body: If you’re thinking about getting an MBA, today’s the day you’ve been waiting for: Our new list of best B-schools is live. Plus: What it takes to get your first job on Wall Street (free link).

Bloomberg Businessweek’s Best Business Schools Rankings for 2026-27 are live now, and, for the eighth year in a row, Stanford Graduate School of Business is No. 1 in the US. Thanks in part to its close ties to Silicon Valley, Stanford came in best for networking and entrepreneurship. IMD, in Lausanne, Switzerland, is the top MBA program in Europe. It ranks first on two of the key indexes, Learning and Networking.

You can dive into the rankings to sort schools by US region or explore international programs. See the industries where recent MBA graduates found work and calculate what your return on investment might be, if you’re headed back to school.

The release of this year’s rankings is the right time to consider how AI technology has created a dilemma for faculty and B-school leaders: At a moment when more people are calling to slow down AI implementation, business schools are racing ahead to deploy it. But they’re walking a tightrope, trying to balance the new tech skills with essential incumbent skills — like writing — that risk getting crowded out.

Got questions about B-schools? Bloomberg’s Lisa Mateo hosts a live interactive conversation with Dimitra Kessenides, Liam Knox and Jo Constantz on Friday at noon in New York. While anyone can listen to the Live Q&A, Bloomberg digital subscribers and Terminal clients have the exclusive opportunity to ask our team questions to answer in real time.
If you’re a college sophomore with investment banking ambitions and you haven’t started preparing for the job market, you’re already behind.

Investment banking is more competitive than ever. Total compensation can exceed $180,000 for first-year analysts, leading to a career that delivers prestige and pay that can reach into the millions. An internship is the golden ticket to an entry-level job. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and JPMorgan Chase & Co. say their internship acceptance rates have dropped to less than 1% in recent years, as hundreds of thousands of applicants vie for spots in programs that typically lead to full-time job offers. A growing number of students are pursuing a career in the industry, according to data from entry-level job site Handshake, with investment banking internships drawing more than three times as many applications on the platform than the typical internship. As banks jockey to have first pick, recruiting timelines have crept earlier, pushing students to master an elaborate playbook to break into the industry.
The path to Wall Street starts soon after college freshmen arrive on campus, write Misha Manjuran Oberoi and Jo Constantz. Here’s how the fierce competition works.
