items.title: Bessent to Meet Chinese Counterpart Ahead of Trump-Xi Summit
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he will meet this weekend with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, ahead of a summit between President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping later this month.

Bessent made the remark Tuesday before the House Financial Services Committee, where he is testifying about the state of the international financial system. Bessent said he looked forward to speaking with the Chinese vice premier about sanctions related to the war in Iran, as the US increases economic pressure on the Islamic Republic.

The Iran war, now in its seventh month, has been a key factor pushing up borrowing costs and consumer prices in the US and around the world this year. The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to the highest in almost two decades, the latest milestone in a bruising global bond selloff driven by booming capital investment and soaring energy prices that are exacerbating inflation.
Read More: US 10-Year Yield Rises to Highest Since 2007 as Fed Looms

Bessent, speaking to reporters Tuesday outside the hearing room, said he thinks the rise in yields is “largely due to the oil-price rise, and oil prices are going to come down,” according to a clip aired on Fox News.

During the hearing, Bessent took exception to a lawmaker’s comment that it didn’t matter who develops a superintelligence first. Echoing Trump, the Treasury secretary has consistently emphasized the importance of maintaining the US lead over China in artificial intelligence, an area where Chinese firms have been gaining ground on their Silicon Valley rivals.
“It does matter whether the good guys or the bad guys have this,” Bessent said. “As a person who manages the the relationship with China on AI, it matters a great deal.”

Ahead of Trump’s meeting with Xi, set for Sept. 24 in Washington, the competition over artificial intelligence has emerged as key source of friction between the world’s two largest economies. Last week, three US national security agencies accused Chinese AI firms including DeepSeek and Moonshot AI — the maker of the breakthrough Kimi K3 model — of systematically extracting proprietary knowledge from American firms.
While the Chinese companies have refrained from commenting on the US allegations, China’s government has pushed back forcefully on the claims, calling them baseless and threatening retaliation.

Authorities in Beijing similarly have criticized calls from leading US AI developers Anthropic PBC and OpenAI for a slowdown in work on advanced models as “fearmongering,” signaling their concern that American firms could be pressuring the Trump administration to further restrict China’s access to advanced chips and other hardware.
The high-level talks are the latest signal that the meeting between the leaders of the world’s two largest economies remains on track. Beijing has not yet officially confirmed the date of the visit.
Bessent did not specify the date or location of his meeting with He. The two men have typically met before each of the US-China leaders’ summits to lay the groundwork for the talks.

The hearing was disrupted by a number of anti-war protesters, with at least five people being removed by security. “Stop the sanctions that are killing Iranian civilians,” one screamed as Bessent began his opening statement.
“Scott Bessent, you’re a war criminal!” shouted another, holding a banner that read “Sanctions Kill Iranians.”

items.title: Dutch to Propose Capital Gains Tax to Break Reform Deadlock
body: The Dutch government will propose a capital gains levy next year, bringing the Netherlands in line with most European countries on how they tax wealth.
Finance Minister Eelco Heinen announced the move on Tuesday in the Hague as part of a statement on the nation’s budget day.
The measure would tax gains on investments only once they are sold, rather than the current regime that can impose levies on theoretical returns or unrealized increases in value.
The new system will “contribute to the goal of increasing future earning power, improving the investment climate, and stimulating economic growth,” the minister said in a statement.

An earlier overhaul attempt to tax paper profits triggered an investor backlash, and is currently stalled in the Senate. Years of similar wrangling and uncertainty over the Dutch fiscal regime for global assets have drawn criticism from businesses and their workers.

Heinen’s proposal marks a push to break the deadlock in a country that, like other European peers, faces a perennial struggle over budgets. Fragmented parliaments and structurally increasing spending demands often transform routine fiscal measures into matters for protracted negotiations which weigh on markets.

Moving to a capital gains tax incurs a cost. Besides the administrative burden of switching systems, the government will have to wait until assets are sold before receiving revenue, rather than being paid every year. Tax Secretary Eelco Eerenberg declined to say when the tax could be implemented.
Read more: Dutch Workers Strike Over Welfare Cuts to Fund Higher NATO Spend Spend

Prime Minister Rob Jetten’s coalition now faces months of talks to secure a majority, having already struggled to reach consensus among the ruling parties on its deal, narrowly averting a major political crisis.

Tuesday’s budget also follows weeks of union-led strikes against €6.5 billion ($7.5 billion) in welfare cuts that disrupted public transport and affecting operations at Heineken NV and the Port of Rotterdam. Many of these spending reductions, including halving the duration of unemployment benefit, were postponed on Tuesday.
Read more: Why High Yields on Government Bonds Are Causing Alarm: Explainer

items.title: Novonesis CEO Says EU Red Tape Risks Biosolutions Lead to China
body: Europe risks surrendering its status as a global frontrunner in biosolutions to China unless it dramatically speeds up regulation and approvals, according to the woman who runs the world’s largest maker of industrial enzymes.

The biological technologies such as micro-organisms, yeasts and enzymes are one of the relatively few areas where the region still holds an advantage over global competitors, Novonesis A/S Chief Executive Officer Ester Baiget said at an event in Copenhagen on Tuesday. But China is rapidly catching up as it pours money into research, manufacturing capacity and intellectual property, while moving faster on regulation, she said.
“China is not copying anymore. China is so much ahead on innovation” and “moving at very high speed,” she said. “We are going backward relative to where the world is evolving.”
European businesses have grown increasingly frustrated with a regulatory burden they say is stifling innovation and making it harder to compete with the US and China.

For Novonesis, that can mean waiting years to register new products, while China is “investing massively in everything that drives speed,” Baiget said. One result is that China has already built up about 70% of the world’s fermentation capacity, according to the CEO.
Europe shouldn’t change direction, only speed, she said. “What we have here is precious.”

items.title: Merz Calls for Trade Tools to Fight 'Unfair' China Competition
body: Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that Germany will support tough new measures against China’s “unfair” trade practices at a meeting of European Union leaders next month.

“China deliberately combines its market-driven dynamism with state intervention, overcapacity, aggressive pricing, an undervalued currency, and heavily subsidized exports,” Merz said at a foreign trade lobby event in Berlin Tuesday. “We need effective instruments to reduce our dependencies and protect ourselves against unfair competition.”

Merz’s government is preparing a far-reaching package of economic-security measures to shield strategic industries from China that may include new tariffs on hybrid electric vehicles, Bloomberg reported Monday. Ministries are mapping vulnerabilities to China and assessing countermeasures, with potential proposals including mandatory joint ventures, strengthened inbound and outbound investment screening and a bolstered export controls regime.

European leaders tasked the European Commission, the bloc’s executive arm that oversees trade matters, with “sharpening our trade policy toolkit,” he said, and announced that the measures will be discussed at the next summit in Brussels Oct. 15-16.
The work is an indication of the hardening shift in Germany’s China policy, which has traditionally been cautious given Berlin’s export-driven economy and deep commercial ties with Beijing.

The EU’s trade deficit with China exceeds €1 billion ($1.2 billion) a day and Germany’s industrial downturn has produced tens of thousands of announced job cuts, with Volkswagen AG planning to increase global cuts to 100,000.

“This is not about protecting ourselves from competition. Without competition, there is no innovation,” Merz said. “It’s about a level playing field and therefore about framework conditions that make fair competition possible in the first place.”

items.title: Carlyle's Thomas Says AI Financing Echoes Pre-Crisis Mortgages
body: Lenders’ approach to data centers has a troubling similarity to the model applied to mortgages before the financial crisis, said Jason Thomas, head of global research and investment strategy for Carlyle Group Inc.

Specifically, project financing for artificial intelligence development is often supported by the investment-grade credit quality of the financial sponsor, he said Tuesday in an interview with Bloomberg Television. Lenders aren’t necessarily taking a view on the underlying project, he added.

“I do worry though, because this is reminiscent in some ways of 2005 to 2007,” Thomas said. At the time, lenders said they weren’t taking a view on the mortgage loan collateral but instead on the ability of the bank to take it onto its balance sheet if need be. Eventually, that no longer became feasible as liabilities grew, he said.

That’s not the case today, he said, “as it relates to these investment-grade sponsors, but again as the liabilities escalate and as perhaps the implied volatility, or the distribution of outcomes, the revenues associated with the data centers widens, we could get there at some point in the future.”
Risk premiums for AI in both credit and equity have been shrinking as the AI buildout has intensified, he said, adding that he thinks a slowdown is more likely than not.
Read More: Carlyle’s Schwartz Sees Fed Avoiding Aggressive Hike Cycle

items.title: OpenAI Says It's Working With Anthropic, Google on AI Safety
body: OpenAI is working on steps to address artificial intelligence safety issues with its top competitors Anthropic PBC and Google DeepMind, escalating industry efforts to respond to a groundswell of concern that the technology poses an economic and security threat.

Chris Lehane, the global policy chief for OpenAI, said Tuesday that the company’s engagement with Anthropic and Google had been under way for several weeks. He added that OpenAI does not see the need for an antitrust waiver for the three AI firms to coordinate on safety matters.
“It’s better to try to work together to prioritize safety,” Lehane said at a briefing in Washington.

Lehane was one of many to comment Tuesday on the prospects of government measures to regulate AI, including diverse political actors such as US Senator Bernie Sanders and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon, as well as tech industry figures like Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang.

Anxiety about AI’s existential risks burst into the mainstream following a 3,800-word essay posted Saturday by Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei, who urged restraining development of the most advanced systems so researchers can better understand potential threats. Amodei’s missive was quickly embraced by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI chief Elon Musk.
Read More: AI Bosses Clash With Trump on Their Calls to Slow AI Development

US antitrust regulators are already signaling their skepticism toward giving AI companies an exemption to coordinate on safety. Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson said Tuesday he would be “deeply suspicious” of such requests.
Ferguson added that he sees the AI companies as “asking for barriers to entry” that will insulate their business from challengers. “That sure sounds like moat digging,” he added.

During his briefing, Lehane said the AI firms’ work on safety issues has ample precedent and cited the airline industry as an example. “There are many instances over time where companies are trying to help each other on safety,” he said.
Spokespeople for Anthropic and Google DeepMind, a unit of Alphabet Inc., didn’t respond to requests for comment.
Lehane said that he was in Washington to meet with US lawmakers and that OpenAI would support bipartisan proposals aimed at addressing potential catastrophic risks from the technology.

Measures favored by OpenAI include a framework for federal AI governance from Republican Representative Jay Obernolte and Democrat Lori Trahan, Lehane said. The company also supports a Senate proposal taking shape spearheaded by Majority Leader John Thune, Republican Ted Cruz and Democrat Amy Klobuchar that would seek to address catastrophic risks.
“Whatever we can get through,” Lehane said.
Read More: AI Fears Give Bernie Sanders a Rare Moment of Unity With Bannon

At an event in Washington Tuesday, Sanders said he would introduce legislation next week that would ban the so-called superintelligent AI, a level of capability potentially surpassing human control. The Vermont senator, an independent who aligns with Democrats, found rare common ground with the conservative provocateur Bannon in calling for immediate action to shore up AI safety.
“Congress, under both Democratic and Republican control, have been asleep at the wheel and we now have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing,” Sanders said.
Lawmakers have also offered measures aimed specifically at the potential competition concerns raised by coordination on safety by AI firms.

Senator Jim Banks, an Indiana Republican, and Senator Adam Schiff, a California Democrat, have proposed a bill that would give AI companies a narrow antitrust carveout to share information with one other related to loss of control over AI systems, cyber or biological threats and attempts by Chinese companies to exfiltrate data. That legislation has been folded into an annual defense bill, a person familiar with the matter said.
Read More: Trump’s AI Defense Defies Voter Unease Heading Into Midterms

Odds of any proposal passing before the end of the year remain slim. Congress is unlikely to act on any AI legislation anytime soon, with the House slated to leave Washington on Thursday and not return until after the November elections. The brief lame duck session after the election is expected to focus on a plan to boost the Pentagon budget.

President Donald Trump has also voiced his vehement opposition to any effort to impose AI guardrails. In a rapid-fire series of social media posts, Trump on Monday belittled a push led by Anthropic and OpenAI to slow work on cutting-edge systems, invoking bombastic language to dismiss existential fears about AI as “a hoax.”

Other Silicon Valley leaders including Nvidia’s Huang have played down the need for new government measures to address AI’s most dire risks. Huang, whose company is the biggest maker of AI processors, said Tuesday that market forces would be enough to help companies safely innovate, saying it’s a false choice between safe or fast AI development.
“You can definitely have both at the same time,” Huang said at a Salesforce Inc. event. “You pace yourself until you’re confident you’re releasing something that the market would appreciate.”

items.title: Angola Bucks Global Trend And Cuts Key Rate as Iran War Rages
body: Angola’s central bank extended its easing cycle as inflation continued to cool, bucking a global trend of policymakers raising or holding rates as the Iran war rages on.

The monetary policy committee reduced the benchmark interest rate for a second straight meeting to 14.75% from 15.75%, Governor Manuel Tiago Dias told reporters Tuesday in the capital, Luanda. That brings cumulative rate cuts in the past year to 475 basis points.

The southwest African nation joins a small group of economies such as Israel in lowering borrowing costs since US-Iran hostilities flared up in late August, causing oil prices to spike to more than $100 a barrel.

Unlike our peers in the US and Europe “we are seeing a continued decline in inflation and we believe that, fortunately, inflationary pressures in our economy are easing substantially,” Dias said, “That is one of the factors leading us to lower our policy rates.”
Inflation slowed to 8.78% in August from 9.3% a month earlier, its lowest level in at least 11 years, and is still expected to end the year at 8.6%, the governor said.
Angola’s costly fuel subsidy has shielded consumers from the soaring prices. Despite being Africa’s third-largest oil producer, Angola imports most of the refined fuel it consumes.
The MPC’s final meeting of the year is scheduled for Nov. 16-17 in the northeastern city of Saurimo, Dias said.

items.title: Meta Touts the Cost-Saving Benefits of Latest In-House AI Chips
body: Meta Platforms Inc. plans to begin deploying a new in-house artificial intelligence chip in data centers during the first half of next year, a move it says will save money and energy when running AI models.

The company, which first announced plans to develop homegrown AI chips in 2023, is testing the third generation of the line, called MTIA 450, or Arke. The next one — dubbed 500, or Astrid — will complete design work in about a month and go into data centers at the end of 2027. Meta expects to use that one even more widely.

“Each one takes on a little bit more risk technologically, and gets us better performance,” Yee Jiun Song, Meta’s vice president of engineering, said in an interview. That includes better performance per watt of energy and per dollar spent, he said.

Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, is developing its own chips as part of a massive push to develop AI infrastructure. The company is working with Broadcom Inc. on the designs and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. on manufacturing — a project aimed at reducing its reliance on Nvidia Corp.’s industry-leading processors.

When measured by energy use — a key benchmark for the data center industry — the company has committed to more than a gigawatt’s worth of the chips over a 12-month period. After that, “we expect it to accelerate,” said Song, who oversees Meta’s custom silicon program. That forecast assumes there’s no crash in the AI markets or in demand, he said.

Meta Superintelligence Labs, the company’s artificial intelligence division, is helping fine-tune the chips by offering insight into coming AI models and the requirements for running them — a stage known as inference. The end result is that the chips can perform more efficiently than “whatever Nvidia is currently shipping” when running AI models, Song said, “just because we’re doing a lot of the engineering ourselves.”

Twelve of the new model chips arrived at Meta from TSMC on Sept. 1 and performance is within 2% or 3% of what the company’s simulations had indicated. On the first day, the team was able to use the processors to operate Meta models, as well as ones from DeepSeek and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.

The tests indicate there’s no design snags with the semiconductors. But there’s still a lot of trialing and tuning to go — a few months of work — while production ramps up in the factory. All four generations of the chips largely rely on high-bandwidth memory and are not aimed at the ultrafast inference market — a category where AI models are expected to respond extremely quickly. “These are the workhorse chips that we’re going to use for general-purpose inference,” Song said.
Read More: Meta Preparing to Deploy Four New Homegrown Chips to Handle AI

The company had previously planned to build a chip code-named Olympus that was aimed at both the training stage of AI models and the inference phase. It would have arrived in 2028 or 2029, but Meta canceled that project to focus on inference — in part because of cost considerations, Song said. “When you start to build up gigawatts and gigawatts of capacity, you really care about cost,” he said. If the chip that handles both training and inference is potentially 30% more expensive, that suddenly seems “completely unacceptable,” Song said.

After work is complete on Astrid, Meta will focus on improving speed and throughput — the amount of AI work handled — with future models. Fiber-optic technologies also should let the chip team improve performance.
“We have a very robust road map,” Song said. “For the next few years, we expect to continue to build chips that are competitive with what our vendors are building for us.”

items.title: Nigerian Inflation Unexpectedly Eases, Boosts Rate-Cut Case
body: Nigeria’s annual inflation rate unexpectedly fell in August, improving the case for policymakers to resume their easing cycle next week.

Consumer prices rose 15.39% from 15.43% in July, data published by the National Bureau of Statistics on Tuesday showed. The median estimate of three economists in a Bloomberg survey was 15.7%. Prices rose 0.7% in the month from 1.6% in July.

The weaker-than-expected inflation keeps the door ajar for the central bank’s monetary policy committee to cut interest rates on Sept. 22, David Omojomolo, Africa economist at Capital Economics, said in a note. “But we think credibility concerns will win out, and the MPC will keep rates unchanged.”
The MPC has kept its key rate at 26.5% for two straight meetings after a 50-basis-point cut in February to assess the impact of global supply shocks on inflation.
The MPC will likely “wait for a more pronounced disinflation trend before restarting its easing cycle,” Omojomolo said
New price pressures are emerging from surging grain, fertilizer and energy costs as the wars in Ukraine and Iran disrupt supplies.
The high cost of living has become a key campaign issue ahead of presidential elections in January, when President Bola Tinubu is seeking another four-year term.

The ruling party has pledged to cut transport costs by Oct. 1 through the use of gas-powered buses and last month Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele announced that the National Economic Council had directed fiscal and monetary authorities to find “measures to moderate interest rates.”
Annual food inflation decelerated to 19.6% in August from 20.3% the month before, and core eased to 13.3% from 14.97%.

items.title: LNG Buyers Look to US to Hedge Future Risk of Hormuz Disruption
body: Liquefied natural gas buyers are accelerating discussions to buy more fuel from the US as the Iran war and turmoil over the Strait of Hormuz forces them to seek alternatives to suppliers in the Middle East.

Companies in Thailand, Pakistan and Bangladesh are in talks to sign long-term contracts with US suppliers, officials said at the Gastech conference in Bangkok. China Gas Holdings Ltd. signed a rare sales agreement this week from US exporter Venture Global Inc. scheduled to start in 2030, despite tensions between Washington and Beijing.

The move comes as disruption to Hormuz — through which about a fifth of all LNG flowed before the war — enter a seventh month and Qatar’s massive export terminal remains largely offline after being damaged by missile strikes. The loss of supply from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates to key Asian customers, coupled by high spot prices, is lifting utility bills and triggering energy shortages across parts of Asia.

“Buyers around the world really are more focused on diversifying their LNG procurement,” Yukio Kani, the chairman of Jera Co., one of the world’s biggest LNG buyers, said on Bloomberg TV. “Some rely too much on Qatar, like more than 50% or 60%.”

Jera — Japan’s top gas importer — has spent the last decade diversifying its sources of supply and now depends on the Middle East for about 5% of its LNG, Kani said at the Gastech conference in Bangkok. It imports most of that through long-term contracts — a strategy that other nations should follow to reduce exposure to the volatile spot market, according to Kani.

Inpex Corp., the Japanese energy producer, is considering investing in an LNG export project in the US, Chief Executive Officer Takayuki Ueda said in an interview. The flow of LNG through the strait, he said, “will not return to the previous status quo.”
“Diversification of our portfolio — in our words, portfolio resiliency — is important,” Ueda said.

To be sure, companies are looking beyond the US as well. Inpex is exploring projects in South America, Ueda said. Thai company officials at Gastech, meanwhile, showed interest in LNG from Canada and the Asia Pacific.

US suppliers tend to offer among the lowest prices for longterm contracts, in part because the agreements are linked to the nation’s Henry Hub benchmark and vast shale reserves have kept domestic prices low. Shipments from the US under long-term contracts are being delivered to Asia at $8 per million British thermal units, according to officials at US and Japanese companies.
For comparison, LNG prices in the spot market for Asia are about $30 per million Btu as European and Asian buyers compete for a limited pool of supply.

However, the prices of some US contracts have increased, due in part to supply chain bottlenecks and a reaction to the current tightness in the market, according to company officials and traders. That, plus a general shift to reduce exposure to LNG, may act as a hurdle to any fast deals.

US supplies also have the flexibility to be delivered to both to Asia and Europe. This also means that a buyer can import US LNG shipments into their domestic market if there are requirements, or resell it if there is demand or more profitable places overseas.

New LNG supply from North America has replaced more than half of the Middle Eastern volumes lost from the global market this year, Cederic Cremers, Shell Plc’s president of integrated gas, said Monday.

The US is the world’s largest LNG exporter and is poised to roughly double exports by the end of the decade. ExxonMobil Holdings Corp. expects US LNG to account for about 30% of global supply by 2030, senior vice president for LNG Peter Clarke said Monday. Projects including Woodside Energy Plc’s Louisiana LNG and Cheniere Energy Inc. expansions are currently marketing LNG supplies for delivery starting by around 2030.
“America wants to sell you gas,” James Danly, US Department of Energy deputy secretary, said during a panel at Gastech. “I’ve been yelling it from the rooftops.”

items.title: Pipeline Strike and Houthi Advances Complicate Iran War
body: Welcome back to Bloomberg’s Defense Monitor, a weekly rundown on the companies, geopolitics and finances of the future battlefield. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.

Like the headline says, things have, somehow, gotten worse in the Gulf region, with a damaged pipeline crimping an alternative export route and Houthi anti-ship weapons crimping the ability to sail safely through the Red Sea.

Japan may increase its defense spending to 3.5% of gross domestic product, a heavy lift for its economy and its politicians.NATO aircraft shot down a drone that poked through Lithuanian airspace, although no one has said yet whose drone it was.
A Russian warship fired flares — to be clear, devices that aren’t weapons — at a Danish helicopter.
US President Donald Trump demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian refineries. A few hours later, Ukraine struck Russia’s Syzran refinery.

All this tumult in Europe led to some interesting developments you’ve read about in this very newsletter. One of them — France’s desire to wrap the continent in the warm embrace of its nuclear umbrella — is picking up steam, as you’ll see in the Breakout. ...
— Gerry Doyle

We’ve been talking about nuclear weapons a lot lately, both in worrying and reassuring terms. Here’s one more discussion point: the US’s turn away from Europe is already affecting the continent’s nuclear posture.
This week, Finland said it was joining France’s nuclear deterrence initiative.

“Nuclear deterrence” is just a fancy way of saying that atomic weapons give an adversary a good reason not to do anything seriously adversarial. Extended deterrence, or a nuclear umbrella, means that one country’s weapons are used to provide deterrence for its friends.

France is trying to fill that role in Europe, following months of quiet conversations that led to public statements by President Emmanuel Macron in March. Eight countries already signed up for the French initiative, which is vague so far but could involve deployments of strike aircraft and joint exercises.

To be sure, the US hasn’t officially withdrawn its nuclear umbrella, which would be a huge strategic shift. But the involvement of yet another European country in France’s deterrence project shows the seriousness of thinking among Washington’s partners about, at the very least, needing a hedge against an unreliable ally.
“This is a natural step as our close allies Norway, Sweden and Denmark have already joined the initiative,” Finnish Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen said.
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering whether to help Saudi Arabia respond to attacks from the Houthis in Yemen amid British concerns about a worsening economic hit from the escalating conflict.

The US fired so many munitions at Iranian targets during the first few months of Operation Epic Fury that it “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” Pentagon officials told the Defense Department’s independent watchdog.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and US counterpart Pete Hegseth are expected to sign an agreement designed to deepen cooperation between manufacturers so European companies can produce certain US weapon systems via licensing.

Saudi Arabia’s closing of a major crude pipeline following attacks had an immediate impact on the oil market, as you might expect, by disrupting a route that’s been key to bypassing the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Iran war. Houthi rebels, meanwhile, captured key coastal towns in Yemen, giving them greater control over shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb strait, another vital maritime chokepoint.
Expert analysis provided by Bloomberg Intelligence. Links exclusively for Terminal subscribers.

Iran’s seizing of an Anduril Dive-LD underwater drone underscores two advantages of lower-cost autonomy: losses needn’t risk sailors or costly crewed platforms, and sensitive technology is protected. That design can help the Pentagon deploy autonomous systems without turning every lost platform into a major technology compromise. Anduril’s Navy selection and $98 million fiscal 2027 budget allocation can strengthen its maritime-autonomy position. —Wayne Sanders, senior aerospace and defense analyst

The US ramp-up in Patriot Advanced Capability-3 interceptor production can lift Lockheed’s segment revenue to $8 billion by 2030 from $2.5 billion in 2025, while aiding Boeing, L3Harris and other suppliers. Lockheed aims to boost yearly output to 2,000 missiles from about 600, which will make the program 8% of sales and 9-10% of profit at margins near 14%. Demand can hit 2,500 missiles annually by 2032, adding about $270 million of profit above the baseline. —Wayne Sanders, senior aerospace and defense analyst

items.title: Russia Boosts Oil Exports as Middle East War Sends Prices Soaring
body: Russia’s crude shipments jumped by the most since May last week, just as an attack on a key pipeline crossing Saudi Arabia sent oil prices soaring, providing a big boost to the Kremlin’s war chest.

In the four weeks through Sept. 13, overseas crude flows rose to 3.54 million barrels a day, tanker-movements data compiled by Bloomberg show, following the biggest advance in weekly shipments since mid-May.

Fortuitously for Moscow, the jump in flows comes just as oil prices are soaring again after drone strikes shut down Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, on which the kingdom has relied to continue getting its oil to market in the face of Iran’s effective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. The attack has sent Brent crude to the highest since May, and pulled up Russian grades.

The higher Russian exports will be welcomed by refiners in China and India, who face disruption to their Middle Eastern supplies from a resurgence of fighting in the region. In addition to the pipeline halt, the flare-up has also seen attacks on tankers by Iran-backed Houthi rebels that have blocked the kingdom’s oil flows via the southern Red Sea. Separately, a US blockade of Iran-linked ships has stopped about 1.5 million barrels a day of crude that flowed to China.

Moscow has boosted shipments of its crude through the Baltic port of Ust-Luga, diverting Kazakh cargoes to the more vulnerable Novorossiysk terminal on the Black Sea. That move has allowed Russia to lift its own Ust-Luga crude shipments by about one-third, or 160,000 barrels a day, so far this month, compared with August.

Still, strikes on Russian oil and gas-condensate processing plants continue to be an almost nightly occurrence, despite mounting pressure on Kyiv from US President Donald Trump, who blames them, rather than the war in the Middle East, for rising diesel prices.

Higher international crude prices are boosting Russia’s war chest. Moscow’s barrels delivered to India earned the most since early May last week, according to data from Argus Media, helping to drive the value of weekly exports to a near-four-month high. Prices paid by Chinese refiners are also soaring, with Pacific benchmark ESPO offered at more than $20 a barrel above Brent futures, on a delivered basis.
Amid these soaring prices, Russia is diverting some of the crude that can’t be processed domestically into the export stream, but not enough to allow it to maintain production levels.

Output fell to 8.72 million barrels a day last month, dropping for a ninth straight month, according to secondary source estimates published by the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. That was more than 1 million barrels a day below the country’s permitted production level under a long-running agreement with its OPEC+ allies.

In the week to Sept. 13, some 38 tankers loaded 27.06 million barrels of Russian crude, vessel-tracking data and port-agent reports show. The volume compared with 23.88 million barrels on 33 ships the previous week.
Loading operations have accelerated at Novorossiysk after resuming in late August following Ukrainian drone strikes on the port.
Weekly shipments can be volatile, affected by weather, maintenance work, sanctions, military activity and the timing of departures.

There were two shipments of Kazakhstan’s Kebco grade from Novorossiysk during the week. Moscow has diverted all shipments of Kazakh crude this month through the Black Sea port, freeing up more capacity for its own barrels at Ust-Luga on the Baltic, which is seen as safer.

The amount of Russian crude on the water has edged higher in the past two weeks, reflecting the recovery in shipments from a 16-week low seen in the final seven days of August, even as refiners in India took more than 2 million barrels a day of Moscow’s oil for a third straight month in August.

On a four-week average basis, the gross value of Moscow’s exports rose to $1.9 billion a week in the 28 days to Sept. 13, up by $180 million a week from the figure for the period to Sept. 6 and the highest since the period to June 28. The increase was driven by a combination of higher prices for Russia’s key crudes and a modest increase in flows.

On a weekly basis, the value of exports jumped by about $620 million, driven by a combination of higher shipments and soaring prices, which rose in line with global benchmarks. At $2.42 billion, the weekly value was the highest since the seven-day period to May 24.

China and India remain the biggest buyers of Russian crude by a considerable margin. But it’s not always possible to assign a final destination to individual cargoes until well into their voyage, leaving many of the more recent shipments on tankers showing interim destinations, such as Suez or Port Sudan, marked as “Unknown Asia.”

Observed shipments to Russia’s Asian customers, including those showing no final destination, rose to 3.41 million barrels a day in the 28 days to Sept. 13, up from 3.35 million in the period to Sept. 6.
Flows to Turkey, Russia’s biggest buyer west of Suez, in the period to Sept. 13 slipped to about 50,000 barrels a day, down from 80,000 barrels a day for the period to Sept. 6.

Flows to Syria have fallen to zero since August after the Mediterranean nation agreed to  “drastically” reduce Russian oil imports in negotiations with the US on lifting remaining sanctions. Separately, shipments to Egypt, Russia’s newest east Mediterranean customer, rose to about 80,000 barrels a day in the four-week period,  up from about 30,000 barrels a day seen during the 28 days to Sept. 6.
This story forms part of a weekly series tracking shipments of crude from Russian export terminals and the gross value of those flows. The next update will be on Tuesday, Sept. 22.

All figures exclude cargoes identified as Kazakhstan’s KEBCO grade. Those are shipments made by KazTransoil JSC that transit Russia for export through Novorossiysk and Ust-Luga and are not subject to European Union sanctions or a price cap. The Kazakh barrels are blended with crude of Russian origin to create a uniform export stream. Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Kazakhstan has rebranded its cargoes to distinguish them from those shipped by Russian companies.

Bloomberg classifies ship-to-ship transfers as clandestine if automated position signals appear to be switched off or falsified — a tactic known as spoofing — to hide the two vessels involved coming together to make the cargo switch.

Vessel-tracking data are cross-checked against port-agent reports as well as flows and ship movements reported by other information providers including Kpler and Vortexa Ltd. and satellite imagery covering Russian ports.
If you are reading this story on the Bloomberg terminal, click for a  link to a PDF file of four-week average flows from Russia to key destinations.

items.title: Miami, Dallas Join US Airports with Private Terminals for Commercial Flights
body: The champagne is chilled, the caviar is served, and you don’t have to worry about your luggage. Pink couches covered in green palm trees are very Miami. Lounge chairs around a reflecting pool offer a quiet escape.

From a private suite with a balcony, you can order croquetas and Cuban panzanella, or request a massage, manicure or haircut. When it’s time to board, a driver is waiting to chauffeur you in a BMW across the tarmac, directly to your commercial flight at Miami International Airport.
It’s the perks of flying private, without actually flying on a private jet.

Air travel has never been more crowded, with long security lines, packed terminals and overflowing lounges. Some travelers are so fed up that they are paying more than $5,000 for access to a private terminal to bypass the hassles of the airport.

Luxurious private terminals are being built across the US, widening the economic divide at the airport. One company called PS operates all four of the existing private terminals in the country. It expanded to Miami and Dallas in recent months, adding to its locations in Los Angeles and Atlanta. Airports serving San Francisco and Washington, D.C., are planning similar swanky areas.

Most fliers would balk at spending thousands of dollars on top of the cost of their plane tickets. Airports say the spaces meet demand from a wealthier clientele who prize convenience and privacy, but not so wealthy that they have a private jet.  Plus, the private terminals give airport operators a financial boost with long-term lease payments and revenue sharing from the independent companies that run them. The extra revenue can help airports fund capital projects.

When Joi Gibbs, 45, walks into the PS terminal at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the staff whisks her luggage away and hands her a glass of Billecart-Salmon, her favorite bubbly. She typically orders a burger or a salad and has a couple of drinks before being driven to the plane.
Gibbs pays a fee to tag along with her friend who has a PS membership, and she said it’s worth the price, particularly for the separate security check and skipping the line at the gate.
“There’s no waiting. I don’t have to lift a finger,” said Gibbs, who works in technology operations in healthcare and as a content creator. “There’s no people when I go into that private lounge.”

Customers of PS, formerly known as The Private Suite, can bypass the main airport terminal entirely and go through a separate security check for departures or through a dedicated US Customs and Border Protection screening on arrival. Travelers can pay for access to the “Salon,” a shared lounge limited to those 21 and older, or for a fully private room.

The all-access membership costs $4,850 a year, and each visit then costs $895 a person for the Salon or $3,650 for a group of up to four in a private suite. Non-members can pay $1,295 a person for a visit to the Salon, but they have to sign up for the waitlist and can only get in if the location has space that day. Once inside, food, drinks and most amenities are included, though tipping is encouraged.

It still costs far less than NetJets Inc., where access to private jets starts at $215,000. Holders of the American Express Centurion, or “Black Card,” can get a complimentary PS membership and a reduced rate of $825 a person for each visit to the Salon.
“We’ve emerged as a third category between commercial and private air travel,” said Amina Belouizdad Porter, chief executive officer of PS.

American airports are playing catch-up. Travelers around the world have had access to private terminals for years, including a beer garden with Bavarian Alps views in  Munich and wine and cigar experiences in Istanbul.
Latin America’s first private luxury terminal opened at Sao Paulo’s airport a couple of years ago and cost roughly $20 million to build.
Even as higher airfares and economic pressures keep some travelers at home, those who are taking trips are increasingly willing to spend more on premium experiences.

Affluent leisure travelers make up 26% of global travelers but account for 57% of reported airport spending, according to a 2026 survey by Airport Dimensions. Among the 11,000 travelers surveyed, 62% said they are willing to pay for upgraded airport experiences such as lounge access, fast-track services and premium retail.

“The definition of luxury has changed a lot, and it’s so much more about time, privacy, certainty and control,” said Porter. “People are willing to spend more money to get their time back, and I think this was very much accelerated by the pandemic.”
Travelers like Tyler Brown, an industrial systems engineer in Miami, would prefer airports to focus on improving the experience for frequent fliers, not just the people who can pay the most.

“I don’t see the terminal as doing anything that isn’t just coming up with a new model that costs more than the last one, just to keep weeding out more and more people,” said Brown, 27. “I get it, but air travel has definitely gotten so much worse in recent times.”
Soon, PS won’t be the only company to run a private terminal in the US.

Washington Dulles International Airport got the green light from the airport authority in July to move forward with a private terminal project, awarding Ireland-based daa International a 20-year contract to develop and operate the facility. The contract is valued at $125 million. Final plans are still in the works, but the contract proposes that the VIP space will sit on a roughly 51,000-square-foot parcel.
The Metropolitan Washington Airport Authority, which operates Dulles, and daa International didn’t provide further details because the plans are still in the early stages.
San Francisco International Airport is looking for a developer to build and operate such a terminal, with an opening planned for late 2028.

“There is clearly a demand amongst travelers for paying for an elevated experience,” said Doug Yakel, a spokesperson for San Francisco’s airport. “We see other airports taking on remote terminal concepts, so we think the time is right for our airport.”

The Bay Area airport plans to award a contract to a developer in early December, he said. The developer will be responsible for building out and maintaining the terminal, while the airport will collect a percentage of the revenue and rent from the lease.
“If you think about the San Francisco Bay Area, the innovation and industry that exists around here, you could definitely make a use case for it here at SFO,” Yakel said.

Since the downturns in the aftermath of Sept. 11 and the Covid-19 pandemic, airports have made a concerted effort to reduce their reliance on airline-related fees. Globally, non-aeronautical revenues — from things like retail, parking, restaurants and real estate —  account for nearly 37% of airport revenue and offset roughly 48% of total airport costs, according to a March report from Airports Council International.
A private terminal works in a specific kind of market with enough well-off consumers or business travelers and where the airport has the physical space available.

At Miami International Airport, for example, PS converted the former Pan American Airways headquarters into its private terminal, complete with gold paneling and stones preserved from the historic building.

In the two-story lounge on the outskirts of the airport, a good 10-minute drive from the commercial gates, the bar is stocked. Carts in the salon offer an evolving selection of freebies like Peter Thomas Roth eye patches and Summer Fridays lip balms. The suites have snacks, cocktails and private bathrooms with showers, and the scent of Le Labo Santal 26 candles and fresh orchids lingers in the air. For families, concierges can ready suites with children’s books and diapers, or treats for pets.
Brittany Callaghan, a 30-year-old stay-at-home mom, is a regular at the PS terminal in Los Angeles, where she and her husband have visited both the Salon and a private suite.

“LAX is currently under construction, and we just found it a hassle just dealing with checking in, walking for 30 minutes to our gate and then waiting,” Callaghan said. “It’s really convenient to show up like an hour or two before, and then it’s just like hanging out in your private area.”

PS said its global client base grew 21% over the past year to more than 89,000 customers across its Los Angeles, Atlanta, Dallas Fort Worth and Miami locations. About one-third of its visitors hold non-US passports. Members tend to be business travelers or families, though the company has seen growing demand from travelers who splurge on the service occasionally for a special trip. Previously backed by private equity, PS is now owned by Groupe ADP, one of the world’s largest airport operators.
Before a recent shorter flight, Callaghan said she made the mistake of not going to PS. She ended up waiting over an hour to get into the American Express lounge in the regular terminal.

“Nowadays everybody has an Amex, which is great, but now we can't even use the lounge. And we pay a lot of money annually for the platinum,” she said. “We might as well just pay the money to go to PS.”

items.title: Why Are Tesla and SpaceX Separate? Musk Says 'Great Question'
body: Elon Musk again teased the idea of his AI and rocket firm SpaceX combining with electric-car maker Tesla Inc., noting the extensive cooperation between the two companies he leads as chief executive officer.

During a virtual appearance at All-In Summit 2026, an event put on by several technology investors in his inner circle, Musk was asked about an upcoming showcase of Tesla’s next-generation Roadster. The CEO said years ago that Tesla will offer a SpaceX option package, where small rocket thrusters will boost the car’s acceleration and top speed.
One of the All-In co-hosts, David Friedberg, then asked: “Elon, why do you still have two separate companies?”
“Great question,” Musk responded. “Who could imagine what action one might take when there’s so much close collaboration in so many areas?”

Speculation has mounted this year that Musk might merge SpaceX and Tesla. His business empire has gone through significant transformation, with SpaceX acquiring the artificial intelligence firm xAI in February, and the combined company going public in June in the largest IPO of all time.
Read More: Are SpaceX and Tesla Hurtling Toward a Merger?

Musk has fed the speculation by frequently talking about “convergence” among his companies. SpaceX and Tesla are working together on a massive joint project called Terafab, a planned fabrication plant that aims to manufacture semiconductors in the US, starting in Texas.
SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell appeared in-person at All-In ahead of Musk, with another one of the event’s co-hosts joking with her about the possibility of the company combining with Tesla.
Shortly after discussing SpaceX’s acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor, another All-In co-host, Jason Calacanis, asked Shotwell: “What other companies are you planning on buying?”
“Good one,” Shotwell said.
“Do you like electric cars?” Friedberg asked.
“I have a bunch” she said.

items.title: Intel-Backed Chipmaker Altera Files Confidentially for IPO
body: Altera, a chipmaker backed by Silver Lake and Intel Corp., filed confidentially for an initial public offering.

The company, which makes programmable chips for applications including artificial intelligence, industrial automation and robotics, hasn’t determined the number of shares it will offer or the price range, according to an announcement Tuesday.

Altera traces its history to 1983, according to its website. Intel acquired the company in 2015 for around $16.7 billion. Silver Lake acquired a 51% stake in Altera last year, with MGX, an Abu Dhabi-backed investment company, joining the deal later.

US IPO activity has soared as companies capitalize on a frenzy of AI investment. First-time share sales have raised $160.6 billion, excluding blank-check firms and other financial vehicles, setting 2026 up to be the biggest year for debuts since the pandemic, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

items.title: China and US Discuss Cutting Tariffs on Agriculture and Energy
body: The US and China are discussing slashing tariffs on certain goods, including on American energy and agricultural shipments — a potential sign the leaders’ summit next week will lead to an extension of the one-year trade truce.

The meetings between the two sides are also likely to result in an agreement to lower duties on Chinese inputs for manufacturers, according to people familiar with the matter. The moves are expected to be carried out under an earlier plan for reciprocal tariff cuts on roughly $30 billion in trade.
Most-favored-nation rates would be applied to some items from China, said the people, who requested anonymity in order to discuss private conversations.

Highlighting the central role that agriculture is likely to play in the talks, representatives from state-owned food trading firm Cofco may join Chinese President Xi Jinping when he travels to the US to meet with counterpart Donald Trump, according to two people familiar with the matter. More than a dozen firms are also being considered for a CEO delegation, though a final decision has not been reached, according to the people.

While such a deal would be limited — bilateral trade hit more than $400 billion in the first eight months of the year — it would signal that the sides are engaging enough to maintain the tariff truce reached in October 2025.

An agreement would also show that Washington and Beijing can keep ties on track despite an expanding divide on how to handle artificial intelligence, export controls and the status of Taiwan. And it would signal that the Board of Trade, announced when Trump met Xi in Beijing in May, is able to produce some results.

China is making steady progress on its pledge to buy 25 million tons of US soybeans annually through 2028, recently passing the halfway mark for this year — a bright spot in trade relations between the world’s two largest economies. Beijing has also committed to buy at least $17 billion of US agricultural products annually on top of the soybean purchases, with the target prorated for 2026, the White House said in May.
The Office of the US Trade Representative, China’s Ministry of Commerce and Cofco did not respond to requests for comment.

Trump has said Xi would visit the White House on Sept. 24, an event that would also include a state dinner. China hasn’t confirmed dates for Xi’s travel yet, something it tends to do only days in advance.

For his state visit in May, Trump brought more than a dozen CEOs to China, including Nvidia Corp.’s Jensen Huang and Tesla Inc.’s Elon Musk. The executives met with Li Qiang, and Xi told them that US enterprises “are deeply involved in China’s reform and opening up, a process from which both sides have benefited.”
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News this month that he expected to see “announcements on agriculture and non-tariff barriers related to agriculture” during Xi’s visit.
Greer also said he expected the Board of Trade to make other announcements on toys, games and fireworks that might protect them from future tariffs or other trade measures.

items.title: Carney Expands Tax Break to Broad Range of Investments
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney is expanding the scope of a major investment tax write-off, adding oil and gas pipelines, oil production equipment, mining property and more to the list of assets eligible for immediate expensing in Canada.

Carney announced the tax measure — dubbed the productivity mega deduction — Tuesday as his government hosts an investment summit. Dozens of firms have gathered at Toronto’s Four Seasons hotel to discuss possible stakes in Canadian projects in natural resources, manufacturing and other sectors.

A number of those projects will now qualify for immediate expensing of some of their capital spending, under the new rules. It’s one of the most significant changes in decades to the tax treatment of business investments in Canada, and is poised to ease the income tax burden for many companies.

Normally, businesses can write off only a percentage of a capital asset’s cost each year. Allowing them to deduct those outlays right away encourages firms to invest sooner, since they can reduce their taxes immediately or choose to save those credits for later.

The expansion of the tax write-off means it will now apply to businesses that spend on aircraft, fiber-optic cables, Canadian-made passenger vehicles, computer equipment, bridges, roads and other assets. It’s expected to cost C$36 billion ($25.9 billion) over the next five years.

The government says it expects the change to have an economic return of 1.4 to 3 times the federal cost, totaling C$22 billion worth of output annually and increasing employment by 80,000 jobs per year a decade from now.
Reform is needed because “we have had a productivity issue in this country,” Carney said in an interview with Bloomberg News. “We need more investment in machinery, equipment, intangibles, R&D.”
The change covers roughly two-thirds of the categories of assets that companies invest in, up from 15% currently, Carney said.

The government states that extending and expanding tax relief will reduce Canada’s marginal effective tax rate on new business investment to 6.4% from 13% — the lowest among Group of Seven countries, and half the rate in the US.
The new measure, which requires a legislative change, applies to property purchased on or after Sept. 15, and is permanent.

Carney’s government had expanded immediate expensing for some assets in its 2025 budget. That measure covered a limited range of investments such as buildings used in manufacturing and zero-emission vehicles, and was to be phased out by 2034.
In the spring, it was extended to liquefied natural gas equipment, but only if it met certain carbon costing requirements. Those emissions-intensity criteria have been removed, the government said.

“This very much fits in with what Canada’s overall strategy is, which is to drive investment in sectors where we can export our products to the world,” said Avery Shenfeld, chief economist at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce.
“It makes perfect sense that we’re taking a tax measure that originally was much more restricted to parts of manufacturing and broadening it to sectors like mining and technology,” he added.

Canada’s economy has struggled to boost capital spending for years, and the Bank of Canada has called the country’s meager productivity gains an emergency. Last year, Deputy Governor Nicolas Vincent warned that the country was in a “vicious circle,” wherein weak productivity leads to reduced investment.

As uncertainty about its relationship with the US continues to hang over Canada, Carney’s government is trying to show investors it’s serious about addressing lingering concerns about taxes and regulation. The prime minister has pledged to mobilize C$1 trillion worth of private and public investment over five years.
The government has already announced billions in new investments for pipelines and other infrastructure, along with financial support for sectors hit hard by the trade war.

Over half of economists surveyed by Bloomberg last month said they expect deeper deficits, even as higher energy prices add to federal coffers. But Carney insisted his government will meet its pledge to balance its operating budget, saying the added expenses will be categorized as capital because they stimulate investment. His government is set to release its next budget in the coming months.
“We’re moving to the lowest deficit in the G7,” he said. “So we’re going to maintain that and have far and away the most competitive tax environment.”
In April, the government projected C$242 billion in deficits over a four-year period.

Previous federal governments have allowed companies to speed up the write-off of capital costs, but the measures were often temporary or limited in scope. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s government, for example, applied the provision to clean technologies and for certain property bought by small businesses.

items.title: Next Africa: Bitcoin Mining in Ethiopia Has a Weather Problem
body: Welcome to Next Africa, a daily newsletter on where the continent stands now — and where it’s headed. Sign up here. In today’s edition, we look at:
The El Niño weather phenomenon is taking an unanticipated toll on a key industry in Ethiopia.

The Horn of Africa nation lured more than 30 Chinese Bitcoin miners to invest by offering them some of the world’s cheapest power. But its ability to deliver is being thwarted by reduced inflows of water into hydroelectric dams.

The Ethiopian Electric Power Corp. reduced the amount of energy it makes available to the miners that consume almost a third of the nation’s total production of 9,730 megawatts as a precautionary measure. That enabled it to protect supplies for manufacturers and households, according to Ashebir Balcha, the state firm’s CEO.
“When we noticed the dry season was approaching, we reduced the supply to 75%,” he says. “When there was no improvement we reduced to 50% and now we reached 23%.”
The situation will be reassessed by next month, and there will be deeper cuts if necessary.
The risk of that happening is high if El Niño — which occurs as the atmosphere reacts to warming across the equatorial Pacific Ocean — intensifies as expected.
The US Climate Prediction Center last month estimated there was a 69% chance that conditions toward the end of this year will be the most severe in records dating back to 1950.
Some 39 Bitcoin-mining companies signed power-purchase agreements with Ethiopia’s state supplier, and 31 had already began operating.
Now they face an uncertain future. Options include suing for damages, relocating elsewhere or sitting tight and hoping the situation improves.
The utility meanwhile faces losing customers that generated 35% of its revenue in its past financial year, and the government will have to contend with a loss of foreign currency and investment.
That’s a severe setback for a country still recovering from a two-year civil war and wading through a prolonged debt restructuring.

Demand for shares in the Dangote refinery overwhelmed some Nigerian investing apps soon after the IPO opened on Monday. Minutes after it was officially announced, Bamboo posted on X that it was working to get its app up and running again. There were 40% more account openings in the past week than in all of May, previously the investment platform’s best month on record.

South Africa’s National Treasury proposed a three-year intervention to stabilize the Johannesburg municipality, which has been beset by governance and financial challenges, Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana says. Years of political instability and mismanagement have left the nation’s biggest city unable to pay its bills or provide reliable services. The plan will continue even if a new administration wins control of the council in Nov. 4 municipal elections.

Algeria and Mali agreed to collaborate on regional security, cementing a diplomatic thaw as the North African nation rebuilds its sway on the fringes of the Sahara with military-led governments that have close ties with Russia. OPEC member Algeria is increasingly re-engaging on its vast southern flank, where it has battled Islamist militants and Tuareg separatists, and is trying to advance projects such as a trans-Saharan gas pipeline.

Zimbabwe’s transition to a single currency will be driven by market conditions, according to central bank head John Mushayavanhu. The government initially set 2030 as the deadline to phase out use of dollars and make its gold-backed ZiG the official unit of payment. The switch will only happen once there is stable, single-digit inflation and the country has enough foreign exchange to cover at least three months of imports, the governor says.

Gabon’s foreign bonds surged after the government announced that an audit found the oil producer’s debt was almost a fifth lower than an initial estimate. The findings put Gabon’s loans at 69% of GDP, giving the central African nation a stronger balance sheet as it seeks a new IMF program and tries to settle a backlog of unpaid debts.

Sasol has started selling sustainable aviation fuel to a company that organizes luxury trips to Antarctica, tapping into a new market that may help reduce its environmental footprint. The biggest producer of fuel from coal and one of South Africa’s biggest greenhouse-gas emitters, is making fuel from used cooking oil at its Natref refinery. Tour operator White Desert, whose offerings range from one-day trips from Cape Town that cost $16,500 to a seven-day excursion for up to $120,000, has been signed up as a first customer.

items.title: EU to Levy Fines of Up To 6% of Tech Companies' Sales in Kids Act
body: Welcome to the Brussels Edition. I’m Gian Volpicelli, a European technology reporter based in Brussels, bringing you the latest from the EU. Make sure you’re signed up.Ahead of Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union speech, tomorrow, one thing is clear: she’ll talk about kids. In her annual Strasbourg address, the president of the European Commission is set to pitch her masterplan to keep young teens off social media — a policy the mother of seven has framed as a personal battle. The law enacting her vision, called the EU KIDS Act, is going to be officially presented on Thursday, setting in motion a legislative process that could take months or years to complete.

The draft regulation, whose full name is the backronym “EU Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy,” would establish legal age limits for access to social media and other online services blamed more and more for damaging kids’ welfare and mental health.

According to a working draft of the law Bloomberg reported yesterday, children between three and 13 years old would only be allowed access to services tailored for them and with full parental supervision, while those aged 13 and 14 will be allowed accounts on mainstream platforms only with significant restrictions and parental controls. That would set the age for independent use of social media at 15.

The KIDS Act’s rules would apply to more than just social networks, encompassing video-sharing platforms, app stores, online games, and AI chatbots — all of which would be required to verify users’ age using EU-approved methods. Penalties for failing to do so could reach up to 6% of the offending company’s annual global sales.

The proposal might still change before its Thursday debut — in fact, eleventh-hour negotiations are ongoing — but whatever the law’s final form, in two days the EU will join a growing coalition of countries age-gating social networks. The von der Leyen commission has been under pressure from member states to introduce bloc-wide rules, following the example of Australia, which first introduced curbs last year.

The Australian experiment’s results have been mixed, partly because the law did not mandate any specific age-verification technology. The KIDS Act would plug that hole — but whether that’s enough remains to be seen.

Canada wants to see the creation of a global “technology stability” body to help oversee artificial intelligence and ensure it is safe, Prime Minister Mark Carney told Bloomberg in an interview. “There’s a need for coordination,” Carney said. “Ultimately, a technology stability board, in our view, along the lines of the Financial Stability Board would make sense.” Speaking ahead of his visit to Strasbourg this week, the Canadian leader said that he is hoping for an arrangement with the EU “above and beyond” the trade deal that already exists, also pointing to “enhanced labor mobility” and educational opportunities.

Investors are increasingly looking east as they seek out the best opportunities in Europe’s sovereign bond markets. Bulgaria, Hungary and Lithuania are among the top picks thanks to an improving economic and fiscal backdrop, as well as the yields on offer, a combination that’s harder to find among their western neighbors. Political regime change and growing adoption of the euro, which comes with stringent economic requirements set by Brussels, further boost the investment case.

The European Central Bank’s top banking watchdog warned against watering down regulations for the industry, as authorities in the region explore changes to stimulate growth. Claudia Buch, who chairs the ECB Supervisory Board, said that the current regulatory debate carries “a certain risk” of weakening the standards without any real long-term benefits. The EU is debating whether to follow in the US’s footstep in loosening rules for lenders. Banks are calling for capital requirements to be lowered so that they can better compete with peers elsewhere and free up funds to back the supply of credit. Buch pushed back against that argument, saying well-capitalized banks are better positioned to support lending.

items.title: AMC-Robinhood Feud Tests Who Gets to Put Stocks on Blockchains
body: Five years after Adam Aron and Vlad Tenev became two of the defining figures of the meme-stock boom, the AMC Entertainment Holdings Inc. chief and Robinhood Markets Inc. co-founder are clashing over a new question: who gets to create a tradable version of a public company’s stock?

Aron hit out this month after discovering that a token linked to AMC was trading through Robinhood without the theater chain’s involvement. He called the practice “contemptible” and “outrageous” and demanded that Robinhood stop. “What’s the concern?” Tenev replied on X.

Their spat points to a broader question emerging as crypto firms race to put US stocks on blockchains: how much control should companies have over products tied to their shares? Those products can be structured in very different ways. Some are backed by actual stock, while others simply track the price. Sometimes the company is involved. Sometimes a token carrying its name can start trading without it. Many trade around the clock.

Johann Kerbrat, Robinhood’s general manager of crypto, said the backlash reflects a misunderstanding of tokenized stocks, which he compared with established products such as stock options and exchange-traded funds. “Issuers do not have to approve those,” he said. “We see tokenization as just another way to offer access to US stocks.”

Tenev expanded on that argument in a post on X, saying companies should control the rights attached to their shares, but not every financial product built around them. Putting those products on a blockchain shouldn’t give issuers a veto they don’t have in traditional markets, he said.
Read more: AMC-Robinhood Feud Shows Cracks in Tokenization Spree

All these nuances matter because the products can give investors very different rights. Robinhood offers debt securities outside the US that track and are backed by US shares but remain distinct from the underlying stock. Tenev said Monday on X that Robinhood plans to add voting rights for token holders and allow investors to swap shares for tokens, bringing some features of conventional stock ownership to the product.

Other platforms offer tokens that track a stock’s price without being backed by the securities themselves. Firms including Superstate and Securitize, meanwhile, are working directly with public companies to bring tokenized shares to US crypto markets, preserving rights such as voting and dividends.

For now, most tokenized-equity trading happens overseas and the market remains small. About $2.84 billion of tokenized stocks are outstanding worldwide, up 14.5% from 30 days ago, according to RWA.xyz. The number of holders has jumped 164% to 3.5 million over the same period.

Most of those products are so-called wrappers, essentially securities designed to track shares rather than the shares themselves. As more crypto venues push tokenized stocks and US regulators move toward opening the market, the risk is that a growing number of retail investors may struggle to tell the difference.

“Retail investors need to understand that if they are buying tokenized stocks issued by third parties, the federal securities laws may not protect them in the same way as if they were buying traditional shares in the company,” said Benjamin Schiffrin, director of securities policy at Better Markets.

The backlash has already reached some of the best-known names in tech. “Please be careful,” OpenAI said in a post last year, distancing itself from Robinhood’s OpenAI tokenized shares. Elon Musk was blunter: “Your ‘equity’ is fake.”

Wall Street is preparing for something larger. Nasdaq Inc. is investing $100 million in Payward, the parent of cryptocurrency exchange Kraken, as the firm expands tokenized-stock infrastructure and offerings. BlackRock has created one of the largest tokenized funds through Securitize, while the New York Stock Exchange is developing a blockchain-based venue for round-the-clock trading in tokenized stocks and exchange-traded funds. Coinbase is pushing ahead too, with CEO Brian Armstrong saying on X that voting rights for its tokenized stocks are coming soon.

Crypto firms see a chance to bring the multitrillion-dollar US stock market onto the rails of digital assets, where trading can continue around the clock. Companies such as AMC see something else: products bearing their names trading in markets they neither created nor control.

“Many issuers we’ve spoken to don’t like other firms tokenizing their shares without their consent,” said Bryan Choe, head of research at RWA.xyz. “They don’t want a product carrying their own name that they have no control over.” AMC didn’t return a request for comment.
Overseas, the line between traditional shares and their onchain versions is already becoming easier to cross.

Earlier this year, Backpack began allowing approved investors to convert shares held in brokerage accounts into tokens that can trade on the Solana blockchain. An investor could, for example, exchange 1,000 Apple Inc. shares for 1,000 tokens representing those shares and trade them beyond regular US market hours.

Backpack, founded by former FTX and Alameda Research employees, doesn’t offer the feature to US investors. Its model nevertheless provides a glimpse of the choices US regulators are beginning to confront as tokenized securities move closer to domestic markets.

Backpack says its stock-to-token conversion feature is another way to gain exposure to public companies. Its tokens differ from synthetic versions offered by some crypto platforms overseas that aren’t backed by actual shares.

“I only want to own equities, not some synthetic derivatives,” said Kyle Samani, a Backpack board member. “These kinds of things” — such as synthetic tokens not backed by actual shares — “are fine until they are not fine,” he said.
Thin liquidity can create another problem: a token’s price can diverge sharply from the stock it tracks. Companies may also have legal recourse when third parties market products using their names.

“The most likely claim that could be brought — you are using our company name, trademark for this product, and that’s not authorized,” said Ashley Ebersole, former SEC senior counsel and founder of real-world assets marketplace tx. “There are other intellectual property theories. You are getting people false impression that this is the official product of the stock issuer. People are getting this impression because of they way you are marketing it.”
Read more: BlackRock Partner Securitize Rides Wall Street Tokenization Wave

Proponents say tokenized stocks can also offer fractional ownership and near-instant settlement, while allowing assets to move between traditional markets and blockchains outside regular trading hours.

Much of the debate over tokenized stocks in the US remains theoretical. That could soon change as the Securities and Exchange Commission prepares its so-called innovation exemption for tokenized securities.

The SEC had planned to unveil the exemption in May, but decided to delay it amid questions from stock exchanges, public companies and other market participants. One contentious issue was whether third parties could offer tokenized products tied to companies without those companies’ consent.

The exemption could give issuers the ability to object to third-party listings tied to their stocks, Bloomberg has reported. That may reassure companies such as AMC, but it could also sharply restrict the number of tokenized stocks that are available in the US.
That gets back to what Aron and Tenev are really arguing about: can someone create a tokenized version of a company’s stock without asking the company first?
“What we really need to set the facts straight is, what’s legal and what’s not legal?” said Yoshi Yokokawa, CEO of Alpaca, a crypto brokerage and financial infrastructure startup.
