items.title: India's Inflation Raises a Red Flag for an October Rate Hike
body: Welcome to India Edition, Bloomberg’s daily dive into what’s moving the worlds of business, markets and politics in this dynamic, fast-paced economy. I’m Menaka Doshi. If you didn’t receive this directly in your inbox, you can subscribe here, and share feedback with us here.
Today, I look at the gathering inflation clouds and my colleague Samie Modak examines the sudden rush in India’s IPO market.
Onion prices are up 50% over last year, sugar is 24% more expensive and vegetable oil 9% — making the Indian thali more expensive than even the rise in headline inflation would suggest.
Consumer prices rose 4.82% in August from a year earlier, the highest inflation reading in 20 months. Wholesale inflation climbed to 9.92%.

Headline inflation remains within the central bank’s 2%-6% tolerance band, but has now exceeded its 4% target for three straight months. A patchy monsoon and high crude prices are likely to keep it elevated, economists say.

Rural inflation outpaced urban inflation in August, while services inflation has begun to pick up more meaningfully, HSBC economists said in a report on Monday. “Inflation is likely to jump in September, and average above 5% for nine consecutive months; we expect the Reserve Bank of India to hike policy rates by 25 basis points each in October and December,” they concluded.
To be clear, many agree that inflation isn’t broad-based yet, though there are signs it is getting there.

The median inflation rate across all 358 items was 2.9% year-on-year, well below the weighted headline reading of 4.8%, QuantEco Research said in a report today. Some 38% of items had inflation below 2%, while 19% recorded rates above 6%. QuantEco economists maintain their call for a 50 basis point rate hike over December and February, while acknowledging “the emerging risk of an early rate action in Oct. 26.”

Strong economic growth is adding to the case for an earlier hike. With demand robust, producers are increasingly able to pass higher fuel and input costs on to consumers, Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at Crisil, said in emailed comments. “The window for a prolonged wait-and-watch approach appears to be narrowing, and we expect the next phase of policy tightening to commence soon,” Joshi said.

Two other factors will also influence RBI’s next move. The spurt in government bond yields after the central bank announced moves to drain liquidity from the system. And what the US Federal Reserve decides at its meeting this week. A majority of economists saw the Federal Reserve holding interest rates steady, according to a Bloomberg survey.
The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to the highest in almost two decades, driven by surging energy prices, mounting debt and inflation.
Indian bonds declined after the central bank said it would sell sovereign notes to drain cash from lenders.
Amazon’s India quick delivery service is set to hit annual sales of more than $1 billion, intensifying competition with homegrown firms.
Stock exchanges and brokers may be among the biggest beneficiaries of India’s proposed changes to the newly launched closing auction system.
Don’t Miss

Want more? Sign up for Markets Daily India, a subscriber-only newsletter featuring key insights before the trading day starts. Keep track of the twists and turns — and the global fallout — of the war with Iran here.
Hello, I’m Samie, Bloomberg’s Asia Equities reporter in Mumbai.
India’s initial public offering market is suddenly busy again. Nearly 50 companies have hit the mainboard since August, as issuers race to get deals out before a regulatory deadline.

Following a one-time relaxation from markets regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India, companies now have until Sept. 30 to use approvals that were due to expire between April and September, after geopolitical turmoil earlier in the year pushed several IPOs back.
Normally, companies have 12 months after SEBI clears their offer documents to launch the IPO.

The revival has so far been driven largely by smaller offerings. Most recent deals have been below 10 billion rupees ($104.5 million), creating a crowded IPO calendar without generating the fundraising volumes seen in previous boom years.

That is set to change with National Stock Exchange of India’s 225.6 billion-rupee offering, by far India’s biggest IPO this year. The previous largest was SBI Funds Management’s 98.1 billion-rupee offering in July.

The NSE IPO should take India’s fundraising tally this year past 1.1 trillion rupees, while Jio Platforms could add about 380 billion rupees if it lists next month or in November. Even after that, India would need more than 270 billion rupees of additional IPOs to beat last year’s record 1.75 trillion rupees.

That looks like a tall order. The final quarter is usually the busiest time of year for stock offerings, but beyond the deals already in focus, no other IPOs of $1 billion or more are currently lined up, a banker told me.

NSE’s deal itself underscores the limits of the revival. The exchange had a shot at surpassing Hyundai India’s 2024 offering as the country’s biggest-ever IPO, but lowered its valuation and reduced the number of shares following investor feedback. A section of the market is also worried that tighter derivatives rules could slow revenue growth at exchanges.

And NSE is not the only company having to make concessions. Other issuers have also tempered their ambitions, while some prominent candidates have stepped away altogether. PhonePe deferred its listing plans amid geopolitical turmoil and market volatility, while quick-commerce firm Zepto put its IPO on hold and opted instead for a pre-IPO fundraising round after investors pushed back on the terms being sought.

There has been an unprecedented number of global exhibitions devoted to Indian art and artists in recent months, with shows in London, New York, Berlin, and St. Petersburg. India’s booming economy and growing population of newly rich citizens have led to a surge in the country’s art scene, with a new class of collectors and patrons driving demand.

Is Indian art a part of your home and portfolio? I’d love to know more if you are a collector, budding or veteran. Write to me here. Thanks for reading India Edition. —MenakaSave the date: Bloomberg New Economy Forum - New Delhi: This October, the Bloomberg New Economy Forum convenes its global community of business and public-sector leaders under the guiding theme, “A World in Play: Defining the New Levers of Power.” This year’s Forum, held Oct. 13-15 in New Delhi, will examine the shifting geopolitical landscape and explore the risks and opportunities reshaping the global economy. Visit BloombergNewEconomy.com/India to learn more.

items.title: Switzerland Needs Reforms to Keep Its Global Lead, OECD Says
body: Switzerland must embrace tax and pension reforms to preserve its status as one of the world’s top economies, the OECD said, raising its growth forecast for the country.

The Paris-based organization now anticipates expansion of 2% this year, up from 1.1% predicted in June, following a surprisingly strong performance in the second quarter. Officials cautioned that risks of trade impediments and a renewed appreciation of the franc remain elevated for the export-oriented economy.

Looking ahead, the OECD stressed that Switzerland faces housing shortages, an aging population and growing geopolitical challenges that will create long-term spending pressures, requiring the government to increase tax revenue.

“Prudent macroeconomic management, including a successful debt brake rule, have been key to withstanding repeated shocks,” it said in a report released Tuesday. “But reforms will be needed for Switzerland to remain one of the world’s most competitive and innovative economies.”

Recommendations include an ambitious pension overhaul which links the retirement age to gains in life expectancy, advice it also recently gave France. Switzerland should also reform its property tax so older and wealthier households get incentives to leave large dwellings.

“Switzerland has every reason to look to the future with confidence,” OECD Secretary General Mathias Cormann told reporters in Bern. “The task in front of Switzerland to keep the strong momentum going into the future is to secure fiscal sustainability as people live longer, to broaden productivity growth across more firms and sectors and to unlock housing supply.”

Ahead of a vote on new treaties with the European Union, the OECD urged Switzerland to preserve its access to the European single market while also diversifying its trading partners. Exports amount to about 78% of gross domestic product, with the EU accounting for almost 40% of Swiss shipments and the US for more than 20%.
The OECD also said Switzerland’s rules governing lobbying lack transparency and called for a code of conduct and a register of lobbyists.
The organization joined the IMF and all local regulators in supporting the Swiss government’s strict stance on new capital requirements for UBS Group AG.

items.title: Brazil Top Court Puts Off Moraes Decision, Clouding Election
body: Leia em português.

Brazil’s Supreme Court delayed a decision on whether to open an unprecedented investigation into one of its justices after a tense public hearing in which members traded accusations of political bias and spreading falsehoods about each other.

Judges gathered for a televised session on Tuesday to decide on a probe into Justice Alexandre de Moraes, a powerful member of the body facing scrutiny over his alleged ties to the man at the center of a massive bank scandal.

The allegations triggered an internal dispute between Moraes and Justice André Mendonça that has plunged the court into its deepest crisis in recent memory just weeks before Brazil’s presidential election.

The saga has contributed to declining public sentiment about the court and clouded the election, with the conflict between Moraes and Mendonça mirroring Brazil’s broader political polarization ahead of a race that pits leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

A decision to open a probe into Moraes, a controversial judge who has long drawn the ire of the Brazilian right, would mark the first time in the court’s 135-year history that it authorized an investigation into one of its own members. But Justice Flávio Dino requested more time to review the case as the session descended into chaos, a procedural move that will put off a decision.

Dino lodged the request while justices were holding a preliminary vote on whether to delay proceedings regarding Moraes until next week, when they will also assess a complaint Moraes filed against Mendonça. Dino’s move could delay the vote on Moraes’ case by as long as 90 days, potentially pushing it past the Oct. 4 first-round election and a likely runoff three weeks later.
The high-stakes hearing quickly exposed faultlines within the divided court as Moraes labeled the requested investigation “fraudulent” and politically motivated.

The judge, who rose to prominence for confronting Elon Musk over social media disinformation and his role in the conviction of former President Jair Bolsonaro on coup charges, accused Mendonça of working “in the service of a political group that attempted a coup against Brazil.”
Late Monday, Moraes issued a 44-page document in which he’d previewed his defense, denying links to Vorcaro and accusing Mendonça of pursuing the investigation out of electoral motivations.
His calls were echoed by allies like Dino and Justice Gilmar Mendes, the body’s longest-serving member.
“That’s a lie,” Mendonça yelled in response. The judge denied any irregularities in the probe.

At a campaign rally late Tuesday, Flávio Bolsonaro sought to tie Moraes to Lula, insisting that the president’s allies on the court he dubbed “shock troops” had only postponed “the end of impunity” by delaying the vote. The candidate singled out Dino, who before joining the court served as Lula’s justice minister.
“A vote for Lula is a vote for Alexandre de Moraes,” he told supporters.

The root of the current crisis is a long-simmering rivalry between Moraes and Mendonça, who was appointed to the court by Jair Bolsonaro. He’s since emerged as the chief internal critic of Moraes’ use of the court’s expansive powers, which have for years drawn accusations of political bias from allies of the right-wing former president.
The dispute erupted into public view when Mendonça unsealed private messages sent by former Banco Master SA head Daniel Vorcaro to a phone number attributed by investigators to Moraes.
Vorcaro and Banco Master are mired in what authorities have called Brazil’s biggest-ever bank fraud, a case that has eroded trust in governing institutions like the top court.
The fight has threatened to turn the presidential election into a referendum on the court’s future and given an apparent boost to Bolsonaro, the eldest son of Jair Bolsonaro.

The 45-year-old senator has used the allegations against Moraes to deflect from his own ties to Vorcaro while re-upping his calls for the judge’s impeachment. He’s gained on Lula in polls as he’s painted the president as a close ally of Moraes and an increasingly unpopular court.
A majority of Brazilians, 56%, said they don’t trust the Supreme Court in a Quaest poll released Monday, a 10-point increase from a month ago.
The move to delay the proceedings could further damage the court’s image if it deepens perceptions that Moraes’ allies are attempting to shield him from scrutiny.

Lula has appeared conscious of the political risk the saga poses to his reelection bid. He’s repeatedly tried to distance himself from the turmoil in recent days, calling for transparency and full investigations into anyone linked to the Banco Master crisis.

The incumbent president called for a “deep reform” of the judiciary in an interview with local broadcaster TV Record on Tuesday night, including potential term limits for top judges and revamped criteria for picking them.
“And one thing has to be clear,” he said. “Anyone who becomes a justice cannot get rich. We need to establish standards to ensure integrity.”
Lula also called for the complete disclosure of phone records related to the Banco Master case as he accused Mendonça of “releasing only what suited his interests.”

Brazil’s election has tightened into a statistical tie, according to recent polls. Lula led the race comfortably two months ago, but the court crisis, corruption allegations against one of his sons and a weakening economy have weighed on his popularity.

The top court is scheduled to convene on Sept. 23 to consider allegations Moraes made against Mendonça. In an official document issued earlier this month, Moraes accused Mendonça of abuse of power and directing investigators toward specific targets for personal and political reasons, calling on Chief Justice Edson Fachin to open an investigation.

“I’m deeply dismayed and saddened that the Supreme Court has caused civic unease among Brazilians,” Justice Cármen Lúcia said, while voting in favor of considering the Moraes probe as scheduled on Tuesday. “The judiciary exists to reassure the people, and we have generated unrest.”

items.title: Vodacom to Appeal Kenya Court Ruling on Safaricom Stake Sale
body: Vodacom Group Ltd. said it will appeal a Kenyan High Court decision invalidating the government’s sale of a stake in East Africa’s biggest mobile-network operator to the South African-based wireless carrier.

The court ordered that the 15% stake in Safaricom Plc be returned to the government, ruling that the sale violated public-finance management laws and failed to fully comply with public-participation requirements, judges Francis Gikonyo, Roselyne Aburili and Tabitha Ouya said in a decision handed down Tuesday in Nairobi.

“As interim steps, Vodacom will lodge an appeal against today’s decision with the Court of Appeal and will also apply for a stay pending the determination of the appeal,” the company said in response to questions sent by text message.
Vodacom shares fell nearly 4%, the most since July 27, in Johannesburg trading after the ruling before retracing losses. Safaricom shares jumped as much as 2.2% during Kenya’s trading session.

The divestiture was undertaken in contravention of the constitution and the law and was therefore “invalid, null and void,” the judges said. “The 15% shares are hereby restored to the government of Kenya,”
If the appeal is unsuccessful Kenya’s cash-strapped state may need to refund about $1.9 billion it’s already received for the stake.

Critical transactional documents such as the share-purchase agreement and a dividend rights purchase pact weren’t disclosed for public scrutiny, while the state didn’t explain in court why it settled on Vodacom as a buyer without a competitive selection process, the judges said.

In addition, the upfront monetization of future dividends violated the constitution by disenfranchising citizens and the transfer of control of a strategic asset to a foreign shareholder threatened national security, they ruled.
“The divestiture involved the acquisition of effective control,” the ruling states. “It was a takeover. This detail of information was not disclosed to the public.”

Vodacom agreed to buy an additional stake in Safaricom from the Kenyan government in December, increasing its shareholding to about 55% from almost 40%. The Kenyan Treasury’s interest was reduced to 20%.

The court said the parties didn’t apply for exemption from takeover requirements and there was no evidence that the Competition Authority approved the transaction. Transaction advisory services were also procured from KCB Investment Bank Ltd. in contravention of the nation’s laws.
Vodacom said the transaction was completed on June 30 following the lifting of the conservatory order by the Court of Appeal and the fulfillment of all relevant conditions precedent.
The sale raised about 204.3 billion shillings ($1.6 billion), along with an additional 40.2 billion shillings from the securitization of future dividends.

President William Ruto’s administration is privatizing state assets to raise project financing needed to fire up the $141 billion economy. His administration has a $39-billion infrastructure pipeline that includes railways, airport upgrades, roads, power lines, dams and irrigation projects that he says will create jobs and cut transport and energy costs.
The build out will be partly funded by cash raised from the sale of assets including Kenya Pipeline Co. and co-investment from the private sector, according to Ruto.

items.title: Indonesian Power Politics, Not Just Markets, Forced Out Finance Chief Purbaya
body: The end came quickly for Indonesia’s finance minister.
Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa was interrupted by a phone call from a top presidential aide while speaking in parliament in Jakarta on Monday. Within about two hours, his replacement had been announced.

In a little over a year on the job as President Prabowo Subianto’s handpicked fiscal chief, Purbaya was outspoken and brash but unable to restore confidence among investors spooked by his boss’s policy unpredictability.

Under his watch, the country’s stock market tanked and its currency hit record lows. The long-serving and respected central bank chief was forced out after repeated disagreements. Economists constantly noted that the administration needed to reassure investors.

Ultimately, however, Purbaya crossed one final internal red line last week, launching a sudden, massive personnel overhaul centered largely on the ministry’s tax and customs arms, angering their powerful heads and causing widespread confusion, according to people familiar with the situation.

Suahasil Nazara, a deputy finance minister for the past seven years who would soon replace Purbaya, sent staff a text message saying he regretted the personnel change and had unsuccessfully urged Purbaya to postpone it.

“The Ministry of Finance, as a major institution, will fall into disarray if we operate in this manner,” he wrote in the message, which was shared with Bloomberg. “When making decisions, we must not simply rely on authority and power.”
Suahasil didn’t reply to requests for comment.
On Monday afternoon, Purbaya had stepped out of the parliamentary hearing to take a call from State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi, who told him that Prabowo had decided to replace him.
Purbaya on Tuesday suggested that the personnel change at the finance ministry was “partly” the reason for his dismissal. “The rest,” he added without elaborating, “was the president’s prerogative.”

The heads of the tax and customs offices that Purbaya apparently crossed — Bimo Wijayanto and Djaka Budhi Utama, a retired army lieutenant general — weren’t the usual senior civil servants. Both entered the finance ministry with unusually direct presidential backing, with Prabowo summoning the pair to the palace before their appointments last May and personally assigning them to strengthening state revenue.
Utama denied any friction with Purbaya when asked by reporters about the issue on Tuesday after a handover event at the ministry. Wijayanto didn’t respond to the same questions.

Purbaya’s appointment and his style had underscored Prabowo’s unilateral and personal approach to governing, which has included major policy pronouncements that took even top officials by surprise. While markets reacted kindly to his exit, the rush doesn’t necessarily signal a new era of market-friendly predictability and stability.
Read More: Prabowo’s Economic Team Reset Leaves Investors Wanting More
Two other recent episodes also reveal steps Purbaya took to bolster state finances that appear to have crossed lines within Prabowo’s government.

Last month, he announced that the president had approved moving $6.8 billion from the sovereign wealth fund, Danantara, to the state budget. Danantara Chief Executive Officer Rosan Roeslani later said there had been no discussion about such an arrangement.

Purbaya also tried to hold on to government revenue by pausing the processing and payment of tax refund requests from firms through the end of the year, according to the people. The Indonesian Chamber of Commerce complained to the Industry Minister Agus Gumiwang Kartasasmita, who aired the issue in Parliament late last month. Purbaya then promised to investigate.

Prabowo hasn’t publicly stated his reasons for replacing Purbaya. The Government Communications Agency said Tuesday that the reshuffle reflected a “focus on strengthening execution rather than altering the government’s policy direction,” which it said remained unchanged. It thanked Purbaya for his service and didn’t list specific reasons for the dismissal.

For much of his tenure, Purbaya argued that Indonesia could move faster and use its fiscal resources more aggressively to lift growth. The Purdue-trained economist was willing to challenge analysts, ratings agencies and even his own country’s central bank in public, while pushing through aggressive changes inside the ministry.

That confidence was part of what initially attracted Prabowo. In a March interview with Bloomberg, the president said he saw Purbaya as someone who “knows what he’s talking about” and was “optimistic.”
Read More: Defiant Prabowo Spars With Indonesia Tycoons and Market Skeptics

Purbaya and Prabowo shared the view that wealthy Indonesians and companies, particularly major commodity exporters, weren’t paying their fair share of taxes, with under-invoicing and lapses within the tax authority enabling the practice.

Inside his ministry, Purbaya promised to “clean house” and welcomed anti-corruption raids targeting tax and customs officials to break up networks involved in bribery, under-invoicing and tax evasion. He told Bloomberg in April that he wanted to stop leakages from illegal imports, which he argued were hurting domestic demand and economic growth.

Purbaya, who earned the moniker “cowboy” for his unfiltered, straight-talking style, brought that confidence to his tenure as finance minister as well. He rated himself an eight out of 10 in the interview, saying: “I think I’m good enough.”
Read More: Indonesia Finance Chief Takes His Growth Bet to a World on Edge

Earlier this year, Purbaya chastised a Citigroup Inc. economist over his forecast that the budget deficit could breach the legal ceiling, questioning the analyst’s qualifications. He also called out the World Bank for its lower growth projection for this year as a major mistake.

After Moody’s Ratings and Fitch Ratings lowered Indonesia’s sovereign outlook to negative, Purbaya repeatedly argued that the agencies had misread Indonesia’s economic and policy outlook and that growth was poised to accelerate.

Economic growth did rise during Purbaya’s tenure, moving closer to his 6% target. But economists still raised questions about how fiscal, monetary and other government policies were being coordinated, and whether the push for faster expansion was keeping pace with the need to preserve fiscal buffers and policy predictability.

They have also increasingly questioned how much of the headline growth reflects underlying demand, arguing that government spending on priority programs has provided a significant boost while household and private-sector demand remain less convincing.

For Suahasil — Prabowo’s third finance chief — the challenge now goes beyond just keeping the budget deficit below target, according to Achmad Nur Hidayat, an economist and public-policy expert at UPN Veteran Jakarta. A sub-3% deficit doesn’t mean the budget is healthy, he said, particularly if fiscal obligations are shifted off balance sheet or spending cuts put pressure on regional budgets and subsidies.

“A minister of finance is not merely a treasurer tasked with raising money to fund all of the government’s political promises,” Hidayat said, adding that the boundaries between the wealth fund’s commercial activities, government mandates, state dividends and potential fiscal risks need to be clarified.

The 2027 budget will also serve as an early test for Suahasil’s leadership, analysts said, with the government facing a long list of spending priorities, including Prabowo’s free-meals program, energy subsidies, food security, education, health, infrastructure, defense and cooperatives.

If the deficit is kept below 3% “without improving the quality of spending, revenue collection, Danantara’s governance, and fiscal accountability, then this change in the finance minister will only result in administrative stability,” said Hidayat. “Indonesia needs more than that.”

items.title: México pierde a turistas que más gastan y apuesta por China
body: Read story in EnglishMéxico busca la manera de reactivar el crecimiento en sus destinos de playa, que alguna vez estuvieron en auge y donde las visitas de turistas de alto poder adquisitivo se ha desacelerado, otra señal preocupante para una economía que atraviesa dificultades.

El tráfico aéreo de pasajeros ha disminuido durante dos años consecutivos en Cancún, Los Cabos y Puerto Vallarta, destinos de fama mundial y emblemas del turismo mexicano. En lo que va del año, las llegadas de pasajeros internacionales han caído un 6% en Cancún, un 8% en Los Cabos y un sorprendente 20% en Puerto Vallarta, reduciendo la afluencia a playas y hoteles que suelen estar abarrotados.
Suscríbase   aquí   al boletín Morning Briefing Español y conozca nuestro canal de   WhatsApp

Esto pone de manifiesto la debilidad subyacente del enorme sector turístico de México, pese al aumento del número total de visitantes extranjeros, y supone otra señal de alerta para una economía que depende en gran medida de su capacidad para atraerlos. La industria turística mexicana, de US$150.000 millones, representa alrededor del 9% de la actividad económica anual —más que cualquier otro sector— y constituye una fuente estable de divisas, en gran medida protegida de las perturbaciones comerciales.

La economía mexicana se ha mantenido prácticamente estancada durante años, con un crecimiento que se prevé en torno al 1% este año, mientras las autoridades se esfuerzan por atraer más inversión privada a pesar de las dudas sobre las futuras relaciones comerciales del país con Estados Unidos.

La caída entre los turistas de mayor gasto obedece a una combinación de tarifas aéreas más altas, una menor demanda estadounidense, la fuerte competencia de destinos del Caribe y otros rivales, y la apreciación de la moneda, que ha encarecido a México, señaló en una entrevista reciente la secretaria de Turismo, Josefina Rodríguez.

“El tema de la turbosina es lo primero que pega a los vuelos y las frecuencias entre México y EE.UU.”, señaló Rodríguez. “Dos, es la inflación en EE.UU.; la gente no está viajando tanto”, añadió, refiriéndose al principal mercado turístico del país vecino.

Otro de los factores disuasorios son los recurrentes estallidos de violencia entre grupos criminales, al igual que la proliferación de desagradables acumulaciones de sargazo que cubren extensos tramos de la costa caribeña de México.

La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum suele destacar el crecimiento de los “visitantes internacionales” —que aumentaron un 14% el año pasado—, lo que atribuye al atractivo de las riquezas naturales y culturales de México. “México está de moda”, sostiene. Pero esa cifra —que incluye a visitantes extranjeros que no pasan una noche en el país— suma a millones de personas que apenas gastan dinero. Por ejemplo, quienes desembarcan en México desde cruceros gastaron en promedio US$84 por escala, mientras que quienes cruzan a pie la frontera desde Estados Unidos, muchos para visitar a familiares en México, gastaron US$59 por visita, según datos oficiales.
Por el contrario, los turistas extranjeros que llegan en avión generan aproximadamente cuatro quintas partes del gasto. El año pasado desembolsaron más de US$1.200 por viaje.
Incluso el impulso de los “visitantes internacionales” se ha moderado. Durante el primer semestre de este año, el crecimiento se desaceleró a menos del 8%.

A comienzos del verano, justo cuando arrancó el Mundial, la debilidad del sector fue especialmente evidente. En los aeropuertos operados por Grupo Aeroportuario del Sureste (ASUR) —siendo Cancún, por lejos, el de mayor tráfico—, el número de viajeros internacionales cayó un 12% en junio.
En agosto, los pasajeros que llegaron en avión a Cancún disminuyeron un 15%. El mes pasado, la caída alcanzó 17% en Los Cabos y 26% en Puerto Vallarta.

Lo más preocupante es que el número de turistas con mayor poder adquisitivo que llegan en avión se ha reducido más del 4% en lo que va del año hasta junio, incluso mientras su gasto promedio aumentó a unos US$1.300 por viaje.

Mientras disminuye la llegada de turistas en avión a los tradicionales destinos mexicanos de sol y playa, las autoridades de turismo están poniendo la mira en un enorme mercado aún sin explotar para contrarrestar la tendencia.

Rodríguez explicó que apunta a China como una nueva fuente de demanda. Su apuesta es que los viajeros chinos de larga distancia, menos interesados en los principales balnearios de México, puedan ser atraídos por la gastronomía, los festivales y los sitios históricos.
Alrededor de 150 millones de viajeros chinos vacacionan en el extranjero cada año, señaló Rodríguez. “México solo capta 200.000, que no es nada”.

Su secretaría estima que un turista chino gasta más del doble que el turista internacional promedio, o unos US$3.000 por viaje. “El perfil del turista chino, primero, no busca sol y playa”, señaló Rodríguez. “Su segmento es más cultural. Enloquecen con el Día de Muertos, es un tema más gastronómico y cultural”.

México cuenta con unos 13.000 guías turísticos y las autoridades quieren capacitar a más de ellos para que hablen mandarín. Según los planes, hoteles y atracciones traducirían la señalización y también adaptarían las opciones de pago para adecuarlas mejor a los visitantes chinos.

Rodríguez señaló que quiere aumentar la presencia de México en las principales plataformas de redes sociales WeChat y Weibo. También busca organizar mejor tanto a los creadores de contenido mexicanos que viven en China como a los residentes chinos en México para formar una red de embajadores turísticos.

La actual campaña del gobierno para impulsar el sector se centra en Ciudad de México, Baja California, Michoacán, Guanajuato y Quintana Roo. La selección es deliberada: la capital y los cuatro estados elegidos ofrecen importantes atractivos culturales e históricos. Tijuana, la ciudad más grande de Baja California, también ofrece vuelos directos a China, y Cancún, el principal destino del país, ubicado en Quintana Roo, sirve como puerta de entrada a los impresionantes sitios arqueológicos de la antigua civilización maya.

Los planes de crecimiento del sector podrían verse limitados por los relativamente escasos recursos del Estado. Además de años de caída del financiamiento para sitios culturales, el gobierno presupuestó este año apenas 43 millones de pesos, o unos US$2,5 millones, para su principal oficina de promoción turística. Rodríguez señaló que la secretaría obtuvo otros 100 millones de pesos para una campaña durante el segundo semestre de 2026 y espera un financiamiento similar en el presupuesto del próximo año, que actualmente está siendo revisado por los legisladores.
Incluso así, México compite con destinos de sol relativamente cercanos, como República Dominicana, pero también con lugares vacacionales mucho más lejanos, como Turquía, según Rodríguez.

La secretaria de Turismo reconoció que esos destinos gastan más en publicidad, pero aun así se muestra optimista sobre lo que considera la gran fortaleza de México: su abundancia de opciones para promocionar.
“Tenemos más oferta de la que sacamos ventaja”, afirmó.Traducción editada por Paulina Munita

items.title: Merz Promises German Drivers Relief on Surging Gas Prices
body: Chancellor Friedrich Merz said his coalition will take action on “price gouging” by gas suppliers and promised German motorists relief amid mounting calls to alleviate the burden on consumers from surging fuel prices.

“The situation in the Middle East is escalating, energy prices and fuel prices at the pump are rising,” Merz told a business conference on Tuesday in Berlin. “For many people who need their cars daily, a breaking point has been reached.”

The coalition is reeling after an overwhelming election victory by Germany’s far-right party this month, with many voters listing rising prices as a reason to defy the country’s political establishment. Senior officials and lawmakers in the governing alliance have begun to call on action to keep prices in check.
Merz said his government is working with state authorities to come up with a policy plan, but didn’t lay out what concrete measures his government is planning.
“The exact instruments have not yet been determined,” he said. “However, you can expect us to present a proposal very soon.”

The government approved a fuel-tax reduction earlier this year after the US-led war on Iran sent prices skyrocketing. Those measures lapsed at the end of June, spurring criticism that the action was only temporary. The measures were also scrutinized for lacking benefits for low-income earners particularly affected by surging prices at the pump.
Energy prices were a primary driver of German inflation last month, with consumer prices gaining an annual 2.9% in August compared with a 2.8% gain the previous month.

items.title: Traders Game Plan What 10-Year Yield at 5% Spells for US Stocks
body: Markets already had plenty to worry about as a historically volatile period for stocks kicks into high gear. A jump in the 10-year Treasury yield above 5% for the first time in almost three years upped the pressure even further.

Unlike October 2023, when the S&P 500 Index traded some 10% below its all-time high amid worries about the ripple effects of a global bond rout, the benchmark gauge is currently sitting within 2.5% from its last record in August. Could this mean the S&P 500 is yet to price in the risks?

To strategists at firms including Wells Fargo & Co., the exact impact on US equities will likely hinge on the speed of the yields’ advance going forward, as a sharp move up would sow anxiety on Wall Street. The backdrop puts even more focus on the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision on Wednesday and Chairman Kevin Warsh’s press conference right after.

“If the Fed indicates they will raise rates just once and then tap the brakes, traders will be relieved,” said Max Wasserman, senior vice president and portfolio manager for the Miramar Team at Wealth Enhancement. “But if there isn’t assurance on just how many hikes could be coming, or any hint that inflation may take awhile to bring down, then yields above 5% will require long-duration tech stocks to drop as investors reevaluate pricey multiples.”

Higher bond yields pose a threat to equities by lowering today’s value of future profits and making them less appealing next to low-risk assets. They also raise corporate expenses, putting a dent on margins. Prior to 2023, the 10-year yields was this high at the onset the Global Financial Crisis, which pushed policymakers to lower rates to near zero and deploy large-scale quantitative easing to support the economy.

Traders now see a nearly 90% chance that the Fed will lift rates on Wednesday after a highly anticipated inflation report showed consumer prices marched higher last month. Investors will listen carefully to Chair Warsh’s press conference for hints on whether more hikes would be warranted by the end of 2026.

“Investors would likely welcome a “message of one and done,” Ohsung Kwon, the chief equity strategist at Wells Fargo & Co., said by phone. “If they don’t hike, it will be bearish for equities,” he said, as the long end of the Treasury curve will probably spike.

Wasserman sees the psychological tipping point for the S&P 500 between 5% and 5.25% on the 10-year yield. Andrew Graham, partner at Jackson Square Capital, says a yield north of 5.10% would jump-start a correction in US stocks. And to 22V Research’s Dennis Debusschere, the 10-year yield hovering in the 4.8%-5% range would pose some restraint on economic growth.

To be sure, the S&P 500 has brushed off the risks so far, rising 20% since a trough in late March and adding $11 trillion in market value during that time. Even amid Monday’s bond selloff, Wall Street’s chief fear gauge, the Cboe Volatility Index, remained near 17 — a level that doesn’t typically signal market stress. The 500-member gauge traded down 0.2% at 9:36 a.m. on Tuesday.
But to Stephanie Roth, chief economist at Wolfe Research, bond yields need to come down in order for US stocks to resume their advance.
“If rates or oil rises further, a more meaningful equity correction is likely,” Roth said in a note to clients.

High-growth, high-multiple technology stocks are often seen as vulnerable to rising rates because many of them are valued on projected profits delivered years in the future. The present value of those expected earning is worth less as yields rise. Portfolio managers, including long-term bulls on the sector, see the risk of fresh losses ahead for rate-sensitive tech stocks — as all signs suggest Warsh will make good on his policy threat given prices for goods and services are still stubbornly high.

“The Fed isn’t going to disrupt this bull market run in stocks — as long as hikes aren’t aggressive,” said Tim Chubb, chief investment officer at Girard, a Univest Wealth Division, whose firm is overweight US equities and is buying the dip in equities on any selloffs. “But a potential overreaction and vulnerable corner of the market is likely tech shares with lofty multiples.”

The equity risk premium, or the difference between the earnings yield of the S&P 500 and that of the 10-year Treasury yield, is one metric that’s under intense scrutiny. The measure, often used to gauge the attractiveness of stocks versus other assets, is hovering near the lowest level since 2002, suggesting stocks are likely to become more sensitive to moves in bond yields.

JPMorgan Chase & Co. strategists led by Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou see the equity risk premium shrinking to 100 basis points below historical average amid three reasons, one being a higher sensitivity of stocks to bond yields.
Others are betting that the selloff in global bonds may indeed be reaching an exhaustion point, which may in turn help support stocks.

“With investor sentiment already deeply bearish on bonds and speculative short positions in 10-year Treasuries near record highs, the move appears increasingly overextended,” according to Larry Adam, chief investment officer at Raymond James. “That suggests yields may be closer to a peak than the start of a new, sustained leg higher.”

items.title: Reform Considers European Court in Fight to Keep Record Gift
body: Reform UK is considering a legal challenge under the European Convention on Human Rights if the Labour government’s bid to retroactively cap overseas political donations is successful.

Nigel Farage’s party recently accepted two record £36 million ($48.5 million) donations from individuals who could be inadmissible under the proposed legislation. A senior Reform figure, granted anonymity to discuss private conversations, said colleagues were mulling the irony that they may end up attempting to overturn that through rights conferred by the ECHR, whose authority the party rejects, and which it has committed to leaving if it were to win the next general election.

Over the weekend, Reform announced that it had accepted the combined £72 million from cryptocurrency investors Christopher Harborne, who was until recently based in Thailand, and Ben Delo, the founder of cryptocurrency platform BitMEX who relocated back to the UK from Hong Kong earlier this year explicitly so that he could fund the party without falling foul of any restrictions. The donations amount to more than Labour and the Conservatives spent fighting the last election, put together.

If Reform resorts to challenging Labour’s donations cap, its leader would be borrowing from the playbook employed by right-wing peers like France’s Marine Le Pen and US President Donald Trump, who’ve both railed against legal process to burnish their anti-establishment credentials. Farage has criticized the legislation — which Labour vowed to introduce before the donations were made, in March, under the leadership of former Prime Minister Keir Starmer — as a partisan attempt to restrict Reform’s income.

Under the Representation of the People Bill, which is yet to pass through Parliament, Labour has said it would cap all donations from overseas parties to an annual £100,000, and that the restriction would continue to apply to donors who move back to the UK for a full calendar year after they relocate. When the government announced its plans earlier this year, it said the legislation would apply retroactively from that date.

In the UK, retroactive applications of the law are unusual but far from unprecedented. The War Crimes Act 1991 allowed proceedings to be brought against British citizens who’d committed atrocities in Germany during the Second World War, even if they weren’t British citizens at the time, while other examples cover the domestic status of caravans and the regulation of government activities in Antarctica. Reform itself is proposing to retroactively abolish so-called settled status, which permits indefinite leave to remain in the UK, for people who’ve immigrated from abroad.

While Reform’s insurgency has been fueled by a sense that it is challenging the status quo, appealing to the ECHR would be an unexpected turn for Farage’s party. As one of the main architects of the UK’s decision to leave the European Union, Farage is also a keen critic of the human rights convention, blaming it for Britain’s inability to deport some failed asylum seekers and criminals from overseas.

The Reform leader has vowed to withdraw from the ECHR as quickly as possible, should his party win a general election due by mid-August 2029, in order to pursue a hard-line plan to deport people seeking asylum.

It was unclear on Tuesday which of the court’s articles the party might rely on if they were to challenge the ban. Adam Wagner, a barrister at Doughty Chambers, said if the government makes keeping the donations a criminal offense, Reform could rely on Article 7 which prevents anyone from being convicted of a crime which wasn’t an offense at the time it happened.

“That’s how electoral law tends to be enforced — through criminal offenses,” he told Bloomberg. “Article 7 potentially would apply if they go after these donations that were made before the legislation was enacted.” He also saw some possible arguments to be made under Article 10, which protects freedom of speech, saying: “It becomes particularly interesting if you can show that the change in the law was not politically neutral — if it was targeted at a particular party.”
Wagner said the European Court tended to give a wide margin of discretion to countries on electoral issues, but that “if I was advising Reform, I’d say it’s worth looking at.”

The party has previously had some luck with challenging the government through the courts — it caused Labour to drop plans to postpone some local elections, just days before the case was due to be heard in the high court.

The UK will introduce an enhanced residency test for political donors to ensure foreign money is kept out of British politics, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s spokesperson Tom Wells said Tuesday. He declined to provide details, saying the policy would be set out soon, and disputed criticism that the Labour government was trying to change the rules to prevent Reform from receiving the donations.

Some Labour MPs had been in favor of a broader cap on donations, limiting gifts from any individual at £100,000. However amendments to that effect were dropped after ministers argued that it could restrict funding from trade unions — Labour accepted almost £5 million from such organizations last year.

In a Monday post on X, Farage said he would “fight any attempt by Labour to retrospectively change the law on donations.” In an interview with the BBC, he added that he was sure the donations are “100% compliant with the law today.” Asked if that would still be the case when the elections bill becomes law, Farage declined to comment on the specifics of Delo and Harborne’s moves.

Both Harborne and Delo appear to have moved their residency back to the UK this year in order to keep donating to Reform. Electoral records show Harborne registered to vote at a UK address over the summer, while recent Companies House filings list Delo’s place of residence as the UK, rather than Hong Kong.

Reform has now received at least £61 million from Harborne, and £44 million from Delo. While those would be small sums in US, the UK applies strict limits on campaign financing. In the year preceding a general election a party can spend only £54,010 in each constituency, meaning they can spend just over £34 million if contesting all of them, according to the Institute for Government. Those limits represents an 80% increase to the previous one, after a change in 2023.
The UK’s previous record for a single sum donated to a political party was also held by Reform, after Harborne donated £9 million in the third quarter of 2025.

The party’s donations have raised wider questions about the influence of major donors in UK politics, and the effect they are having on Reform’s policy priorities specifically. Harborne and Delo have both been heavily involved in crypto, which was the first area to be addressed by Reform with a draft bill in 2025.

They come at at a time when the party is also under scrutiny over undeclared donations, which include a £5 million sum Farage received personally from Harborne, and which is the subject of a Parliamentary investigation. Farage denies wrongdoing.

items.title: US Stocks Fall as 10-Year Yield Hits Highest Level Since 2007
body: US stocks fell on Tuesday after the benchmark Treasury yield touched the highest level since 2007 ahead of a Federal Reserve interest-rate decision on Wednesday, when traders expect an increase.
The S&P 500 Index closed 0.4% lower and the Nasdaq 100 Index dropped 0.6%. The US 10-year yield rose four basis points to 5.03%, a rate not seen in 19 years, before retreating to 5.01%.

“Stocks now face real competition from risk-free assets,” Mark Malek, chief investment officer of Muriel Siebert & Co., wrote in a note. “After years when cash yielded almost nothing, investors can earn roughly 5% without taking equity risk, forcing stocks to justify their valuations with a larger prospective return.”
Oil moves also weighed on the stock market. Brent crude rose above $108 per barrel, climbing as equity declines accelerated in the late morning and held steady throughout the session.
Elevated borrowing costs have already put downward pressure on stock valuations, UBS Group AG analysts led by David Lefkowitz wrote in a note to clients.

“For long-term yields to rise materially from here and put further pressure on equity valuations, investors would likely have to price in an even more aggressive path for monetary policy,” they wrote.

Equities have continued to generate strong returns despite higher yields because their impacts have been offset by robust earnings growth, Barclays Plc analysts led by Stefano Pascale wrote in a note.
But “that balancing act may become more difficult if yields continue to rise,” they wrote.

While it makes sense to focus on the Fed, “the biggest medium-term risk to the equity outlook remains the trajectory of AI infrastructure investment,” especially since higher interest rates can increase the cost of capital, the UBS analysts wrote.

Enthusiasm around risk assets is fading as investors worry about a chaotic rise in bond yields and the results of US midterm elections, according to a survey from Bank of America Corp., which found that a net 49% of fund managers are overweight global equities compared with 56% last month.

Nvidia Corp. was among the top Magnificent 7 performers on the day after Jensen Huang, the chipmaker’s chief executive officer, took a live phone call from Donald Trump during a panel discussion Monday, allowing the US president to dismiss artificial intelligence dangers as a “hoax.”

JPMorgan Chase & Co. shares gained 0.7%, erasing earlier declines, after the bank’s Co-President Doug Petno said at a Barclays conference that he expects third-quarter investment banking fees and markets revenue to be up by mid-to-high teens.

items.title: Brightshore Capital Launches $250 Million Property Platform
body: Global real estate firm Brightshore Capital, formerly known as GTIS Partners, has launched its first real estate debt investment platform with initial capital of $250 million at a time when homebuilders’ financing needs are mounting.

The launch of Brightshore Credit comes amid elevated building costs and high interest rates, as well as a wall of debt maturities coming due. That creates pressure points for developers looking for support, Brightshore Capital founder and President Tom Shapiro said in an interview.

“We certainly see growing the platform to several billion dollars, but we’re solely focused right now, not on raising more capital, but doing a really good job investing the current capital that we have,” Shapiro said.
The $250 million can be stretched to larger deals by selling senior notes, potentially supporting more than $1 billion of transactions, Shapiro added.

Large asset managers including Blackstone Inc. have also pushed into the market with a lending platform for homebuilders. Last year, Apollo Global Management Inc. launched Olympus Housing Capital to provide builders with money to buy and prepare land for construction.

Founded in 2005, Brightshore has $5.6 billion in assets under management, with a focus on residential and industrial investments in the US and residential, industrial, office and hospitality investments in Brazil, according to its website.

The New York-based Brightshore has invested about $1.5 billion in debt through different vehicles, according to Shapiro. The difference is that this time it has a dedicated debt vehicle that will focus on origination and high-yield credit including stretch senior, mezzanine financings, preferred equity and B-notes.
“When we look at an overall deal, we try to figure out where we want to play in the capital stack,” he said.

Shapiro breaks down the real estate market into multiple pieces and by geography. One attractive market is San Francisco, he said, citing improved conditions on the back of Mayor Daniel Lurie’s efforts to curb crime and boost the availability of mental health treatment to reduce homelessness.

Brightshore bought about a dozen apartment buildings in San Francisco over the past six months, he said. In June, it acquired The Wilson, a 67-unit apartment in the city’s SoMa, or the “South of Market Street” neighborhood.
“We very much want to be in the equity in San Francisco because we believe in the upside of where that is,” Shapiro said. “San Francisco is in a massive recovery right now.”

Elsewhere, Shapiro pointed to oversupplied Sunbelt markets such as Austin where properties coming out of lease-up, or new developments that have reached full occupancy, may need to refinance construction debt at much higher interest rates. Lower rents and higher operating costs are also putting stress on some projects, leaving deals in need of recapitalization, he said.

Brightshore’s re-branding follows the 2025 buyout of GoldenTree Asset Management, its minority partner, and reflects its new structure as a fully partner-owned investment firm. The leadership remains unchanged.

items.title: The Debasement Trade Splits as Gold and Bitcoin Bets Diverge
body: With Treasuries sinking and the dollar falling this year, Bitcoin and gold are again being touted as hedges against currency debasement.

Yet in the options market, the great debasement trade is splitting in two. Gold traders are pushing their targets higher with little protection against a reversal. Bitcoin traders are pushing higher too, but hedging against a fall.

The divide is particularly stark around Sept. 18, a major expiry two days after the Federal Reserve’s next rate decision. In SPDR Gold Shares, more than five bullish call options were outstanding for every put, which typically offers protection against a decline. In BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, the ratio was closer to four calls for every three puts.

That is the fault line inside the debasement trade, the idea that heavy government borrowing and loose monetary policy will diminish the value of the dollar over time. Gold and Bitcoin may be responding to the same macro fears, but investors are not positioning for them in the same way.

Gold traders have steadily shifted their targets higher, and the preference for calls extends well beyond the Fed meeting into longer-dated options. Bitcoin traders have raised their sights too, while also building substantial protection near current prices.

“Gold investors continue to lean bullish via options,” said Aakash Doshi, global head of gold strategy at State Street Investment Management. The volatility skew “remains firmly bid for calls versus puts across both short-dated and long-dated tenors,” he said.

For the gold ETF, about $75.8 billion of notional options are due to expire on Sept. 18, by far the biggest expiry on its calendar, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The Bitcoin fund has about $5.8 billion expiring that day, its largest expiry of 2026.

Of the two, gold’s bullish options tilt is more persistent and less tied to a single event, with investors also recently purchasing calls in October and into next year. It also has a buyer Bitcoin lacks: central banks, whose purchases provide a source of demand outside the options market.
Read more: Gold Bulls Turn to Exotic Options, Spreads in ‘Orderly’ Rally

Griffin Ardern, co-founder and options portfolio manager at Primal Fund, said that official-sector buying gives bullion an underlying source of support even though those purchases do not show up in GLD’s options market.
“Gold wins in every branch of the fiscal-dominance scenario,” Ardern said.

Bitcoin presents a less straightforward payoff, he said. It can benefit strongly if investors come to expect greater monetary support or currency debasement, but it can also trade like a risk asset when inflation and bond yields rise and investors pull back from equities.

“That isn’t scepticism about the debasement thesis,” Ardern said. Rather, traders are keeping exposure to further gains while adding protection because Bitcoin’s performance depends more heavily on which path the macro economy takes.

Bitcoin’s recent surge helps explain the caution. After spending much of the bear market around $63,000, it shot toward $80,000 and has yet to establish a durable new trading range. Investors want to stay exposed if the breakout resumes, but they are also protecting against a reversal.

“After that squeeze, institutional flows returned to the Bitcoin spot market and to IBIT — albeit mostly at much higher prices, close to current market levels. For those recent buyers, it makes sense to hedge their positions while the sentiment recovery is still nascent and its resilience has not yet been tested,” said Andreja Cobeljic, head of derivatives trading at Amina Bank.

The open interest data can’t by itself prove whether traders are bullish or bearish. Large option positions can also be parts of more complicated strategies. In the case of GLD, much of the call option positioning is in the form of spreads, where a long position in one strike is offset by a short at a higher level, reducing the cost of the bullish bet but also limiting the gain if prices rally.

“The strike level numbers do not settle conviction versus caution, because open interest is a stock of matched positions: it tells you contracts exist, not who holds them or which side opened them,” said James Harris, chief executive officer at asset manager Tesseract.
The broader macro backdrop helps explain why gold has been the cleaner expression of the debasement trade, according to Harris.

The Fed rate decision and followup comments from central bank chairman Kevin Warsh add another complication to the longer-term picture. Investors have become increasingly convinced that interest rates could go higher rather than lower, pricing in a nearly 92% chance of a hike at the meeting Wednesday. That compares with a 32% probability on Aug. 19, when the Treasury Department unexpectedly announced that it would at least double the purchase of long-dated bonds.

“Inflation remains above target, and Warsh made clear at Jackson Hole that unless the Fed can be confident it is moving towards 2% at sufficient speed, it still has work to do,” Harris said. “The September debate is now between raising and waiting, not tightening and easing.”

items.title: Mexico Tourism Hit by Falling Beach Visits from Big Spending Foreigners
body: Lea en español
Mexico is trying to figure out how to reignite growth at its once-booming beach destinations, where visits by big-spending travelers have slowed in another bleak sign for a struggling economy.

Air passenger traffic has declined for two years running in Cancún, Los Cabos and Puerto Vallarta, global leisure hotspots that serve as a beacon of Mexican tourism. So far this year, arrivals from international passengers have fallen 6% in Cancun, 8% in Los Cabos and a staggering 20% in Puerto Vallarta, leaving typically crammed beaches and hotels light on crowds.

The declines highlight underlying weakness in Mexico’s massive tourism sector even as its overall number of foreign visitors has grown, and to an economy that leans heavily on its ability to attract them. The country’s $150 billion tourism industry accounts for roughly 9% of annual economic activity — more than any other sector — and serves as a steady source of foreign currency that is largely insulated from trade shocks.

The Mexican economy has been essentially flat for years, with growth this year seen coming in around 1% as officials scrabble to lure more private investment despite doubts over future trade ties with the US.

The downturn from the biggest-spending tourists stems from a collision of higher airfares, softer US demand, stiff competition from Caribbean and other rivals, and a stronger currency that has made Mexico more expensive, Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez said in a recent interview.

“Jet fuel is the first thing that hits flights and frequencies between the US and Mexico,” Rodríguez said. “Second, inflation in the US; people aren’t traveling as much,” she added, referring to the country’s top tourist market next door.
Regular eruptions of gangland violence mark another deterrent, as does the growth of foul sargassum algae blooms that pile up on large stretches of Mexico’s Caribbean coastline.

President Claudia Sheinbaum often stresses the growth in “international visitors” — up 14% last year — a jump she’s chalked up to the allure of Mexico’s natural and cultural riches. “Mexico is in fashion,” she argues. But that figure — foreign visitors who don’t spend a night in the country — adds millions who barely open their wallets. For example, those who step foot into Mexico from cruise ships spent on average $84 per stop, while those who cross the US border, many to visit relatives in Mexico, spent $59 per visit, according to official data.
By contrast, foreign tourists who arrive by plane generate about four-fifths of spending. They coughed up more than $1,200 per trip last year.
Even the momentum for “international visitors” has cooled. During the first half of this year, growth slowed to less than 8%.

In early summer just as the World Cup kicked off, the sector’s weakness was especially evident. At airports run by Grupo Aeroportuario del Sureste (ASUR) — Cancún by far its busiest — a 12% decline was posted for international travelers in June.
In August, those flying into Cancún slid 15%. Last month’s downturn reached 17% for Los Cabos and 26% for Puerto Vallarta.
Most troubling, the highest-spending tourists arriving by plane has shrunk this year through June, down more than 4%, even as their average spending rose to about $1,300 per trip.
As tourist planeloads dip to Mexico’s traditional sun and sand getaways, tourism officials are eyeing a giant untapped market to counter the trend.

Rodríguez explained she’s targeting China as a new source of demand. Her wager is that long-haul Chinese travelers less interested in Mexico’s top beach resorts can instead be lured in by food, festivals and historic sites.
Roughly 150 million Chinese travelers vacation overseas every year, Rodríguez noted. “Mexico gets 200,000, which is nothing.”

Her ministry estimates that a Chinese tourist spends more than double the average international vacationer, or about $3,000 per trip. “The Chinese tourist to Mexico, first of all, isn’t looking for sun,” Rodríguez said. “It’s more of a cultural segment. They love Day of the Dead, and it’s more about food and culture.”

Mexico has about 13,000 tourist guides and officials want to train more of them to speak Mandarin. Under the plans, hotels and attractions would translate signs, while also adapting payment options better suited to Chinese guests.

Rodríguez said she wants to grow Mexico’s presence on major social media platforms WeChat and Weibo. She’s also looking to better organize both Mexican content creators living in China and Chinese residents in Mexico into a network of tourism ambassadors.

The government’s current campaign to grow the sector is focused on Mexico City, Baja California, Michoacán, Guanajuato and Quintana Roo. The mix is deliberate: the capital and four target states offer significant cultural and historical attractions. Tijuana, the biggest city in Baja California, also offers direct flights to China, and Cancún, the nation’s top destination located in Quintana Roo, serves as a gateway to the country’s awe-inspiring ancient Maya sites.

The sector’s growth plans could be limited by the government’s relatively scant resources. Beyond a years-long fall in funding for cultural sites, the government budgeted just 43 million pesos, or about $2.5 million, this year for its main tourism-promotion office. Rodríguez said the ministry obtained another 100 million pesos for a campaign in the second half of 2026 and expects similar funding in next year’s budget, which is currently under review by lawmakers.
Even then, Mexico is competing with sunkissed destinations relatively close to home, like the Dominican Republic, but also vacation spots much further away, like Turkey, according to Rodríguez.
The tourism chief acknowledged that those places spend more to advertise, but she’s nevertheless bullish on what she argues is Mexico’s overarching strength: its wealth of opportunities to market.
“We have far more options that we really need to take advantage of,” she said.

items.title: Crusoe Signs Perplexity AI Deal to Provide Cloud Capacity
body: Data center operator Crusoe struck a multiyear cloud deal with Perplexity AI Inc., an AI search company, continuing its push to win more business renting out artificial intelligence chips and related software.

Perplexity will use Nvidia Corp. AI chips from Crusoe to train and run models, as well as relying on Crusoe to manage the technology over its lifetime, Erwan Menard, a Crusoe senior vice president who oversees the cloud product, said in an interview. Crusoe will give more than 1,800 employees Perplexity’s Enterprise Max product as part of the agreement.
The companies declined to comment on terms of the deal.

Crusoe is best known as a data center operator for large projects like OpenAI’s flagship Stargate data center in Abilene, Texas. The company has been trying to expand a unit that competes with so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave Inc. and Nebius Group NV in providing customers with AI chips and software, and Crusoe recently signed a $13 billion deal with Jane Street for its cloud unit.

At the same time, some of Crusoe’s massive data center projects haven’t gone to plan. OpenAI and partner Oracle Corp. declined to take up a lease on an expansion of the Abilene site — although Microsoft Corp. agreed to rent it — and partners pushed Crusoe off a project to build a data center in Wyoming for Alphabet Inc.’s Google.

Crusoe Cloud offers Nvidia chips and those from Advanced Micro Devices Inc., which is unusual — most neoclouds specialize in one type, usually Nvidia’s graphics processing units. Crusoe has cloud deployments in the US, Iceland and Norway and will soon add Israel, Menard said.

While Perplexity is a large customer of Amazon.com Inc.’s cloud unit, Amazon Web Services, and other major providers, Crusoe is helping the startup gain more access to Nvidia’s GB300 chips, which are important for its work, said Nate Kupp, vice president of engineering, enterprise and infrastructure at Perplexity.
Crusoe also has access to the latest Nvidia processors, called Vera Rubin, and has other contracted customers currently using them, Menard said, without specifying.
Having a cloud offering helps Crusoe attract customers who don’t want a massive data center of their own, while boosting revenue and profitability, Menard said.

“We love doing data centers at gigawatt scale and above because we make a big difference,” he said. But for smaller customers who just need access to chips or services, “we’ll give you that value-add under the hood.”

items.title: Vitol Paid Out $75 Million to Trader Convicted of Corruption
body: Lea en español

Vitol Group paid $75 million to buy out a former employee who was charged with conspiring to bribe government officials — and kept making the payments even after his landmark corruption trial, according to court documents.

The payments were revealed in a submission by lawyers for ex-Vitol trader Javier Aguilar, ahead of a sentencing hearing later this week. Aguilar was found guilty after a New York trial in 2024, marking one of the first times that an executive at a major trading house had ever stood trial for corruption.

Evidence shown during the trial revealed that Aguilar’s shares in Vitol, which is wholly owned by its employees, were worth $75.5 million in 2020, the year he was indicted. He owned 0.55% of the trading house from 2017 to 2019, according to separate legal filings. A senior Vitol executive testified to the court that the world’s largest commodity trading house had the ability to forfeit the shares of an employee who commits a crime, but did not say how the company was treating Aguilar’s shareholding.

In the submission, Aguilar’s lawyers said that Vitol “paid out the remaining tranches of Javier’s equity in full, before and after trial.” They argued that the continued payments were evidence of Vitol’s own complicity in the corruption, claiming that “Javier’s flaw was that he did not refuse to participate in an entrenched corporate culture of bribery.”

Vitol itself admitted to having bribed government officials in Brazil, Ecuador and Mexico over more than a decade between 2005 and 2020 in a deferred prosecution agreement with the US that predated Aguilar’s trial by several years.

A Vitol spokesperson declined to comment on specific payments to any current or former employee, and said that the facts in relation to Vitol’s involvement had been detailed in the deferred prosecution agreement. The DPA was “dismissed” in June 2024, the spokesperson noted, meaning that a court found that Vitol had fulfilled the conditions of the agreement and the US agreed not to bring charges against it.
Vitol Chief Executive Officer Russell Hardy told Bloomberg in 2024 that the company had “changed a lot” since the resolution of the DOJ investigation into it.
Read: How the Top Oil Trader’s Brazen Corruption Was Caught on Tape
In their submission, Aguilar’s lawyers sought to portray him as a mere pawn in a broader corruption scheme that was masterminded by others.

“The bribery infrastructure was in place long before Javier’s involvement,” they wrote. “Javier was a trader who joined, used, and directed an existing regional practice that Vitol, its counterparties, and its intermediaries already knew how to operate.”

“Senior Vitol executives — individuals far above Javier in the corporate hierarchy — were also implicated in the same type of conduct,” they said. They acknowledged that other Vitol executives had not been charged with wrongdoing in relation to the case.

The Vitol spokesperson said: “At no point in the DPA or during Aguilar’s trial did the Department of Justice allege anyone in Vitol’s executive management, had knowledge of, or involvement in, any misconduct by Aguilar or others.”

Prosecutors have asked the court to sentence Aguilar to at least 12 years’ imprisonment. The lawyers for Aguilar, who is a Mexican citizen, asked for his punishment to be a non-custodial sentence and self-deportation.

items.title: UK to Shield Poorest as State Pension Becomes Liable for Tax
body: Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey will protect the poorest recipients of the basic state pension from income tax after wage data put the benefit on course to exceed the threshold for paying the levy next year.
Under a longstanding “triple lock” guarantee, pensions rise annually by the highest of inflation, wage growth or 2.5%.

Wages are almost certain to be the binding factor, with official figures earlier Tuesday showing they rose an annual 3.9% in the three months through July. It means pensions are set to rise above £13,000 ($17,500) a year from April, a level that exceeds the £12,570 threshold for paying income tax.

That in theory would leave elderly Britons wholly reliant on the basic state pension facing a small tax bill for the first time. But within hours of the wage figures, the government moved to head off a potentially damaging development for new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

“Pensioners who only just exceed the personal allowance will not have the administrative burden of paying a small amount of tax,” Burnham’s spokesman, Tom Wells, told reporters. He said work on the matter is “ongoing” in the Treasury and that the chancellor would lay out details in his first budget on Oct. 28.

The prospect of some of the lowest-income people in Britain being dragged into the tax net presented awkward optics for Burnham, who has put help with the cost of living at the center of his agenda since taking office in July.
His predecessor Keir Starmer faced a widespread backlash when he proposed restricting winter fuel payments to pensioners early last year.

However, the steep increase in the state pension has renewed questions about the fairness and sustainability of the triple lock, with pensions now accounting for more than one in 10 pounds of all government spending at over £150 billion a year.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank has called it unaffordable and the Office for Budget Responsibility has shown that it is costing the exchequer billions of pounds. Critics say the commitment is consuming money that could otherwise be spent on public services and investment or used to cut taxes.

In total, around 13 million people aged 66 and over receive the payment, most of whom will not qualify for any exemption. On current projections, the standard state pension will see an uplift of at least £488 this year to £13,036.
The triple lock is based on annual wage growth including bonuses in the three months through July and CPI inflation in September.

Wage growth for the period may yet be revised, and inflation of 4% in September would make the pension uprating even steeper. However, that seems unlikely despite the recent surge in energy costs. Bloomberg Economics forecasts CPI growth of 3.3% for the month.

Proposals to exempt pensioners with no alternative sources of income from tax were proposed by the Starmer government, but no mechanism was set up and it was unclear whether Burnham would retain the pledge.

One option for Healey would be to raise the personal allowance, which is set to remain frozen through the end of the decade. However, that would come at a significant fiscal cost at a time when the chancellor needs every pound he can get to shore up public finances hit by the energy price shock.

items.title: California Is Test Case for US Fuel Demand as Prices Soar
body: Welcome to our guide to the commodities driving the global economy. Today, US oil reporter Will Kubzansky explores the impact of the global fuel crunch on drivers in the Golden State.

Considering how central the automobile is to life in California — think of its interstate highways, LA’s urban sprawl, a thriving car culture — it’s ironic that the state has the highest fuel prices in the US.
The squeeze on global supplies is now pushing those costs up further.

While US average gasoline prices are above $4 gallon, Californian motorists are paying more than $6. Diesel is in excess of $8 a gallon, again significantly above what every other state is shelling out.
At one station in San Diego, the trucking fuel was listed at $9.99 a gallon on Friday, the highest possible price on most electronic marquees.

That premium is a long-running feature of economic conditions in the state, which is cut off from America’s extensive fuel pipeline network. In recent years, much of California’s gasoline demand has been met by imports from South Korean and Indian refineries, which have now been curtailed by the impact of the Iran war.

For months, energy analysts have warned of global demand destruction owing to high prices, a consequence not only of the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz but Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refining capacity. On Friday, the International Energy Agency further slashed its oil consumption forecast.
So far, most of the drop-off in demand has occurred outside the US. Despite its higher-than-average exposure to energy inflation, California’s gasoline and diesel purchases haven’t collapsed.
But the state has seen a more gradual decline in fuel consumption in recent years due to improved efficiency and adoption of electric cars.

California’s gasoline prices are now around 15 cents off the wartime high set in May. The cost of diesel — the lifeblood of commercial trucking and agriculture (California is the largest farming state by revenue) and much else — is setting fresh records every day.
Unless prices stabilize or retreat soon, more motorists in the Golden State could be compelled to make a permanent change in behavior.
—Will Kubzansky, Bloomberg News
Yuan-priced crude futures in China rallied to a record as refiners in the largest importing country ramped up purchases and the shutdown of an oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia hurt global supplies.
Ukraine said it hit a refinery in Russia’s Volga region as the two nations continued attacks on each other’s critical infrastructure despite US President Donald Trump’s claim of an energy truce.
UK household energy bills are poised to jump about 25% in January, according to a Bloomberg Economics forecast that threatens to upend a government drive to ease the cost of living.
Chinese aluminum production climbed to a record last month as smelters rushed to fill a global shortfall caused by the Iran war.
Gold held a decline as further disruptions to oil flows from the Middle East reinforced expectations the US Federal Reserve will raise interest rates as soon as this week.

Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. has been cleared to acquire a stake in a battery firm linked to one of China’s largest carmakers, highlighting Beijing’s growing support for consolidation in the sector.

China is expanding its fleet of coal-fired power plants despite rapid deployment of renewables. BloombergNEF estimates 342 gigawatts of new coal capacity will be added by 2030, driven by the need to support renewable integration and meet rising peak demand.

Bloomberg Green returns to New York on Sept. 23 during Climate Week, convening industry leaders, policymakers and climate innovators to explore what’s next in the transition to a more resilient and future-ready world.
