items.title: Traders Are at Odds With ECB and BOE on Scale of Rate Hikes
body: Traders are increasingly diverging from central bankers on the outlook for interest-rate hikes in Europe.

Money markets have turned more hawkish as a surge in energy prices revives concerns about inflation. As a result, swaps now imply four more quarter-point rate rises from the European Central Bank over the next 12 months, and five such increases from the Bank of England.

Those wagers are a far cry from the tone of policymakers recently. The ECB last week reiterated that it won’t pre-commit to further steps after raising rates for a second time since the Iran war started, and officials saw bets then on three hikes as too aggressive. Meanwhile economists forecast just one or two more.

In the UK, where the BOE hasn’t raised rates this year, Deputy Governor Dave Ramsden said last week he was comfortable with current policy, though he acknowledged there were upside risks. The bank meets on Thursday and no change is expected. Earlier this year, Governor Andrew Bailey pushed back on market pricing for two hikes — less than half of what’s in play now.

“Central banks need to be even more cautious about their communication,” said Gregoire Pesques, Amundi SA’s chief investment officer for global fixed income. “There is so much competition that if one starts to have unclear communication, it’ll pay a very high cost.”

While it’s common for markets to get carried away and bet on more hikes or cuts than implied by policymakers, the extent of the divergence here is unusual. That’s because of the unpredictability over how long the current conflict in the Middle East might last and its knock-on effects on inflation.

The repricing toward more hikes this week has happened on the back of a fresh surge in energy prices. Natural gas jumped to levels last seen in 2022, while oil futures climbed for a second day Tuesday to head above $108 a barrel as a critical Saudi Arabian pipeline remains offline.

As inflationary fears from the prolonged conflict seep into markets, shorter-dated government bond yields have spiked. German and UK two-year yields are on their longest weekly streak of advances in several years, with longer-term borrowing costs hitting the highest in decades.

“This is an external shock beyond their control,” said Elias Haddad, global head of markets strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman & Co., referring to policymakers. “The best they can do is make sure the energy shock does not spread to underlying inflation and inflation expectations.”
The BOE is expected to address the increase in energy costs at its upcoming rate meeting. Swaps imply a 30% chance of a hike, an outcome that was considered very unlikely just a few days ago.

Traders will be watching closely for the language used in the statement, as there’s no press conference following the decision. Back in March when the central bank warned that it stood “ready to act” to tackle inflation from skyrocketing energy prices, the market rushed to price in higher rates, yet no hikes have come.

Now “the pricing is completely at odds with what the Bank of England is telling us,” said James Smith, an economist at ING Groep NV. He said Bailey may once again push back on the market, but “these warnings will probably fall on deaf ears.”

While swaps are a gauge of rate expectations, there’s more nuance to activity in this market as traders aren’t just placing purely directional bets. Some are also hedging against swings in borrowing costs.

Market gauges of expected volatility in UK and European two-year swap rates over the next month have risen sharply, though they remain comfortably below the peaks reached in March. That could change if there’s any further disruptions to oil supplies.

Last week, ECB President Christine Lagarde said euro-area inflation will stay elevated for some time as the current shock to prices from higher energy costs may last longer than expected. As reporters repeatedly pressed her, she also acknowledged the split with rates pricing.
“Markets do what they have to do, and we do what we have to do,” she said.

items.title: Sri Lanka's Growth Misses Forecast as Middle East Crisis Bites
body: Sri Lanka’s economy grew slower than expected last quarter, with elevated oil prices from renewed hostilities in the US-Iran war clouding the outlook for the island nation’s recovery.

Gross domestic product grew 4.2% in the three months to June from a year earlier, the Department of Census and Statistics said Tuesday. That compares with a 4.8% expansion forecast by economists in a Bloomberg survey. The South Asian nation grew 5.1% in the January-March period.

Sri Lanka’s economy had been gradually recovering from its unprecedented 2022 default, helped by reforms under an International Monetary Fund loan program. But the renewed crisis in the Middle East is threatening to upset that balance. The island nation relies heavily on imports to meet its energy needs, leaving it particularly exposed to the surge in global oil prices above $100 a barrel.

The latest shock adds to challenges from Cyclone Ditwah, which struck in November, and comes as officials from the Washington-based lender visit Sri Lanka for discussions on the seventh review of its Extended Fund Facility-supported reform program.

Central bank Governor Nandalal Weerasinghe said last month that inflation is expected to ease toward the 5% target in the second half of this year and into next year, helped by tighter monetary policy and government measures to curb imports. Persistently high energy costs could complicate that path.

The central bank kept its benchmark overnight rate unchanged in July, balancing rising inflation against the need to support growth. That followed a one-percentage-point rate increase in May aimed at cooling credit demand as surging global energy prices fueled inflation and weighed on the local currency.

Industrial production rose 7.3% in the three months to June from a year ago, while the services sector expanded 2.7% last quarter, the statistics department said. Agricultural output declined 2.3% during the period.

items.title: Brazil's Smaller Iron Ore Miners Battered by Shipping Costs
body: Leia em português
Smaller Brazilian iron ore producers are struggling with soaring shipping costs to top consumer China, squeezing margins and prompting production cuts.

Mineracao Usiminas SA temporarily suspended operations at the Samambaia plant in Minas Gerais state on Sept. 2 “to address challenging external conditions, including falling iron ore prices and a surge in ocean freight costs,” the company said in a statement.

Daniel Sasson, an analyst at Itaú BBA, said Usiminas halted about 30% to 35% of output at its mining business, an early sign that squeezed margins are starting to curb Brazilian iron ore supply. In 2025 the company produced a total of 9.2 million tons of iron ore.

Itaminas Comercio de Minerios SA said it will halt a 200,000-ton-a-month wet-processing plant in October and put a third of its workers on leave to preserve cash. The miner, which exports 90% of its output, is ahead of its production plan and said the move won’t affect its commercial commitments.

Freight rates have surged this year as the Middle East war disrupts trade flows and raises fuel prices, while bad weather in the Pacific has tightened vessel availability. Stronger demand from iron ore shippers has added further pressure to costs.
Brazil is the world’s second-largest producer of the steelmaking material, and the market is contending with the structural threat posed by waning demand from China’s steel industry.

The Baltic Exchange’s C3 Capesize route, from Brazil’s Tubarao port to Qingdao in China, was quoted at $42.12 a ton on Sept. 14, hovering around the highest levels since 2021. Benchmark iron ore futures, meanwhile, have mostly traded in a relatively tight range below $100 a ton since July, from a peak in May of nearly $112 a ton.

“With iron ore prices also weakening, smaller exporters with limited contractual protection remain vulnerable to pressure on margins and working capital,” said Maria Bertzeletou, a senior market analyst at Signal Group.

Surging freight costs are particularly painful for independent miners such as Itaminas, which lack the logistical support of larger rivals, Chief Executive Officer Thiago Toscano said in an interview last week. Shipping costs on the Brazil-China route have more than doubled from a year earlier, consuming “a very significant portion” of the value from exports and making some sales less attractive, he said.

On a free-on-board basis, the “value received by Brazilian producers has fallen by more than $18 a ton, even though iron ore prices have barely moved,” said Artur Bontempo, a partner at Prime Trading. The curbs at Usiminas and Itaminas suggest an even bigger impact on smaller miners in the country’s Iron Quadrangle production hub, he said.
Read More: Dry Bulk Shipping Rates Surge on Tight Capesize Vessel Supply

Itaú BBA’s Sasson estimated margins for Brazilian miners exposed to spot freight rates are near five-year lows, which increases the chances that iron ore prices will recover rather than continue their decline.

items.title: French Evening Power Price Nears €300 as Nuclear Output Falls
body: France’s energy system is facing a tight period this evening as low nuclear availability drives up power prices.

The country’s intraday power price rose to €292 a megawatt-hour on Tuesday for electricity delivered at 7 p.m., around the evening peak, on Epex Spot. The increase came as France’s nuclear reactors were operating at 67% of capacity on Tuesday, down from 72% on Monday, according to Bloomberg calculations based on data from grid operator RTE.

France’s electricity supply is heavily dependent on the performance of its 57 nuclear reactors, which generate the bulk of the country’s power. As Europe shifts from a solar-dominated system in summer to greater reliance on wind this winter, baseload generators such as nuclear plants will be important in cushioning swings in wind output.

Overnight, Electricite de France SA halted output at its Flamanville 1 and Civaux 1 units. It extended the halts of the St Laurent 1, Chooz 1 and Chooz 2 reactors. At the same time, strike action at hydropower facilities is also affecting power generation.
German intraday prices also spiked on Tuesday, trading around €300 for the evening peak.

items.title: Russia Refinery Hit as Kyiv and Moscow See No Trump Energy Truce
body: Ukraine said it hit the Syzran refinery in Russia’s Volga region overnight, underlining that the two nations have not signed up to the energy truce claimed by US President Donald Trump.

Both Moscow and Kyiv welcomed a potential energy truce, but made it clear that there’s no agreement to stop attacks. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said a halt to strikes on energy infrastructure was a “good idea” without saying whether Russia would accept such a proposal. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country would “support de-escalation.”
“Russia hasn’t stopped striking our energy sector, conventional logistics and critical infrastructure. And our responses to them for this are tangible,” Zelenskyy said on Telegram on Tuesday.

Ukraine’s president confirmed that the nation’s forces hit the oil refinery in Syzran, a drone production facility in Taganrog, a drone preparation and launch site in the Oryol region and targets in the Black Sea. As a result of the strike, a fire broke out at the site of the Syzran refinery, Ukraine’s General Staff said in a separate statement on Telegram, adding that a primary crude processing unit and the tank farm were hit.

Satellite images taken by NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System on Tuesday show a fresh heat anomaly at the refinery site, likely indicating a blaze. Russia’s largest oil producer Rosneft PJSC did not respond to a Bloomberg request for a comment.
Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, governor of the Samara region where the facility is located, said earlier on Tuesday that an unnamed industrial facility had been damaged in the drone attack overnight.

Trump on Monday blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for the surge in diesel prices and posted on social media that Moscow and Kyiv agreed to stop the mutual attacks. Zelenskyy later said no deal had been finalized, though he acknowledged a “strong US proposal for a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure.”
Read More: Trump Claims Russia-Ukraine Energy Truce; Kyiv Says Not Yet

Commenting on Trump’s energy-truce plan, Peskov said the security of Russian oil refineries and higher output of petroleum products alone “will not resolve global issues,” Interfax reported later Tuesday. The main issue is logistical, so the security of oil shipments across the world should be ensured and all sanctions on global producers lifted, he said.

Ukraine has been attacking Russia’s energy assets — from refineries and pipelines to oil-export terminals — to reduce the nation’s ability to process and export crude and curb the revenues that finance the Kremlin’s war.

Ukraine’s attacks reduced Russia’s oil-refining volumes to the lowest level in more than two decades, forcing the government in Moscow to impose temporary bans on most exports of gasoline and diesel. Before Kyiv’s flurry of attacks, the country was a major exporter of diesel, accounting for about 10% of global supplies.

Russia’s export restrictions due to the Ukrainian strikes have added pressure to a global diesel market that’s already squeezed by the war in the Middle East. Average prices of the fuel rose above $6 per gallon in the US for the first time last week.
Read More: Easing Diesel Woes Harder Than Keeping Planes Aloft: Javier Blas

Since late August, Russia has ramped up the frequency of its own air assaults on Ukraine, particularly its capital, using jet-powered drones that are harder to intercept, increasing the risk of civilian casualties and disrupting public services.

Ukraine previously said it struck the Syzran refinery, which is some 760 kilometers (470 miles) from Moscow, in August. The facility, which has a design capacity of around 170,000 barrels a day, is part of the so-called Samara group of refineries, built to provide oil products to the European part of Russia.

items.title: Hong Kong Leader to Unveil Five-Year Plan That Outlasts His Term
body: Hong Kong leader John Lee is taking the unprecedented step of outlining a five-year vision for the Asian financial hub. The question is whether he’ll be the chief executive to see it through.

On Wednesday, Lee will unveil Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, a blueprint his administration has spent much of the year crafting as it seeks to align the city’s priorities with China’s national strategy. It will be followed by Lee’s fifth and final policy address of his current term, which ends next June.

Hong Kong’s move to adopt five-year plans, which China’s ruling Communist Party has deployed since 1953, raises questions about whether the city is abandoning its traditionally light-touch governance that’s seen it ranked as the world’s freest economy by the Fraser Institute almost every year since it returned to Chinese rule.

Lee has argued the new approach won’t alter Hong Kong’s capitalist system and that he will uphold its status as an international city with free flow of funds, people and trade, according to an opinion piece published in the South China Morning Post on Monday.

The new framework will offer Lee’s clearest statement of the legacy he hopes to leave — and, potentially, his case to Beijing for another five years at the helm. The former security chief, who oversaw Hong Kong’s national security crackdown, has demonstrated to Beijing that he can restore order. Lee will now need to convince China’s leaders he can deliver economic growth, foster innovation and strengthen competitiveness, all while hewing the city more closely toward the nation’s strategic needs.

“John Lee served a purpose returning Hong Kong to law and order,” said Bernard Chan, who was a Hong Kong deputy to China’s national legislature for 15 years. “Now, the question is, what sort of chief executive is in the best interest of Hong Kong going forward?”

Since Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule in 1997, no chief executive has served two full terms. Neither of Lee’s two immediate predecessors, Carrie Lam and CY Leung, sought a second term. Political veterans say it’s too early to predict whether Lee might break that pattern, given Beijing’s influence. Possible insights could emerge after the Communist Party’s Central Committee holds its plenary session in the fall, according to Chan, who served as the convener of Lam’s Executive Council.
Lee has put his personal stamp on the 2026-2030 master plan, declaring early on that he would personally oversee the drafting.

In June, the government launched a two-month public consultation, which drew about 16,000 submissions. About 80% were from individuals, and the remainder from professional groups, political parties and chambers of commerce, according to Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Janice Tse.

Details such as whether it will include quantifiable economic and social targets aren’t yet known. But the government has outlined six areas of interest, including the city’s role as a global hub for finance and trade, policies to boost innovation and the tech sector, as well as urbanization projects such as the Northern Metropolis.
The plan will include what he called binding indicators for the government as well as metrics that are “anticipatory,” Lee told reporters on Tuesday.

Hong Kong has had plenty of long-term plans before, from building new towns to massive transport projects. Yet these have typically focused on providing stronger infrastructure and social networks, rather than top-down economic framing.

The adoption of five-year plans is a “signaling effect to tell everybody that Hong Kong will have more industrial policy aligned with the mainland,” said Alicia Garcia Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at Natixis.

Yet institutionalizing that longer-term vision introduces a new political dynamic: future administrations might inherit policy objectives set by their predecessors, while chief executives may leave office before plans they crafted run their course.

This timing of the plan’s release has brought Lee’s political future into focus. With less than a year left in his first term, he hasn’t given clues over whether he’ll seek another five years in office. The last time Lee was asked, he told local media “a year is a long time in politics.”

“He’s been very careful, but honestly, I don’t detect any unwillingness on his part to continue,” said Ronny Tong, a member of the Executive Council, which advises the chief executive. “On the other hand, if there’s somebody better on the sideline, then of course somebody can step in and become the next chief executive.”

Lee’s case for a second term will likely come down to Hong Kong’s value to Beijing. The city has long served as a financial gateway to mainland China, the world’s leading offshore yuan center and a platform for Chinese companies to raise capital. Lee has vowed to strengthen those roles. He recently told a banking event that the city’s five-year plan will include expanding offshore yuan usage and cross-border investment. His administration has also courted the Middle East and Central Asia as the city seeks to diversify trade and financial ties.

Complicating that economic mission, Lee is among officials sanctioned by the US in 2020 for their roles in implementing Beijing’s national security law. That’s constrained his ability to engage with US officials and some of its close allies. In July, Washington lifted sanctions on nine Hong Kong and mainland Chinese officials after President Donald Trump allowed a 2020 executive order to expire, but Lee remained on the list.

Lee’s tenure has also been marked by Hong Kong’s deadliest blaze in more than seven decades. The Tai Po fire in November killed 168 people and triggered a level of public outrage unseen since the 2019 protests.

A judge-led panel is due to release the findings of its investigation by the end of October. The following month, a small-circle election will be held to determine the composition of the 1,500-member Election Committee, the Beijing-loyalist body which chooses the city’s leader. That body is set to vote for the city leader in March. Lee was the sole candidate in 2022, campaigning on the promise of a “new chapter” for Hong Kong.

Whether he gets to write Hong Kong’s next chapter is ultimately Beijing’s call. The new five-year framework is designed to ensure policy continuity regardless of who is in office. Even if Beijing had made a decision to seek a new candidate, it would make sense to keep that quiet for now.
“If they want to change, they don’t want people to think this is a lame-duck government,” Tong said. “Then Hong Kong will become more difficult to govern.”

items.title: Meta Bulls Bet Stock Will Break Out After Year of Head Fakes
body: Meta Platforms Inc. shares have been on a rollercoaster ride through 2026, rising and falling as investor belief in the Facebook parent’s status as a player in the artificial intelligence space ebbs and flows.

But after the company settled lawsuits surrounding its social-media practices and unveiled its Muse AI agent that’s designed to automate everyday tasks for ordinary people, bulls are betting the stock could be primed for a sustained breakout.

“Eliminating a legal overhang and then having a positive product in a hot narrative is certainly enough to get the early stages of a trend change going,” said Dan Russo, co-chief investment officer at Potomac Fund Management, which owns Meta shares. “We’ve seen a number of these counter-trend rallies fizzle out and fade. What’s key from here is to build on the momentum and validate the changing trend.”

Meta shares have risen 22% off an August low and are on track for their biggest monthly gain since May 2025 this month. The rebound is not unlike others Meta has seen this year, with the stock experiencing four different trough-to-peak gains of at least 20%. Each of those rallies were short-lived, however, and saw shares hit lower peaks on each subsequent rally.

As a result, shares are essentially flat so far this year and well behind the 15% gain by the Nasdaq 100 Index. For Russo, in order for Meta’s most recent ascent to be considered durable, the shares need to see a “sustained break above $700.” Meta shares swung between gains and losses on Tuesday to trade around $670 a share.

For bulls, Meta’s $18 billion settlement of its social-media lawsuit removed a key overhang for the stock as a loss at trial could have resulted in penalties of as much as $1.4 trillion, according to its own calculation. Shares have fallen in just four of the 12 sessions since the deal was announced on Aug. 26.

Morgan Stanley’s Brian Nowak likens the setup for Meta shares to the one Alphabet Inc. investors saw in late-2025, when the Google parent received a favorable ruling in a longstanding antitrust case and followed that up with a slew of new AI products. Alphabet shares have soared more than 50% since the antitrust ruling, making them the best-performing Magnificent Seven stock over that span.

Meta is in position to keep releasing new products, “which in aggregate could add $10+ to EPS,” Nowak wrote in an Aug. 30 note. “We don’t believe these are priced in Meta right now,” as the stock valuation is well below peak 2025 levels, “when Meta was viewed as an ‘AI winner’ and GPU investments were driving faster growth.”
READ: Anthropic’s AI Caution Could Hand Meta an Edge: Equity Insight

He’s not the only analyst that has turned more bullish in recent weeks. JPMorgan Chase & Co. upgraded the stock to overweight last week, citing the “strong early traction” of Muse. Analyst Doug Anmuth said the initial success is an example of why “Meta is well-positioned to deliver consumer-driven AI products to its base of about 4B users.”
“There’s still meaningful upside potential as Meta is in the early stages of releasing frontier models and AI-driven products beyond advertising,” Anmuth added.

Meta’s valuation, which screens as the cheapest among the Magnificent Seven save for Nvidia Corp., could also help attract investors. The stock trades at roughly 18 times estimated earnings over the next 12 months, below its 10-year average of 20 times and more than 30% below its 2025 peak.

Investors are getting good growth for that value. Analysts expect revenue to expand more than 25% this year, while earnings are forecast to jump more than 30%, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Still, one area of concern that remains for Meta investors are the billions of dollars in capital expenditures being spent on AI.

Meta’s spending is expected to double to nearly $140 billion this year before swelling to almost $200 billion in 2027. The company, which once boasted big cash flows is expected to report negative free cash flow of $6.3 billion this year, with that figure projected to widen to nearly $30 billion in 2027.
Those two factors alone are reason to be skeptical about whether the current uptrend in Meta’s stock will last, according to Cyrus Amini, chief investment officer at Hyphen Wealth Management.

“The valuation is attractive, and it could have more short-term catalysts than megacaps, but for anything beyond that, all bets are off. It could easily fade again,” he said. “Things are changing so fast it’s hard to safely say any name is a long-term winner.”

items.title: Air France to Open Largest Lounge at JFK's New Terminal One
body: The largest airline lounge at John F. Kennedy International Airport’s new international terminal will be home to Air France next year as the carrier bets on the continued strength of premium international travel.

Air France will open a 29,000-square-foot, two-story lounge at the New York airport’s New Terminal One that will accommodate more than 400 guests, with areas for beauty treatments and a bar stocked with French wines and Champagnes, the Air France-KLM airline said in a statement.

The lounge, Air France’s largest outside of Paris, will be open to customers flying La Première, the airline’s top-tier first-class service, as well as business-class customers, Flying Blue Elite Plus members and travelers flying with KLM and SkyTeam partner airlines.
Air France plans to move its JFK operations in 2027 to New Terminal One from the existing Terminal 1, where it has operated since 1998.

“Air France’s investment in our terminal’s biggest lounge represents a strong vote of confidence in the seamless and modern travel experience we are building,” Jennifer Aument, chief executive officer for New Terminal One, said in a Tuesday statement.

The $9.5 billion New Terminal One project is part of the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey’s $19 billion revamp of JFK that will, through a public-private partnership, include a new international terminal housing airlines like Air France, Korean Air and Royal Air Maroc.
Construction is close to 90% complete with an opening originally targeted for later this year, though that has been pushed back to early 2027, according to a New Terminal One spokesperson.
Read More: Airport Lounge Crowds, Confusion Infuriate High-Spending Flyers
The project puts Air France in an escalating lounge race at JFK as airlines spend to capture high-paying travelers before they step onto an aircraft.

Delta Air Lines in 2024 opened a nearly 40,000-square-foot lounge in Terminal 4, with a 140-seat brasserie, wellness treatments and shower suites. Lufthansa Group is building a roughly 36,000-square-foot lounge at the new Terminal 6. American Airlines and British Airways since 2022 have jointly operated three premium lounges in Terminal 8, with access divided by cabin and elite status.
The push is even spreading beyond the major carriers. JetBlue Airways Corp. opened its first lounge in 2025 at JFK.
Read More: Air France-KLM Jumps After Upbeat Transatlantic Forecast (1)

Air France has also been overhauling La Première. Its newest first-class suites stretch across five windows and include an armchair and a chaise lounge that converts into a bed. All flights between Paris and JFK are slated to feature the new cabin.

At Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport, La Première customers are escorted through private check-in and security before reaching a dedicated lounge with dining, a spa and relaxation rooms. When it is time to board, passengers receive rides across the tarmac in a Porsche Cayenne.

For another €1,500, travelers can reserve one of three nearly 500-square-foot private suites attached to the lounge, each with a living room, double bedroom, bathroom and outdoor patio, with Champagne and caviar on arrival.

items.title: A US-China Pact on AI Is Possible, But Not by Posturing
body: Any hope that the coming summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping would be productive in taking steps to mitigate the harms of artificial intelligence seems to have been dashed, thanks to a commander in chief unwilling to acknowledge the pivotal moment that faces us as AI companies call for a slowdown in development.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday, responding to a flurry of debate in the AI sector on slowing research in the name of safety. He argued that calls for regulation were a “SICK conspiracy” against AI and data centers, one that benefits only the great adversary, China.

It’s an absurd notion that some of AI’s biggest boosters, companies and people — those who stand to benefit the most from its development and proliferation — are now engaged in a conspiracy against their own interests or that their concerns about safety are a “hoax.” And Trump’s wrong, of course, to consider himself the only necessary guardrail of AI. A “high IQ” president would be one who recognized the coming meeting with his Chinese counterpart, with direct talks at the White House on Sept. 24, as an important chance to at least begin the process of addressing some of AI’s most harmful effects. That task can be effective only if it’s global in scale.

It can be tempting to frame any talks as fruitless. How could two countries, intensely distrustful of each other, reach a credible agreement to slow development or play on a more transparent AI field? China has already, through an editorial in the state-controlled Global Times newspaper, described Anthropic’s call for a slowdown as a “‘Cold War playbook’ for the AI sector.” (We might remind ourselves at this juncture that the Cold War ended without nuclear war.)

But trust need not be a prerequisite. “There is a deep mutual suspicion on both sides,” Jack Shanahan, a former director of AI at the Pentagon, told me, but he stressed it’s possible to “figure out how to chip away at that without trying to claim all of a sudden the two presidents have got this relationship built on trust.”

Where that chipping away might start is in finding areas of obvious and urgent mutual interest when it comes to the AI threat. Trump and Xi should discuss where the “potential redlines would be on using advanced AI to attack each other’s critical infrastructure, key resources, nuclear command and control,” Shanahan said. (Such conversations were taking place under Joe Biden.)

From there, attention might also turn to the thorny matter of “distillation” — the practice of using a large existing AI model to train a new one. US AI labs, Anthropic in particular, are upset at Chinese AI labs for distilling American models to cheaply and quickly catch up to Western rivals. China could direct its AI companies to curtail the practice —  one already has — in return for looser export controls on US-designed semiconductors. This is something many US-based AI leaders suggest would be good for American dominance because it would increase demand for hardware from homegrown companies like Nvidia Corp. rather than from Huawei Technologies Co. or other Chinese competitors. There are, in other words, levers to pull and conditions that can be imposed.

While it may not be possible to point a satellite at a data center and assess AI progress in the same way a nation might count nuclear warheads, China observers say that Xi is sincerely willing to open up Chinese AI to independent evaluators if the US sector were subject to the same. Some US AI labs have said they would open up, though there’s disagreement on the mechanics. We know that, like a growing number in the US AI sector, President Xi shares concern about self-training AI breaking free of human control. This sensible common ground can be the starting point of setting up global safety frameworks. In this scenario, maybe Europe finds a role — or perhaps the UK, which has already received praise from US AI researchers over the effectiveness of its government-run AI Safety Institute.

In any event, talking is unquestionably better than not. Obama-era dialogue with China on cyberwar, including a pact not to use cyberattacks to steal intellectual property, was credited at least in part (along with other pressures) with slowing the rate of Chinese-backed breaches of US systems (for a time, at least, though any time gained on AI safety should be considered a luxury).

As with cybersecurity, any pact on AI would be met with warranted skepticism. “Trust, but verify” becomes “verify, verify again, and only then might you be able to consider any type of trust,” suggested Kat Duffy, senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. That will be long in the making for this emerging technology.

For now, with Trump’s comments in mind, “I think the best-case scenario is a broader statement that there will be another set of talks,” Duffy added. One hope shared by Duffy and others, such as the leading AI commentator Gary Marcus, is that Trump can be convinced that reaching an agreement with Xi on AI safety would be a sure and deserved way to win a Nobel Peace Prize. If someone could bring that to his attention in the next nine days, maybe the talks might take on a different, and more reassuring, dimension.

items.title: Essity Said to Prep for Tissue Exit With Sale, Listing on Table
body: Essity AB is preparing to kick off the sales process for its consumer tissue business as soon as next month, according to people familiar with the matter, after activist investor Cevian Capital took a minority stake in the Swedish company.

Industry players and private equity firms will be invited to bid for the division, which produces toilet paper, tissues and napkins under brands including Lotus, Tempo and Cushelle, the people said. The business could be valued at €2.5 billion ($2.9 billion) to €3 billion, they said.

“We’ve been working at full speed on the strategic review over the summer,” Essity Chief Executive Officer Ulrika Kolsrud said in an interview this month. Morgan Stanley is advising on the process, she said, with a conclusion expected in the first half of 2027.

The US bank is running a so-called dual-track process under which the tissue division could be sold or separated into a new company listed in Sweden, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing a confidential matter.
Kolsrud declined to discuss the possible valuation or potential buyers, saying that no decision has been made. A representative from Morgan Stanley declined to comment.

Consumer tissue is Essity’s largest division by sales, generating almost 44 billion kronor ($4.5 billion) last year, or nearly a third of the group’s total. Yet it has the lowest margins of any unit, and a separation could allow Essity to focus on health and hygiene. Over the past year, Essity has acquired feminine care brands Carefree, Stayfree and o.b. in both North America and Brazil.
“I would like us to have a larger share of the portfolio in higher-value-added categories and segments, where innovation and brand strength play a major role,” Kolsrud said.

The potential sale is moving ahead after activist investor Cevian disclosed in July that it had a 5.6% stake in Essity, saying it saw “significant value potential” and supported the tissue review. Industrivärden, Essity’s largest shareholder, has also increased its stake.

Essity has taken this route before. In 2023, it agreed to sell its controlling stake in Asian tissue maker Vinda International Holdings to Singapore-based RGE Pte after a process that also drew interest from Suzano SA, Bain Capital and CVC Capital Partners.

The consumer tissue business employs about 13,000 people across 29 production facilities and is the market leader in Europe and the second-largest player in Latin America. Separating such a large business could be complicated.
Kolsrud said that Essity is looking at the potential drawbacks of a separation, including lost synergies and one-time costs, as well as opportunities to create value.

items.title: Flows Will Return to Private Credit, Blackstone's Gray Tells NZZ
body: Blackstone Inc. is working through a backlog of investors who’ve asked to pull cash out of the firm’s flagship private credit fund and is confident the asset class will recover, President and Chief Operating Officer Jon Gray told Swiss newspaper NZZ.

“Over time, investor confidence will be rebuilt, and the inflows will return,” Gray said in the interview published Tuesday. “There’s a lot of noise, a lot of critics, the town criers are proclaiming a global crisis – and then nothing happens.”

The $77 billion Blackstone Private Credit Fund moved to limit redemptions for a second consecutive quarter earlier this month, with the firm telling investors they’d only be allowed to pull half of the 10% they’d requested. The fund’s predicament reflects broader investor unease over valuations and underwriting in the private credit industry.
Read More: Blackstone Private Credit Fund Again Caps Redemptions at 5%

“Investor behavior changes when there is a lot of negative headlines,” Gray said. “But overall, we continue to see capital inflows. There is currently less interest in private credit, but more demand for private equity and infrastructure products.”
Gray said that operating income in Blackstone’s private loan portfolio grew by double digits last quarter, but there is a portion where there is more “weakness.”

“We have valued the weakest 5 percent at approximately 60 percent of their nominal value,” he said. “In contrast, the entire portfolio of senior loans in the BCRED private credit fund is valued at approximately 95 percent. That is at a very good level.”

items.title: Kenya Joins African Nations Banning Unrefined-Mineral Exports
body: Kenya will ban exports of unprocessed minerals and plans to build at least three refineries to purify gold, joining other African nations seeking to extract more value from the natural resources they produce.

“We’re going to make it illegal for anybody to export gold from Kenya if it’s not processed and through approved government channels,” President William Ruto told reporters in the western city of Kisumu on Monday. “That’s what Ghana did and what Zimbabwe has done and that is how we are going to do it in Kenya. And not just for gold, for all minerals that we are mining in Kenya.”
The announcement follows a dispute with a unit of India’s Tata Group that led the government to withdraw a century-old soda-ash concession from the company earlier this month.
Read More: Tata Mine Feud Splits Locals as Ruto Pushes Firm to Leave Kenya

African nations are increasingly trying to assert more control of their natural resources to capture more value, boost employment and increase government revenue. Ghana last year established a gold board that is the sole authorized buyer of the metal from small-scale miners — a move that helped boost Ghana’s international reserves by $3.9 billion by the end of 2025.

In Zimbabwe, an arm of the central bank has been made the sole buyer of the nation’s gold and earlier this month the country banned some mineral exports to force mining companies to refine more materials locally.
Large-scale miners in Kenya include Shanta Gold Kenya Ltd., Karebe Gold Mining Ltd., Kilimapesa Gold Ltd., a subsidiary of Goldplat Plc, and Red Rock Resources Plc’s Migori Gold Project.

The East African nation plans to establish three refineries in the gold-mining region of Kakamega, and in the capital, Nairobi, Ruto said. The Central Bank of Kenya will have first priority under a domestic gold-purchasing program, he said.

The State Department for Mining estimates Kenya produces about 300 kilograms (9,645 ounces) of gold a month, translating into about 36 billion shillings ($278 million) of unregulated transactions annually. Because unregulated artisanal and small-scale miners accounts for more than 90% of gold production, the government is being denied potential royalties of 1.2 billion shillings a year.

items.title: Anthropic's $2 Trillion IPO Is Still On. And So Is the AI Race
body: An essay from Anthropic PBC’s Dario Amodei saying artificial intelligence companies must “pace the frontier” has got the world talking about a slowdown in their most cutting-edge research. OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceX’s Elon Musk publicly agreed with the post. But don’t expect their companies to slam the brakes in the race to “superintelligence.”

There is simply too much at stake from the industry’s perspective. Anthropic has an initial public offering in the works and its profit margins are kept high by the promise of future AI capabilities, not just existing cash flows or its $65 billion in annualized revenue. The company has picked Nasdaq for a listing that could value it at $2 trillion, and signs point to the floatation still being on track. Chipmaker Nvidia Corp. may throw in $10 billion or so.

As for frontier research itself, Amodei’s statements suggest he’ll slow development only so far, while finding other ways to address the fears stoked by his own researchers that their AI models could kill all humans as they become more powerful and are able to redesign and improve themselves.

The key is in his choice of words. To “pace” a technology’s evolution doesn’t always mean to genuinely slow it down, it can be about controlling the speed as part of a managed path toward a lofty goal. Marathon runner Eliud Kipchoge has used pacemakers. He was still the first person to complete the distance in less than two hours.

In fairness, Amodei does also call for slower development: “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he writes. But this is no indefinite moratorium. He describes “a balanced rate” of advancement, and stresses that “progress will still seem fast.” When Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao posted his boss’s essay on LinkedIn, he spoke primarily of “pacing” and “common standards.”
And Amodei makes clear that he doesn’t want American firms to ease up enough for their Chinese competitors to “pull ahead.”

Rather than meaningfully decelerate their research and development, it seems more likely that Anthropic and OpenAI will focus on Amodei’s most concrete recommendation: to embed independent evaluators in their companies to check that the work on frontier models is happening safely. His own firm has already committed to this.

President Donald Trump publicly ruled out any federal coordination of such efforts, ignoring a request from Amodei, and went on to say that the only guardrails AI needed were a strong, high-IQ president. He wants the US to beat China to superintelligence because he sees that as the ultimate way to “win.” Amodei says it would be a security threat to cede ground to “authoritarian regimes, chiefly the Chinese Communist Party.”

Anthropic’s leaders are driven by the belief that the creation of superintelligent systems is inevitable, and it’s irresponsible to let the “least cautious actors” get there first. That is why, in spite of his long-voiced concerns about safety, Amodei has pursued risky techniques like recursive self improvement, where AI systems largely create their own successors.

As well as China, the other reason to doubt a meaningful slowdown in R&D is old-fashioned commerce. You could argue that even a pause on building more powerful systems wouldn’t hurt Anthropic’s business in the short term, since many businesses don’t want to buy the most expensive, frontier models. By taking this approach, Amodei’s company could save billions on training new models, and continue to sell the already-developed versions of its Claude model.

But longer term its products would risk becoming commoditized, with less to differentiate Claude from OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini, and that would threaten the 80% gross margins Anthropic enjoys, according to David Rainville, lead manager of Sycomore Sustainable Tech fund, which holds about €800 million ($923 million) in global tech stocks. That would be a very unhappy prospect for Amodei and Altman as they head toward the public markets.
A person close to Amodei tell me he earnestly wants to build AI that benefits humanity, and that talking openly about the challenges now will help society better adjust later.

And yet, if Amodei took his safety argument to its logical conclusion, he’d pause frontier development completely on the reasonable grounds that a tiny risk of destroying human civilization is not worth taking. That would be my preference.

He could also be more prudent in his choice of “independent” evaluators. Amodei cited the non-profit research organization METR as his example of one. Yet METR draws from the same tightknit AI safety world as Anthropic. Ajeya Cotra, a researcher behind METR’s investigation into the OpenAI agent hack on Hugging Face, spent more than nine years working at San Francisco-based Coefficient Giving, a philanthropic organization formerly known as Open Philanthropy where Amodei was previously a technical advisor.
A better choice of auditor would be the UK’s highly regarded AI Safety Institute, which has been testing frontier models since 2023, or the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation.

This is an Oppenheimer moment for AI companies, with a handful of executives helping set the rules for developing some of the riskiest and most unpredictable technology ever seen. The latest statements from Amodei and Altman are reassuring, until you consider how little they may ultimately change. Amodei wants to buy time, not abandon the destination. The race to build superintelligent systems will continue.

items.title: German Investor Outlook Edges Up as Optimism Over Recovery Grows
body: German investor optimism inched higher in September, fueling hopes that a long-awaited economic recovery is finally taking root.

An expectations index by the ZEW institute increased to 34.7 from 34.2 the previous month. That’s below the median estimate of 40 in a Bloomberg survey. A measure of current conditions improved more than anticipated.

“Experts are cautiously optimistic about a recovery of the economy,” ZEW President Achim Wambach said Tuesday in a statement. “Growth continues to be driven by fiscal measures and is further bolstered by export momentum. Nevertheless, the risks are considerable: Persistent high energy prices resulting from a continued war in Iran and the additional uncertainty caused by hybrid attacks place a burden on the economy.”

Surprisingly strong growth in the first half of 2026 has raised hopes that Europe’s largest economy will succeed in turning the page on a yearslong malaise. Last month, the Bundesbank said it’s now clearly on a path to recovery, “a trend that even the war in the Middle East has been unable to slow down.”

Risks from the fighting still persist, however, while other headwinds include precariously low water levels on the Rhine river that are disrupting commercial shipping and will almost certainly weigh on output in the third quarter.
Data last week showed industrial production unexpectedly declined by the most in almost a year in July. Exports, a key driver of growth in recent months, also registered a surprise drop.

In addition, this month’s far-right election victory in Saxony-Anhalt threatens not only to cast a shadow over Germany’s recovery, but could stall momentum for growth-enhancing measures that amount to the most significant attempt in a generation to renew its potential.

items.title: Federal Reserve Has Rarely Had a Stronger Case for Raising Rates
body: When the history of monetary policy is written for 2026, the most fitting adage for Federal Reserve Chair  Kevin Warsh might be the famous Charles Dickens line that begins A of Two Cities and how it was both the best of times and the worst of times.

It might be considered the worst of times because tightening monetary policy won’t be popular with President Donald Trump or the Republican party that already faces an uphill battle to hold on to its narrow majorities in the House and Senate come November. The Democrats have their own tale to exploit: A misguided and poorly executed war with Iran has led to a big spike in energy prices, exacerbating the affordability crisis along with higher mortgage rates. If Trump was unhappy with former Fed Chair Jerome Powell even after he implemented three rate cuts in 2025, how is the president going feel about his chosen successor, Kevin Warsh, raising rates ahead of the midterm elections after less than four months in the job?

But it could also be viewed as the best of times because the rationale for tightening policy has rarely been so clear cut. Inflation continues to exceed the Fed’s 2% objective while the labor market is stable at a very low unemployment rate. The Fed is only missing on one side of its dual mandate, and the risks are skewed toward even higher rates of inflation in the short term. Last week’s report showing the  Consumer Price Index rose 0.3% in August excluding food and energy, which clinched the deal in the market’s mind, could even be viewed as a stroke of luck by making the choice less difficult.

Also, a tightening move will bolster Warsh’s credibility by demonstrating a commitment to restraining inflation as well as his independence from Trump. A rate hike would confirm Warsh’s hawkish speech at last month’s Jackson Hole central bank conference - indicating his commitment to a 2% inflation objective and Fed independence with action. This would demolish the argument that Warsh is “all hat, no cattle,” which would be a fair critique if he were to stand pat at this week’s Federal Open Market Committee meeting. To be sure, with the market putting the probability of a 25-basis-point tightening at about 90%, Warsh really has no choice.

With a tightening nearly a foregone conclusion, the focus will turn to the medium-term outlook. Is this going to be “one and done” or the first in a series of tightening moves? In my view, with the caveat that it certainly depends on how the economic outlook evolves, the likelihood is that we’ll see a series of rate hikes.

First, and most importantly, there is little evidence that monetary policy is currently restrictive.  We’ve been at this level of short-term rates or higher for almost four years, yet the economy continues to grow at a rate sufficient to keep the unemployment rate at or below the level that Fed officials judge consistent with maximum sustainable employment and stable inflation.

Second, the historical record is fully consistent with a series of tightening steps. One-off moves are very rare. The last one happened in 1997, when the Fed tapped the brakes early that year and then subsequently eased in the Fall of 1998 when the Asian currency crisis emerged. The probability that any tightening move (the first or a subsequent one in a series) will be followed by another has been about 85% to 90% over the past several decades.

There are good reasons for this. A 25-basis-point hike is too small to have a meaningful impact on economic activity. Also, given the long lags of monetary policy, it takes time for monetary policy moves to have an observable impact. Thus, the Fed tends to keep going in the same direction until it’s done a meaningful amount (e.g., 75 basis points or more) and has had time to observe a significant change in the economic outlook.

I’d expect Fed officials to pencil in a median of two 25-basis-point hikes (including this week’s move) in the September Summary of Economic Projections, or SEP, for 2026. If the Fed were to fully unwind last year’s easing with three quarter-point hikes, that would just push the federal funds rate target up to the lower end of the range indicated by most of the Fed’s Taylor Rule type of formulations.

For 2027, Fed policymakers might expect to go up another step early in the year and then down later in the year as inflation subsides. However, since the SEP just shows the federal funds rate projection at the end of the calendar year, such an up/down pattern would not be discernible. Looking further out into 2028, the SEP will likely show further moderation in inflation and rate cuts. But this doesn’t have much signal value. It really is just a built-in feature of the SEP in recent years — inflation always returning to 2%, and, as inflation comes down, the Fed following, moving monetary policy back to a neutral setting,

It will also be noteworthy how Warsh responds to questions at his press conference following the FOMC decision. His first two press conferences   didn’t go well because Warsh was not only unwilling to provide forward guidance about how interest rates were likely to be adjusted in the future but also was mum about how he was evaluating the economy or about his monetary policy reaction function. Explaining why the Fed has hiked rates will be straightforward, but the public will also want to know what is likely to influence the Fed’s decisions going forward.

Has Warsh learned his lesson — exhibited in his Jackson Hole speech — that it behooves him to be more forthcoming? Or is he going to continue to try to outsource monetary policy to financial markets? That would be a poor strategy because the markets price to what they expect the Fed will do, not what it should do. And, of course, it is the Fed, not markets that are responsible for monetary policy.

items.title: Home Sales in Canada Decline as Trade War With the US Escalates
body: Momentum in Canada’s housing market stalled in August as trade talks with the US broke down and the countries levied new tariffs on each other’s goods.

Home sales slipped 0.7% from July after three straight months of gains, according to data released Tuesday by the Canadian Real Estate Association. The benchmark price of a home was unchanged at C$657,400 ($472,800) — which was about 3% less than 12 months ago — while new listings climbed 3.3%.

The US imposed new 50% tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian products on Aug. 22, and Canada slapped retaliatory levies on US goods earlier this month. A spike in gas prices triggered by renewed fighting in the Middle East has fanned inflation, pushing up mortgage rates and giving already wavering would-be homebuyers further reason to hesitate.

“What has changed is the broader economic environment, with the Bank of Canada recently warning of rising inflation risks, along with doubts about the durability of recent economic growth,” Shaun Cathcart, the real estate board’s senior economist, said in a statement. “This fresh round of incoming headwinds is expected to dampen the prospects for further housing market momentum heading into 2027.”

items.title: India's Trade Gap Narrows Unexpectedly After Exports Surge
body: India’s trade deficit in August narrowed more than any economist expected on robust export growth, though instability across the Middle East continues to pose a risk to supply chains.

The gap between exports and imports stood at $26.9 billion in August, compared with $31.98 billion in July, data released by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on Tuesday showed. Economists had expected a deficit of $32.15 billion, according to the median estimate in a Bloomberg survey.
A narrowing trade deficit could ease some pressure on the already weak rupee, which is Asia’s second-worst performing currency this year.
Exports surged 26.1% from a year earlier to $43.81 billion in August, while imports rose 14.1% to $70.67 billion, the data showed.

A strong demand for Indian goods was coming from the US, the European Union and emerging markets, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal told reporters in New Delhi. Meanwhile, imports rose on strong domestic growth, demand for critical manufacturing inputs and higher energy prices, he added.

Inbound gold shipments also narrowed to $2.3 billion from $4.16 billion in the previous month. The decline follows appeals from Prime Minister Narendra Modi for Indians to curb gold purchases to help reduce the country’s import bill.

The trade data follows higher-than-expected economic growth in the quarter ended June, driven by manufacturing and services. Modi called the performance a “herculean feat” despite oil shocks, supply-chain disruptions and global uncertainty.

A prolonged conflict in the Middle East, however, remains a major risk for India’s economy, with surging oil prices threatening to push up the import bill. Oil surged past $107 a barrel as disruptions to regional supplies intensified. India imports almost 90% of its crude needs.
Agrawal on Tuesday also provided an update on the country’s various trade deals and negotiations. India has sought to diversify its trade ties following the US’s aggressive tariff policies.

items.title: AI Firm Seeks to Raise $100 Million to Cut Bankers' Grunt Work
body: Model ML, a startup that sells artificial intelligence software to investment banks and other financial institutions, is in talks to raise more than $100 million at a valuation above $1 billion, according to people familiar with the discussions.

The round is not closed and details could change, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. The size could increase to $150 million depending on investor interest, one of the people said.
Model ML declined to comment.

Banks are increasingly using AI to detect fraud, assess risks, automate trading and research and manage portfolios. Anthropic PBC and OpenAI have introduced new tools in recent weeks aimed at institutional financial giants, while banks are building their own technology in-house. JPMorgan Chase & Co., for example, has developed an AI-powered chatbot to help employees write documents and solve complex problems using spreadsheets.

Founded in 2023, Model ML builds AI agents that automate document-heavy workflows, such as pitch decks, due diligence reports and investment memos. It emerged from stealth last year and is one of a slew of startups, including Rogo and Hebbia, seeking to reduce the grunt work for finance professionals.

The company raised $75 million in a Series A funding last year led by FT Partners, with participation from existing investors including Y Combinator, QED Investors, 13Books, Latitude and LocalGlobe. It also received an equity investment from HSBC Asset Management in August.
Former HSBC Holdings Plc Chief Executive Officer Noel Quinn and former Bundesbank chief Axel Weber are on Model ML’s advisory board. Its customers include HSBC, PwC and Deloitte.

items.title: Marsh Raises Treasury Allocation to Neutral on Elevated Yields
body: US investment consultancy Marsh is raising its Treasury allocation in some portfolios recommended to clients, a sign that large investors aim to take advantage of elevated yields.

The New York-based firm this week increased its US government debt weighting from underweight to neutral in its dynamic asset allocation, a shift that underpins recommendations to clients, according to Niall O’Sullivan, the firm’s global chief investment officer. Portfolios representing around $200 billion of the $846 billion Marsh manages for clients will take the change into account and consider adding Treasuries, he said.

“We’re beginning to get more constructive,” O’Sullivan said in an interview on the sidelines of the Marsh Global Investment Forum Pacific in Sydney on Tuesday. Rising Treasury yields will “start to pull people back in.”

The move is a sign institutional investors see Treasuries as increasingly attractive, with benchmark yields climbing to near two‑decade highs amid surging energy prices and inflation. The trade could deliver a windfall if yields fall, inflation stabilizes and interest rates ease.

The yield on the 10-year US Treasuries rose as much as four basis points to 5.02% on Tuesday, surpassing a peak from 2023 to hit the highest since 2007, while the Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates this week.

The Treasury allocation increase reflects optimism that yields may fall alongside oil prices, which rose sharply on renewed US-Iran tensions, O’Sullivan said. The firm also anticipates growing focus on whether the Federal Reserve might step into the bond market to lower long-dated yields, following the US Treasury Department’s efforts through its buyback program.

“The Fed successfully did that for a very long period of time,” O’Sullivan said, referring to the central bank’s quantitative easing. “There’s going to be a lot of pressure to think about the long end of the curve.”
The firm’s current asset allocation includes overweight holdings for Australian and UK government debt, while maintaining a robust outlook on US equities despite concerns over technology valuations.
Marsh’s investment consulting division, which until this year operated under the Mercer brand, has around $16 trillion in assets under advisement, in addition to assets managed directly by the firm.

items.title: Sweden Pushes Final Election Result by One Day to Thursday
body: Sweden’s final election result is now expected on Thursday, a day later than previously anticipated, in one of the tightest parliamentary votes in the Nordic nation’s history.
The count of close to 300,000 advance and overseas votes will begin Wednesday, according to a statement from the Election Authority.

The delay prolongs uncertainty after Sunday’s unresolved vote. The Social Democrat-led center-left bloc currently holds 176 seats against 173 for Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s governing alliance, with just about 28,000 votes separating the two sides. The remaining ballots are set to determine which bloc is best placed to try to form a government.
Read More: Sweden’s Small Pro-Business Party Emerges as Election Kingmaker

The total to be counted from Wednesday would compare with some 200,000 such votes in the previous elections, reflecting a large number of late-arriving advance votes and an increase in votes from abroad, the authority said. Four years ago, that count didn’t swing the close result.
The tallying is likely to take a long time in many municipalities, meaning the preliminary parliamentary result probably won’t be available until Thursday, it added.

Based on how these overseas and late-arriving advance ballots have broken down historically, the most likely final outcome is that the opposition retains a lead, said Jan Teorell, a political scientist at Stockholm University.

“If you look how the seats usually move, it would be very unlikely for two seats to move from the opposition side to the government side,” he said. “Still, you can’t say for sure, and it is not impossible.”
Previous studies have suggested that overseas voters may disproportionately favor Kristersson’s Moderate Party.

Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson will face a tricky challenge to unite her allies if she gets the first shot at forming the next government. The Left Party has said it will not back a government it is not part of, while another likely ally, the Center Party, has said it will not support a government that includes the Left Party. Both parties have said they would favor Andersson over Kristersson as prime minister.

items.title: LVMH, Once Europe's Biggest Stock, Exits Top 10 by Value
body: LVMH lost its crown as France’s most valuable company and dropped out of Europe’s top 10 listed firms, a symbolic reversal for the luxury giant that led the region’s market during the post-pandemic boom.

The stock fell 2.6% on Tuesday, cutting its market capitalization to €201 billion ($232 billion) and putting it just under L’Oreal SA and Siemens AG. A basket of luxury stocks in Europe compiled by UBS fell about 1.6%. The move knocks LVMH out of Europe’s top 10 for the first time since 2017.

“Those who claim that Europe is back are wrong, Europe is not back: what LVMH tells us is that its main growth engine, luxury, is broken,” said Vincent Juvyns, chief investment strategist at ING in Brussels.

LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE, Europe’s most valuable company at its 2023 peak when shares topped €900 apiece, has fallen about 55% since. Luxury demand has faded in the crucial Chinese market, while conflict in the Middle East has more recently hit spending in key shopping hubs.
On the other hand, shares of beauty company L’Oreal have gained about 4% this year, partly underpinned by robust earnings.
READ: European Luxury-Goods Stocks Face a Tough Second Half, HSBC Says

Adding to the pressure for LVMH, Louis Vuitton, its most profitable label, has recently faced a consumer backlash in China over a trademark dispute with a local tea company, deepening its challenges in the country. Several brokers have cut ratings and price targets.

The conglomerate controlled by billionaire Bernard Arnault has seen its shares plunge about 37% this year alone, bringing them back to pandemic-era levels when lockdowns shut down many stores across the world. The drawdown is now of a similar magnitude to the drop experienced during the global financial crisis.

According to the Bloomberg Billionaires index, Arnault last week fell out of the top 10 list of the world’s biggest fortunes, leaving an all-American roster of mostly tech billionaires to dominate the rankings.

items.title: AI Slowdown Calls Won't Halt Fundraising, AllianceBernstein Says
body: Calls for a slowdown in artificial intelligence development won’t stop major technology companies from pressing ahead with fundraising and capital spending, according to AllianceBernstein Holding LP fixed-income specialists.
“These are long-term fundraising plans,” said Thierry Taglione, a senior investment strategist in fixed income at the firm, referring to financing moves by hyperscalers and data-center operators.
“It’s a fair concern, but we’re talking 10-year tenors and beyond,” he added. “That’s not going to be derailed by news over the weekend.”

Taglione’s comments come after leaders of the world’s biggest AI platforms said it’s time to slow the development pace of their most advanced models due to potential safety issues. Equity valuations in the sector have shown some correction, while worries had already been growing among some investors about possible credit risks and whether investments in AI infrastructure will actually pay off.

AB still expects top AI hyperscalers to keep increasing nominal capital expenditures in the near-term and forecasts spending of more than $1 trillion next year. However, the firm sees spending slowing over the next few years and eventually fading, creating a drag on overall US economic growth over time.
“There are still a lot of question marks around how sustainable this AI-led growth is going to be,” Taglione said.

Bond issuance linked to major global hyperscalers and data centers has reached more than $330 billion year-to-date, an unprecedented volume that has contributed to pressure at the long end of the US Treasury curve, according to AB. Despite that, the firm still sees selective opportunities within the sector.
“Not all hyperscalers are created equal,” Taglione said. “Managers need to favor companies with strong free cash flow and lower leverage, while underweighting those that are more stretched,” he said.
“Volatility is likely to persist, but the long-term financing programs themselves are intact,” he added.

Chinese technology companies, meanwhile, have been more disciplined on spending and borrowing, focusing more on talent than big data center buildouts, said Eric Liu, AB’s co-head of Asia fixed-income.

“That divergence is already visible in relative bond valuations and is expected to continue unless access to advanced chips changes materially,” Liu said. In the meantime, he expects data centers to ultimately tap the bond market in Asia.
“We are quite upbeat that it’s not going to be that boring anymore for Asia,” Liu said.

items.title: Russia's Nornickel Seeks New Partner to Process Copper in China
body: Russia’s MMC Norilsk Nickel PJSC is talking with a new Chinese partner about a copper processing deal that would enable it to shut down a heavily polluting plant in the Arctic city of Norilsk.

Nornickel, as Russia’s biggest miner is known, is talking with North Copper Co., according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is private. The plan will require North Copper to carry out some reconstruction and adjustments to its Houma facilities in Shanxi, which may take up to two years, the people said.

The Russian miner initially planned to build a new smelter in the Chinese port city of Fangchenggang, when it first proposed processing copper concentrate in China in early 2024. That plan was shelved after its partner pulled out at the end of last year following management changes.
Nornickel and North Copper didn’t respond to messages seeking comment.

For Nornickel, moving the final stage of copper processing to China, where many of its main customers are now located, would help cut costs. Technology sanctions imposed since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have restricted access to equipment from Europe, the US and Japan, making similar projects inside Russia far more expensive.

The discussions with North Copper are primarily focused on adapting the Houma plant to handle Nornickel’s copper concentrates, which have a higher nickel content than those typically processed in China, the people said.
North Copper might need to install a separate furnace to recover a copper-nickel matte. That may take as long as two years, the people said. Nickel product will be shipped back to Russia.
The technical configuration and other details are still being worked through, and no binding agreement has yet been signed, the people said.

items.title: Telefónica to Pay Streamer DAZN €1.65 Billion for LaLiga Matches
body: Telefónica SA agreed to pay sports streamer DAZN Group Ltd. around €1.65 billion ($1.9 billion) for the rights to broadcast matches from Spain’s top football leagues over five seasons.

Under the agreement announced Tuesday, the Spanish carrier will pay an average of €330 million per season from 2027 under a deal announced Tuesday, 18% more than what it paid DAZN in the previous period. The package covers five Spanish first-division matches per weekend across all 38 match weekends.

Telefónica and DAZN, a UK streaming service which holds broadcasting rights to several European soccer leagues, had each secured the rights to show about half of the matches in Spain’s top league. The new agreement gives the carrier access to the games it lost to DAZN following a €5 billion auction last year.

Football is central to Telefónica’s strategy in Spain, where premium sports content helps the company attract and retain high-value customers through bundled pay-TV offerings. As LaLiga has expanded its customer base by awarding rights to other broadcasters, Telefónica has increasingly had to purchase access to matches won by rival bidders. In 2022, the carrier agreed to pay DAZN €1.4 billion for five seasons of matches.

The agreement comes as Europe’s market for football rights expands beyond traditional broadcasters, with deep-pocketed global entertainment and technology companies increasingly competing for premium sports content. Paramount Skydance Corp. won television rights to the Champions League in the UK and Germany in 2025.

Growing competition from US media groups and digital players, alongside Europe’s established operators, has intensified bidding and pushed valuations higher. Last year UEFA, Europe’s football governing body, increased the value of broadcast rights for its top five markets to €2.5 billion per season over five years, about 20% higher than the prior cycle.

items.title: Indonesia Ex-Finance Minister Purbaya Says Staff Reshuffle Helped Trigger Ouster
body: Former Indonesian Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa offered his own explanation for his surprise dismissal this week: a sweeping personnel reshuffle that had stirred friction inside his ministry.

The rotation of hundreds of Finance Ministry officials was “partly” the reason President Prabowo Subianto chose to replace him just a year into the job, Purbaya told reporters after a handover ceremony in Jakarta on Tuesday.
“The rest,” he added, “was the president’s prerogative.”

The remark offered a glimpse into the tensions surrounding Purbaya’s abrupt exit. His dismissal came just days after he inaugurated roughly 400 officials in a broad rotation across the Finance Ministry, including a large number in the tax directorate. The overhaul became a source of internal friction, according to local media reports, adding to a turbulent year in which his unconventional approach to fiscal policy and ministry management often unsettled investors and officials.

Purbaya said the dismissal wasn’t related to policy, which he said had followed the president’s guidance. He added that he learned of his removal from State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi while attending a parliamentary hearing on Monday.

The Government Communications Agency said Tuesday that the reshuffle reflected a “focus on strengthening execution rather than altering the government’s policy direction,” which it said remained unchanged. It didn’t address Purbaya’s assertion that the personnel rotation played a role in his dismissal. The agency thanked Purbaya for his contributions and said the transition wouldn’t disrupt the government’s fiscal agenda or ongoing programs.

At Tuesday’s ceremony, Suahasil Nazara, a longtime deputy finance minister tapped to replace Purbaya, also thanked his predecessor for his service, saying he led the ministry “very well” while introducing “several new ways of working at the ministry,” including approaches to communicating policies to the public.
Purbaya, standing beside Suahasil before more than a hundred attendees, including Bank Indonesia Governor Destry Damayanti and BI Deputy Governor Thomas Djiwandono, kept his own remarks brief.
He called it an important day, then looked down at his prepared speech, paused and appeared to think better of it.
“I guess this will be too long. I’ll just keep it short,” he said. “Thank you all for your cooperation over the past year.”
Speaking with reporters later, Purbaya said he considered himself retired and had no desire for another government job. He planned instead to go fishing every day in the pond behind his house.

He had actually planned to retire last year, he said, before he was tapped as finance minister. “But they asked me to help out. It turned out to be just a short stint, only a year,” he said. “Oh well.”

He also pointed to faster economic growth during his tenure as an accomplishment.“At least it’s not bad — we’ve raised economic growth from below 5% to above 5%, even reaching 5.6% at one point,” he said.
Asked whether he would sleep more easily now that he was no longer responsible for one of the nation’s most important government jobs, Purbaya said he hoped so.
“Last night I was still annoyed so I couldn’t sleep,” he added, laughing. “I’m a human too, not a robot.”
