items.title: Thailand's Vice Finance Minister Says Investment Surging as Stability Returns
body: Thailand, once rocked by years of coups and court-ordered dismissals of prime ministers, is seeing a surge in foreign investment as political stability and policy continuity return, according to Vice Finance Minister Santitarn Sathirathai.

Board of Investment data show inward investment rose about 30% in the second quarter after increasing more than 20% in the first, Santitarn said. BOI-backed projects now account for roughly 30% of total investment in Thailand.

Santitarn, who worked at Credit Suisse from 2010 to 2018, rising to head its emerging Asia economics team, said conversations with multinational companies, investors and credit-rating firms over the past four months have shown a marked shift in perception of one of Southeast Asia’s largest economies.

“I don’t remember the last time that we got this much interest internationally,” Santitarn said in an interview with Bloomberg News Monday. The last comparable period, he said, was during his years at Credit Suisse, when Thailand routinely “popped up really high” in conversations about Asian investment. Today, investors increasingly describe Thailand as “better than I expected,” he said.

At home, the February re-election of conservative Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has given investors greater confidence in the government’s direction and ability to execute. Abroad, trade tensions, the Iran War and ongoing US-China rivalry are pushing companies to diversify supply chains and put a greater premium on stability.

That shift is playing to some of Thailand’s longstanding strengths. While other economies grapple with surging prices, currency volatility and higher interest rates, Thailand has relatively low inflation, strong external finances and accommodative monetary policy.

The baht’s 5.3% decline this year is less than that of Indonesia’s rupiah or the Philippine peso, though Santitarn said the currency’s recent weakening could support Thailand’s economy and competitiveness. Stocks have also been gaining.

“Macro stability, which normally may be something quite boring, now is something important that people cannot take for granted,” Santitarn said. “All of a sudden you have policy continuity. You have macro stability, which has become more scarce globally.”

Santitarn and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas want to lift total investment to 30% of gross domestic product from about 22%-23%, where it has stagnated for years. This year, Thailand has greenlit multiple projects in a variety of sectors from the likes of Nestle SA, Japan’s Datasection Inc., Doosan Electro-Materials Co., Taiwan Union Technology Co. and Fulltech Fiber Glass Corp.

Santitarn acknowledged that renewed protests and political tensions could test the country’s new-found stability. Anutin’s two predecessors were both dismissed by the country’s Constitutional Court, and the country has seen two coups this century. But Santitarn said the government is seeking to insulate its economic agenda from political swings by setting priorities jointly with businesses, allowing them to endure even if the government changes.

“Once you set these directions together with the private sector, even if the government changed, the private sector is still the same,” he said, citing priorities including quality tourism, future mobility and the digital economy.

Thailand doesn’t necessarily have to beat faster-growing neighbors such as Vietnam for every investment. Companies increasingly want production spread across multiple countries rather than concentrated in the cheapest or fastest-growing market, he said.
“You don’t want to put all the eggs in one basket,” Santitarn said. “You still want a diversification play within Asean too. And I think that’s where Thailand looks interesting.”

The challenge is turning that renewed attention into investment and ultimately faster economic growth. Thailand has struggled for years with economic growth of around 2%, a fraction of the blistering pace of Vietnam.

Investment applications through the Board of Investment surged to a record last year and are on track to surpass that this year. The government is now shifting its focus from pledges to projects on the ground, tracking investment realization and working with companies to resolve bottlenecks involving land, water, infrastructure and permits.

With private businesses accounting for roughly three-quarters of investment, the government is seeking to use public infrastructure to crowd in private capital. Officials are also changing how they measure success, with the BOI putting greater emphasis on whether investments create skilled jobs, develop Thai suppliers, transfer technology and support research.

The aim is to capture more of the benefits from investment flowing into artificial intelligence, data centers, electric vehicles, health and clean energy while upgrading Thailand’s established strengths in manufacturing, food and tourism.
Read More: Thailand Eyes $600 Million Tourism Boost With Travel Subsidies

Santitarn likens Thailand’s traditional growth engines to ageing trains that have served the economy well but need upgrading. The country needs to board new high-speed trains led by AI, the digital economy, health and the green transition.
“We’ve been missing trains here and there,” he said, referring to years of disappointing growth. “This is it. This is a chance. The trains are here.”

items.title: Hegseth, Pistorius Ink Deal For Firms to License US Missiles
body: German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and his US counterpart Pete Hegseth discussed how defense companies can deepen transatlantic cooperation and boost weapons production as both sides look to fill low stocks of air defense missiles and deep strike weapons.

During bilateral talks in Washington on Tuesday, Pistorius and Hegseth signed a political agreement designed to deepen cooperation between defense manufacturers so that European companies can produce certain US weapon systems via licensing and vice versa.

“If we pool our strengths even more closely, we can deliver the systems that we and our NATO partners urgently need for deterrence and defense more quickly and in greater numbers,” Pistorius said in a statement before his meeting with Hegseth. “In this way, we are strengthening the readiness of Germany, the United States, and the entire alliance.”

Pistorius pointed to existing company agreements that enable the manufacturing in Germany of fuselage sections for the US-made F-35 fighter jet and the PAC-2 guided missiles for the Patriot air defense system.

Additional projects under discussion include collaborations on Army Tactical Missile System, or ATACM, projectiles, Stinger surface-to-air missiles and Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air missiles, known by the acronym AMRAAM, the German defense ministry said in a statement after the talks.

In unusually warm words, Hegseth — who has frequently slammed NATO allies over the Iran war and defense spending — lauded Germany’s increased defense outlays. He also thanked Pistorius for taking a leading role in NATO’s new burden sharing.
“Defense spending is just the first step,” Hegseth said, adding that Germany needed to put its “very large and historic industrial base to work for the common defense.”
Hegseth said the US-Germany deal the two ministers signed would “significantly intensify our bilateral defense industrial cooperation.”

German officials are pushing US counterparts to also enable the production of the more advanced PAC-3 interceptor, as well as Tomahawk cruise missiles, in Europe. But so far, US manufacturers Lockheed Martin Corp. and RTX Corp.’s Raytheon have shown little interest in granting those licenses to European firms.
Read more: Germany Will Buy US Tomahawk Missiles to Close Crucial Gap

Earlier this year, Germany agreed to purchase the long-range, subsonic Tomahawk cruise missiles to close a dangerous gap with Russia. But numbers and delivery dates remain subject to negotiations, while European governments rush to develop their own deep precision strike missiles.
The US startup Covenant earlier this month revealed plans for the mass production of its heavy-payload Anthem long-range cruise missiles in a new factory near Leipzig in eastern Germany.
Read More: Trump Will Ask US Companies to Make Missiles in Europe

Germany, Britain and France are separately in talks to develop and produce precision deep-strike weapons as they aim to deter Russia from using its Iskander missiles against Berlin and other European capitals.
“Germany has a strong industrial base, highly trained skilled workers, and cutting-edge technological expertise. This enables us to create additional production capacity,” Pistorius said.

The German minister also discussed the future of transatlantic cooperation within North Atlantic Treaty Organization, whose member states President Donald Trump has assailed for not spending enough on defense.

“I will discuss with our American partners how we can lead NATO into a new phase — with a stronger Europe within a strong transatlantic alliance,” Pistorius said. He added that Berlin was “investing resolutely” in its armed forces and is currently “making the second-largest contribution to our joint defense efforts within NATO after the US.”
Read more: Covenant Plans Mass Production of Cruise Missiles in Germany

In July, Pistorius pushed back against calls by Trump that NATO allies should be unconditionally loyal to Washington. NATO was not about blind obedience, Pistorius said at the time, adding that decisions within NATO were taken by free consensus without being dictated by individual member states.
The US had floated the idea of granting political and economic benefits to NATO allies that spend more on defense, raising the prospect of a two-tier alliance.

items.title: Joshua Wong's Freedom Means More Than Cheap Chinese Cars
body: Joshua Wong became a global celebrity as a teenage protest leader in Hong Kong, appearing on the cover of Time magazine, serving as the subject of an award-winning documentary distributed by Netflix and being nominated multiple times for the Nobel Peace Prize. He will spend his 30th birthday in prison next month and faces many more years of incarceration after pleading guilty to a foreign collusion charge in a national security case on Sept. 2. These are lonely days for the city’s jailed activists. The democratic world has a duty not to forget them.

Wong was imprisoned for his role in the city’s vast 2019 pro-democracy demonstrations, as well as his participation the following year in an unofficial primary election that authorities deemed subversive. The protests, which sometimes turned violent, prompted China to impose a national security law on Hong Kong that has been used to criminalize peaceful political dissent. Last week, three organizers of an annual vigil marking the 1989 Tiananmen massacre were sentenced to terms of between five and seven years for inciting subversion. Wong, who has been behind bars for six years, is the only person to be prosecuted twice under the law. A four-year delay in bringing the second case looked calculated to prolong his sentence and keep him in prison beyond his expected 2027 release date.

Wong wasn’t an architect of the 2019 movement. He rose to international prominence as a 17-year-old leader of Occupy Central, a civil-disobedience campaign that blocked city-center roads for several months in 2014. His youth and eloquence made him a potent symbol of the Hong Kong people’s struggle for the democracy they were promised when the former British colony returned to China in 1997. That profile gave him a platform to lobby for overseas support and diplomatic pressure when protests flared again in 2019. The hope of the democracy camp was that global visibility would act as a shield and stay Beijing’s hand. The irony is that this outreach was turned against him. Such advocacy would usually be regarded as legitimate political expression in a liberal democracy; the Chinese security law made it a crime.

Hong Kong’s fight for democracy captured the world’s imagination during the turmoil of 2019. David and Goliath stories have an inherent appeal — and no one embodied that more than Wong, the skinny and bespectacled teenager who confronted Beijing with a clarity and fearlessness that the older generation mostly couldn’t muster. Western politicians from the US to Germany to the UK lionized him and helped elevate him into a global icon. The democratic world owes Wong and his fellow activists its support. But geopolitics has changed radically since 2019 and attention moves on quickly. Just keeping his case in the public consciousness is a challenge.

“It’s really fallen off a cliff,” Andrew Duncan, who produced the 2017 documentary Joshua: Teenager vs Superpower, told me. The US film producer and human-rights activist was in London this month to raise awareness of the case. “It’s time for him to get back on people’s radar screen,’’ he said. “And it’s time for him, more importantly, to get released.”

In Duncan’s view, Britain has a particular responsibility because Wong, although not a UK passport holder, was born in Hong Kong in 1996 when it was still a British-ruled territory. (That hasn’t helped jailed media proprietor Jimmy Lai, who is a British passport holder and whose release the UK hasn’t been able to secure.) Duncan wants to see government action: He points to the number of BYD Co. and other Chinese cars on British roads, suggesting this is a point of leverage, especially given the potential for that open-market access to cause trade frictions with the US.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told parliament on Sept. 1 he would take up Wong’s case, in response to a question from former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith, a China hawk who has been a consistent defender of the rights of Hongkongers. Perhaps Miliband’s pledge will mean something, though Britain has recently appeared keener on repairing business relations than imposing costs on China for dismantling Hong Kong’s freedoms.

Rewatching Joshua: Teenager vs Superpower was a painful experience for me. It’s a portrait of a Hong Kong that has vanished in less than a decade: There is so much youthful idealism on display. Wong first appeared on our television screens (I lived in Hong Kong for 25 years) in the early 2010s, after co-founding, at 14, a student group called Scholarism to oppose the government’s plan to impose compulsory “national education” in schools. A Christian and the son of Lutheran parents, he was clearly an exceptional individual, as composed when facing a row of media microphones as he was fiery when addressing a crowd.

Under the terms of the 1997 handover, Hong Kong was told that its “way of life” would be kept unchanged for 50 years. Being taught to revere China’s Communist Party, which even today has no formal status within the territory, was never part of that life. A teaching manual for the proposed curriculum declared that the party was an “advanced, selfless and united ruling group,” omitted reference to Tiananmen or other human-rights abuses and described Western democracy as “fierce inter-party rivalry that makes the people suffer.”

Scholarism scored a stunning victory over this attempted indoctrination when tens of thousands of young people rallied at government headquarters in September 2012 and the city’s then-leader retreated on the plan. Wong was 15. In retrospect, it was a dangerous success. Emboldened, the group turned its attention to something else promised in the Basic Law (Hong Kong’s constitution, in effect): election of the city’s leader by universal suffrage. But this time it was taking on not just the Hong Kong government, which had traditionally shown itself responsive to the public will, but the Communist Party itself.

Herein lies the core of Hong Kong’s tragedy, which with hindsight can be seen clearly in the Joshua Wong documentary: the incompatible marriage of liberal-democratic freedoms with an authoritarian sovereign. The activist tools that the high-school students took up were part of Hong Kong’s social traditions. Britain never gave the city the right to elect its leader, but it had the superstructure of a democratic society: marches and demonstrations, a free and competitive media, a pluralist political culture with opposition parties and so on.

In such a society, it is natural and legitimate to protest in pursuit of one’s aims. But to a security-focused, one-party state, any autonomous organized network capable of mobilizing large crowds is likely to look more like an attempted color revolution, probably instigated or fomented by foreign actors. This is exactly the party’s view of the 2019 protests, which is a calumny on the intelligence and independent-mindedness of Hong Kong’s young people. Chinese state media has for years branded Wong as an anti-China separatist, traitor and pawn of hostile foreign forces.

The twain will probably never meet. It only remains for us to decide how to respond. The liberal-democratic world has lost confidence in itself in recent years, assailed by the rise of authoritarian populists, perturbed by weak economic growth and intimidated by the growing power of China. That’s no excuse for fatalism. Are we willing to sell our principles for some cheap cars when braver people who were taught our values and acted to defend them languish in prison? I hope not.

items.title: CATL Gets Approval for Battery Deal in Consolidation Push
body: Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. has been cleared to acquire a stake in a battery firm linked to one of China’s largest carmakers, highlighting Beijing’s growing support for consolidation in the sector.

CATL is taking an undisclosed stake in Chongqing Yaoning New Energy Technology Co., a company backed by Geely Automobile Holdings Ltd. that’s currently building a battery plant. Approval for the deal was confirmed in a recent statement by China’s State Administration for Market Regulation.

The green light signals China’s backing for consolidation efforts that are emerging in the country’s fast-growing battery sector, where years of expansion have been driven by the adoption of electric vehicles and a more recent boom in energy-storage facilities.

As competition grows, however, Beijing is trying to ensure that the industry avoids the fate of China’s solar industry, which dominates global manufacturing but has seen its top companies lose billions of dollars after a rapid build-out of factories outpaced growth in demand.

The approval of CATL’s acquisition “signals the government’s intention to promote consolidation,” said Vincent Sun, an analyst at Morningstar Inc. The absorption by major players of stakes in automaker-backed battery units “could prevent redundant expansion and accelerates efficiency,” he said.

However, CATL’s share price dropped 6.2% in Shenzhen, with investor sentiment hit by unverified posts circulating on social media that it may cut production plans and reduce profit forecasts. The company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

At least twice this year, Beijing has warned the country’s leading battery makers to restrict capacity expansion and avoid the destructive price wars that have damaged solar and other renewable-energy industries in the past. China has also suspended construction of new projects to make power and energy-storage batteries pending a year-end review of capacity, local news outlet Caixin reported.
“Consolidation and a ban on new production facilities are two great tools in fighting oversupply,” said Leonid Mironov, portfolio manager at Gavekal Capital Ltd.

items.title: South Korea Finance Chief Nominee Says Economy at Turning Point
body: South Korea’s finance minister nominee said the economy is at a turning point, with an artificial-intelligence-fueled semiconductor boom creating new opportunities even as shifts in the chip cycle, global interest rates and geopolitical tensions pose risks.

Lee Hyoung Il told lawmakers at his confirmation hearing Tuesday that the economy’s recovery is gaining momentum as strong AI demand boosts chip exports and investment. Growth of 3% this year is now within reach, while per capita income is expected to rise into the $40,000 range, he said.

Still, he warned against complacency, saying South Korea must use the upswing to develop new growth engines and make the economy more resilient to uncertainties in global trade and geopolitical risks, including the war in the Middle East.
“Rather than rest on the opportunities before us, we must prepare for the threats ahead,” he said in prepared opening remarks.

Lee, 55, was nominated to become South Korea’s next finance minister after President Lee Jae Myung abruptly replaced his predecessor in a sweeping cabinet reshuffle seen as an effort to regain control of his policy agenda amid falling approval ratings.

The finance minister nominee said his priorities would include easing cost-of-living pressures, improving employment and incomes and ensuring the benefits of growth are shared more evenly across industries, regions and generations. He pledged efforts to stabilize agricultural, livestock and fuel prices while addressing structural sources of inflation by improving distribution systems.

On financial markets, Lee vowed to build on South Korea’s inclusion in the FTSE Russell’s World Government Bond Index by pursuing developed-market status from MSCI Inc. and continuing efforts to internationalize the won. He also called supply-chain security “a fight for survival,” promising to expand strategic reserves and diversify import sources.

“My economic philosophy is clear,” Lee said. “I believe we should uphold the principles of a market economy that encourages creativity and dynamism, while the government should also play an active role in protecting vulnerable groups and supporting people’s livelihoods.”

items.title: China's Aluminum Output Hits Record as Government Cap Looms
body: Chinese aluminum production climbed to a record last month as smelters rushed to fill the global shortfall caused by the conflict in the Middle East.

Output climbed 4.7% year-on-year to just shy of 4 million tons in August, according to the statistics bureau on Tuesday. That brings the year-to-date figure to over 31 million tons — well on the way to busting the government’s annual capacity limit of about 45 million tons.

Smelters have been furiously churning out metal to capture higher margins on exports after the Iran war disrupted about 9% of the world’s supply. But they’ll face some hard choices over the rest of the year if they’re to meet the cap, which was imposed in 2017 to limit structural oversupply, carbon emissions and electricity demand in the notoriously power-hungry sector.

Steel output fell 3.7%, on track to end the year at the lowest level since 2018, as the country’s protracted property crisis continues to suppress demand. Manufacturing and exports are offering a counterweight, but it’s the seasonal lift to construction activity in the autumn that’s likely to determine how much more of a decline is tolerable.

Oil refinery runs rose month-on-month, as more crude slipped through the net in the Strait of Hormuz or arrived from places like Russia, but they were still 6.9% below last year. Private plants have resumed activity following seasonal maintenance while state processors have raised runs to feed a recovery in fuel exports.
Read More: China’s Hunt for Barrels Threatens Oil Market Balancing Act

Both oil and natural gas output rose 0.8%, but coal mining continued to disappoint, dropping 7.7% as producers struggled to get back on track after the Shanxi disaster in May triggered widespread disruptions. Benchmark thermal coal prices have rallied to the highest level since 2023, and China will step up efforts to bolster domestic energy supply, the statistics bureau said.

Thermal power output fell for a second straight month as milder weather held back demand for air-conditioning. The average temperature in China this August was slightly lower than the same month in 2025, according to data from Atmospheric G2, with 23 of 31 days cooler than the prior year.
For the year, fossil fuel power output is now up less than 1% from 2025, keeping alive hopes that China’s top emitting sector will reduce greenhouse gases for a second consecutive year.

China’s consumer spending and investment languished in August, even as industrial output improved more than expected, adding pressure on officials to step up support for the economy. Residential prices fell in August, with used-home values dropping at a faster pace.

Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. has been cleared to acquire a stake in a battery firm linked to one of China’s largest carmakers, highlighting Beijing’s growing support for consolidation in the sector.
China’s taste for an exotic meat and a prized collagen is helping seed an unusual business hundreds of kilometers away in Pakistan’s arid southwest.
China’s hydropower giants are likely to find their profits tested by El Nino and the Nepal floods, said Bloomberg Intelligence.
Early in the US-Iran war, China’s strategic reduction in oil imports acted as a critical shock absorber for energy markets, said Bloomberg Economics. Circumstances look different these days.

China has fulfilled more than half of its annual US soybean purchase pledge, offering a bright spot for trade between the world’s two largest economies ahead of President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington.

Sustained Chinese appetite for US ethane is driving American exports to unprecedented levels. China’s ethylene capacity expansion is set to sharply slow in 2027 amid project delays before rebounding in 2028, according to BI.

items.title: Nickel Producer Halts Plant Ramp-Up on Indonesian Water Shortage
body: Nickel Industries Ltd. halted the ramp-up of one of its Indonesian processing plants due to water shortages, a sign of how an El-Niño linked drought is hurting output in the world’s top producer.

The Excelsior Nickel Cobalt facility in Sulawesi is expected to operate at 30% of nameplate capacity while the water supply constraints persist, the Sydney-listed company said in a statement on Tuesday. Nickel Industries’ other plants have not been affected by the drought conditions, it said.

Indonesia is in the grip of a severe drought, exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern, which has worsened seasonal forest fires and triggered haze conditions across Southeast Asia. The shift also stands to impact nickel production in the country that accounts for about 60% of global supply.

Earlier this month, Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park, where the majority of Nickel Industries’ operations are sited, flagged overall output could be cut by 30% to 40% if new sources of water are not found. Producers at IMIP are also being hit by the high cost of sulfur, a key so-called reagent for high-pressure acid leaching plants like Excelsior Nickel Cobalt.

Less than 4 millimeters of rain was recorded at Nickel Industries’ Hengjaya mine last month, compared with the historical average of 222 millimeters, according to the statement. The mine is located close to IMIP.

items.title: SoftBank-Backed SB Energy's IPO Seeks $500 Million in Japan
body: SB Energy Inc., a data center firm backed by SoftBank Group Corp., is aiming to raise as much as $500 million in the Japanese portion of its planned initial public offering in the US, following other major deals in tapping the country’s deep pools of capital.

The company will start taking investor orders as early as this month, according to a local regulatory filing Tuesday. The proceeds will be used for developing and constructing infrastructure including data centers and power plants. SB Energy, whose strategic investors include OpenAI and Nvidia Corp., this month filed for an IPO in the US.
Read More: SoftBank’s Data Center and Power Firm SB Energy Files for IPO

Mizuho Financial Group Inc., Daiwa Securities Group Inc., PayPay Securities Corp., Rakuten Securities Inc. and SBI Holdings Inc. will act as the selling agents for Mizuho’s US arm, according to the filing. Mizuho is among the arrangers of the SB Energy listing.

The plan looks to tap into Japan’s household financial assets of about $15 trillion, similar to the blockbuster SpaceX IPO in June. The rocket, satellite and AI company raised $2.2 billion in the country, one of a few around the world where retail investors were able to directly participate.

Local offerings as part of large global deals are rare opportunities in a country where sizeable offerings have become relatively rare. Only one Japanese IPO has raised at least $500 million this year, the $607 million listing of taxi operator Go Inc. in June.

The offering is a chance for Japanese investors to buy into the unprecedented spending on AI infrastructure. It’s expected to generate global economic impact of $20 trillion by 2030, according to an IDC estimate cited in the filing. In energy in particular, analysts at UBS Group AG expect $511 billion to be spent by 2030 to close the gap in power demand, largely driven by data centers.

SB Energy combines data centers and solar power and battery energy storage, with 8.8 gigawatts of data center capacity contracted or under construction across its campuses in Texas and Ohio, according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. It also has 5.5 gigawatts (AC) of power projects contracted, under construction or operating.

The company has issued 3.99 million warrants to OpenAI, some of which have already vested, and the remaining 2.25 million expire in 2036, the filing shows. Nvidia agreed to buy $1.5 billion in non-voting shares in a private placement at the equivalent of the IPO price.

items.title: South Korea Plans Fewer Towers in Expansion of Electricity Grid
body: South Korea plans to cut new transmission towers by as much as 40% and put more power lines underground, as it seeks to boost grid expansion to meet rising demand from data centers and semiconductor plants.

The measures, unveiled by Minister of Climate, Energy and Environment Kim Sung-hwan on Tuesday, are aimed at easing local opposition to electricity infrastructure while adding capacity to connect renewable generation to major demand centers.

“We need to reduce social conflict by communicating sufficiently with residents and sharing tangible benefits, while expanding the necessary power grid in a timely manner,” Kim said in a statement. “Power grids are essential national infrastructure supporting the energy transition and the growth of advanced industries.”

The artificial intelligence boom is driving a global increase in electricity demand, which requires investment in grids to handle the heavier loads. South Korea announced an overhaul of its state-owned energy companies earlier this month, with the aim of strengthening its competitiveness at a time of rising power consumption.
Read More: South Korea Set to Merge State-Run Energy Firms to Cut Costs

The government plans to reduce the need for towers by consolidating transmission lines and making greater use of existing infrastructure, Kim said, while expanding underground cables in densely populated areas.

Communities hosting major transmission infrastructure will receive greater financial benefits, including income from renewable-energy projects, the ministry said in the statement. The government also plans to increase compensation and consultation.

items.title: India Bonds in Spotlight as Yield Premium Over Treasuries Hits 22-Year Low
body: Good morning... I’m Savio Shetty in Mumbai, where traders have a lot to chew on after a long weekend, and also a lot to look forward to.The global bond selloff has continued, with the US 10-year Treasury yield surpassing 5% for the first time since 2023 on Monday, when Indian markets were shut for a holiday. Local yields are also expected to rise when trading resumes as India’s central bank has said it will drain 1 trillion rupees ($10.5 billion) from lenders through bond sales, its strongest effort yet to tackle a massive cash surplus in the banking system that poses inflationary risks.Also, oil prices have risen further, and data released on Monday showed inflation accelerated in August, moving closer to the top of the central bank’s 2%-6% target range and making it harder for policymakers to keep rates on hold for long. An advance in local yields may help widen their spread over US Treasuries, which has narrowed to its lowest in more than two decades. (more on that below).Indian equity traders also face a challenging backdrop. While the local market has limited exposure to AI, the selloff in AI-linked stocks bears watching after leaders of some of the world’s biggest companies called for a slowdown in the development of models, citing escalating risks from the technology. India’s benchmark Nifty 50 slid 2.1% last week to cap a fifth straight week of losses, its longest losing run since April.Tata Group stocks will be in focus after the RBI rejected an application from Tata Sons, the conglomerate’s holding company, to surrender its status as a shadow lender. The decision could pave the way for a public listing of Tata Sons.Looking ahead, the Federal Reserve is the first of three major central banks — followed by the Bank of England and Bank of Japan — to announce its policy decision this week. A hotter-than-expected US inflation reading has raised bets on higher interest rates, a move that could have a big impact on bonds, currencies and stocks around the world.
In today’s newsletter, we write about:

Indian bonds have been relatively unscathed by the global bond selloff in recent weeks as a record liquidity surplus in the banking system supported demand for local securities. But the trend may be hard to sustain as the yield gap between domestic bonds and US Treasuries has shrunk to the smallest in over two decades. That is eroding the extra return foreign investors get by holding Indian debt. The shrinking yield advantage may eventually test the RBI’s ability to keep borrowing costs insulated from global markets. With US yields continuing to climb, Indian debt will need higher local yields to remain relatively attractive— a repricing that could come through further weakness in the bond market or a shift toward higher interest rates.
NSE IPO could strain the market

The National Stock Exchange starts taking orders Thursday for its 226-billion-rupee ($2.4 billion) IPO. While that means a test of investor appetite for one of the nation’s most awaited deals, it could also drain liquidity from the secondary market. If fully subscribed, the offering will draw funds equivalent to 2.1 times the average weekly net demand for listed shares this year, data compiled by Bloomberg show. That may add to the pressure on equities as oil prices stay above $100 a barrel and foreign investors remain net sellers. Caution around NSE shares is showing in the unofficial market, where the premium for its unlisted stock fell to about 188 rupees on Friday from 285 rupees on Sept. 7, according to ipowatch.in.
Realty stocks sink as rate-hike bets rise

A gauge of real estate shares tumbled almost 7% last week, its worst drop in four months. The selloff reflects worries that demand for homes may weaken if the RBI raises interest rates amid oil-driven inflation risks and rising US Treasury yields. The realty index is already trading at 37 times current earnings, nearly twice the Nifty 50’s valuation, even as housing sales growth in key cities begins to cool. Supply, meanwhile, is likely to remain elevated through 2027, with developers continuing to launch projects at a brisk pace, according to a recent note by Brickwork Ratings.
Financial-services stocks may make a comeback in 2027

India’s financial-services stocks could narrow the wide gap with global peers in 2027, according to Jefferies. The MSCI India Financials Index has lagged its global counterpart by about 40 percentage points over the past two years, hurt by weaker growth, earnings revisions and the currency. Jefferies expects earnings for the group to grow 14% next year, twice the global pace. A potential rate hike could be another catalyst. Much may also hinge on smooth leadership transitions, according to Jefferies, which has ICICI Bank, SBI and IndusInd Bank among its top picks.

Markets regulator SEBI on Saturday floated a revamp of the closing auction session for stocks amid widespread concerns over sharp price swings and liquidity. The proposals include a rethink of how derivatives settlement prices are calculated. We answer three key questions.What are the main proposed changes?Under one option, the settlement price would be based on a blend of the 30-minute volume-weighted average price and a 10-minute auction window. The second would retain the old VWAP method for a year before shifting to the blended system.
How could the new pricing system help?

In either scenario, the eventual blended price would give more weight to the continuous trading session, where the bulk of market activity takes place. That shift could make the closing process more predictable and reduce the sharp swings seen so far.What will the changes mean for different market participants?

More weight for the 30-minute average price could boost trading volumes and benefit stock exchanges and brokers. Market makers may be at a disadvantage, however, as proposed limits on order cancellations could leave them holding unwanted positions during sharp price moves, likely making them cautious about providing liquidity.

MORE: Check out Bloomberg’s Emerging, a monthly podcast series hosted by Menaka Doshi and Haslinda Amin on the rising economies shaping the global future. In episode two, Menaka explores how the AI boom is reshaping electricity demand and whether it could strain power grids. You can watch it here or listen on iHeart, Apple, Amazon, or Spotify.

Save the date: Bloomberg New Economy Forum - New Delhi: This October, the Bloomberg New Economy Forum convenes its global community of business and public-sector leaders under the guiding theme, “A World in Play: Defining the New Levers of Power.” This year’s Forum, held Oct. 13-15 in New Delhi, will examine the shifting geopolitical landscape and explore the risks and opportunities reshaping the global economy. Visit BloombergNewEconomy.com/India to learn more.

items.title: Pentagon Watchdog Sees Strategic Munitions Shortage
body: The US fired so many munitions at Iranian targets during the first few months of Operation Epic Fury that it “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” Pentagon officials acknowledged to the Defense Department’s independent watchdog.

Acquisition officials said they are “working to streamline procurement processes and production lead times, and to stockpile critical materials, components, and selected munitions to respond rapidly to a contingency,” the Pentagon inspector general said in a report released late Monday.
The IG report, which covers the US military’s operations in the conflict with Iran through June 30, marks an official confirmation of a problem the Trump administration has repeatedly downplayed.

“The U.S. has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types,” Trump posted on social media Aug 6. In another post Sept. 9, Trump said the US has “virtually unlimited amounts” of mid- to high-grade ammunition — “far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War.”

The Defense Department estimated it had spent $22.3 billion worth of expended munitions in the war as of about the end of June, according to the report, while the overall cost through that period totaled more than $33 billion.

The Congressional Budget Office also estimated Tuesday that the direct cost of the first five months of the war in Iran cost $38 billion and will push inflation up 0.5 percentage points by early next year.
Read More: Iran War Has Cost US $38 Billion Over Five Months, CBO Says

The report is the Pentagon IG’s first quarterly assessment of Operation Epic Fury, and reads as a high-level budgetary guide to the cost of the war, with dollar amounts attached. Congress requires these quarterly reports on US military operations where appropriated dollars are spent. The report includes contributions from the watchdogs overseeing the State Department and US Agency for International Development.
A senior Pentagon official said Tuesday that it doesn’t agree with the IG’s findings, “and any report that suggests that the United States’ munitions are depleted are completely false.”

Iran’s military has damaged or destroyed “hundreds” of buildings and structures at US bases in the region, while US diplomatic facilities in four countries sustained physical damage from Iranian strikes, US Central Command told the IG.

The report listed 11 US service members killed in action as of the end of July, with another seven killed in non-hostile events during Epic Fury combat operations. More than 400 service members were wounded in action through the end of June.
The Pentagon didn’t release an immediate comment on the report.

items.title: Indonesia's Prabowo Picked a Good Time to Oust His Finance Chief
body: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto picked a good time to replace his finance minister. Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa, who had been in the post for a year, struggled to gain the confidence of investors. But after months of selling, markets are enjoying a modest upswing. It’s wise to use this opportunity to clean house.

The top economic job goes to Purbaya's deputy, Suahasil Nazara. He was also No. 2 to the highly respected Sri Mulyani Indrawati, who served for almost a decade as finance minister. Nazara doesn't have the public profile to match his two predecessors, and that might just be his main attribute.

Indonesia needs someone who can speak cautiously about growth, jobs and deficits. It was a promising first step that Nazara emphasized the need to keep the budget shortfall within legal limits. His predecessor was unconvincing in his defense of the rule, which has become a litmus test for credibility.Purbaya was often brash and combative. He made personal attacks on a Citigroup Inc. economist who questioned the government's fiscal trajectory; people would do better to heed a Ph.D. economist like him, he insisted. This showed a shoot-the-messenger approach. Nazara should keep his head down and recognize that Indonesia competes for capital. Soothing words can go a long way, even if the thrust of policy is dictated from above.

Purbaya was unfortunate enough to have held the reins when the rupiah was repeatedly hitting record lows, and yields on Indonesian bonds jumped. Only frequent intervention from the central bank prevented the currency from weakening further. It would be unfair to blame Purbaya for every market ruction. At least some of his approach would have been sanctioned by Prabowo, who has intervened more in the nuts and bolts of decisions than prior leaders.

The former general has voiced skepticism about budget rectitude and has been clear that he wants the state to play a bigger role in driving growth. Both he and the new finance boss should use this opportunity to jettison the pipe dream of 8% annual growth, a clip not seen in more than a generation. Lately, Prabowo has been more disciplined in his messaging. Picking a seasoned insider — Nazara spent seven years as a deputy minister — recognizes that a more conventional and less populist approach to governing would be helpful.

It’s a good time to show investors that Indonesia is serious about addressing its challenges. Some stability has returned to markets, with the rupiah on track for a modest quarterly advance and foreigners showing renewed interest in equities, battered by the threat of a downgrade from MSCI Inc. to the status of a frontier market. The benchmark Jakarta Composite Index is still down by almost a quarter this year, so it's an easy decision for Nazara to seek a meeting with MSCI as soon as possible. A side trip to New York to woo Wall Street after attendance at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund in Washington next month would be time well spent.

Nazara should also repair relations with the central bank. Purbaya clashed with Perry Warjiyo, the former head of Bank Indonesia, who was forced out in July in favor of his deputy, Destry Damayanti. The selection of Nazara at the finance ministry shows a similar preference for stability. Having purged his economic team and opted for seasoned hands, Prabowo just may have turned a corner.
With luck, the president has recognized that while he may be head of state, he is required to govern in tandem with markets. Or, at the very least, without their hostility.

items.title: Copper Rises as Traders Weigh New Deliveries, Fed Rate Path
body: Copper advanced as traders weighed easing supply squeeze and bets that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates for the first time in three years.

Futures on the London Metal Exchange rose 0.6% on Tuesday to settle at $14,083.50 a metric ton. Prices have pulled back sharply since rallying to a record high last week, when traders were diverting supplies to the US in anticipation of tariffs on refined metal, leaving the rest of the world starved of supply.

So far, that measure has failed to materialize, and on Monday LME warehouses received their biggest deliveries of copper in almost four weeks. Three-month futures flipped to a premium of $86.75 a ton to copper for immediate delivery, a market structure known as contango that signals ample supply. The premium narrowed slightly on Tuesday to $62.53 a ton.

Economic data from China showed industrial output in the world’s biggest metals consumer improved more than expected in August, even as consumer spending and investment languished. The divergence widens a divide within the economy that complicates the decision facing policymakers over whether to provide additional stimulus.
Also in focus is the Fed’s upcoming meeting, where the US central bank is expected to raise interest rates. That’s typically a negative for non-yielding assets like commodities.
Other LME metals were mixed, with zinc up 0.8% while nickel down 2.2%.

items.title: Traxion Gets Tender Offer as Share Liquidity, Price Drops
body: A company linked to Grupo Traxion’s Executive President Aby Lijtszain Chernizky plans to launch a tender offer for as much as 100% of the Mexican logistics company’s shares, giving investors a chance to sell amid limited trading in the stock.

“The shares are ridiculously cheap,” Traxion’s Vice President of Investor Relations Antonio Tejedo told Bloomberg, citing the weak economic environment and uncertainty over Mexico-US relations, which have hurt demand, volumes and prices.

Traxion will decide its next steps after seeing how many investors take up the offer. A potential delisting remains an option but isn’t currently under discussion and would require a separate process, Tejedo said.

The offer is expected to take place on the Mexican Stock Exchange at an estimated price of 13.18 pesos per share, more than 20% above its average share price over the 60 days through Sept. 11, according to a company statement issued after Monday’s market close. Traxion expects to launch it Thursday and keep it open for 30 days, the executive said.
The move comes as Traxion faces a prolonged slowdown in its freight business, with no recovery expected over the next two or three quarters.
“We don’t know when the Trump administration will stop making noise,” Tejedo said.

Traxion has paused plans to enter the US through an acquisition, but remains interested in reviving them when conditions improve, he said. The company has also sold about 80 trucks in recent quarters and doesn’t plan to replace them, a move aimed at cutting spending and improving cash flow.

The buyout proposal follows a 26% slide in its shares this year. In the second quarter, its net income fell 42% year-on-year, even as revenue growth beat estimates. Company shares were up 1.60% on Tuesday morning.

While Traxion doesn’t yet know which investors will participate, it doesn’t rule out that large holders will be interested in the opportunity, Tejedo said. Some of the company’s largest holders include Discovery Americas, Nexxus Capital and Vanguard Group, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

In 2017, the company sold 239 million shares in an initial public offering to raise 4.07 billion pesos ($237 million), with plans to use the proceeds for acquisitions. Traxion agreed in 2024 to acquire certain logistics operations from Femsa, doing business as Solistica.

For now, the company sees room to grow its existing logistics and technology businesses in Mexico, which require less investment. Traxion also sees little regulatory risk in the country, as foreign companies are restricted from operating freight and passenger fleets on federal routes, the executive said.

items.title: Chinese Economic Momentum Stays Weak With No Stimulus in Sight
body: China’s consumer spending and investment languished in August even as industrial output improved more than expected, widening a divide within the economy that complicates the decision facing policymakers over any additional stimulus.

Retail sales rose 0.4% from a year ago, worse than the 0.8% consensus forecast by economists in a Bloomberg poll, and down from 0.6% in July. Fixed-asset investment plunged 7.2% in the first eight months from the same period last year, slumping slightly more than expected. The jobless rate unexpectedly ticked up.

In contrast, industrial output climbed 5.2% in August, exceeding expectations and accelerating from July’s 4.5% gain. Double-digit growth in exports is largely behind the uplift, as hundreds of billions of dollars flow into the global buildout of data centers and drive up demand for artificial intelligence-related products such as integrated circuits.

The widening divergence between domestic and external demand shows that the rapid expansion in China’s high-tech industries has yet to translate into better incomes and confidence among households. Overall economic growth likely improved little in August from July, though officials may feel emboldened by surging exports and look beyond weakness at home.

“The risk is that policymakers become complacent and fail to introduce sufficient counter-cyclical measures to support domestic demand,” said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at Union Bancaire Privee. That could “leave China trapped in a structural cycle of high savings, weak consumption and persistently low growth.”

The yuan was steady in onshore and offshore markets after the data release and the yield on the government’s 10-year bond was little changed at 1.68%. The Chinese currency has outperformed its regional peers in the past five days despite the dollar’s rebound, as the People’s Bank of China set the daily fixing at a stronger level.

NBS spokesman Fu Linghui said the latest figures showed “the economy was overall stable.” Speaking at a briefing in Beijing, he warned, however, over the negative impact from overseas conflicts and the imbalance between strong supply and weak demand.

Barclays Plc, Oxford Economics and Macquarie Group estimate gross domestic product will expand 4.3% from a year ago in the third quarter based on July and August numbers. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. lowered its forecast of growth for this quarter to 4.4% from 4.6% following the data release.

Without a sharp turnaround in September, that leaves growth increasingly at risk of falling below the official annual target of 4.5% to 5% for a second straight quarter after decelerating sharply in April-June.
Australia & New Zealand Banking Group Ltd. said GDP growth was tracking at 4.2% in July-August, less than the second-half rate needed to meet China’s full-year goal.

Unless momentum improves in the coming months, policymakers are likely to face growing pressure to deploy additional stimulus. And while Beijing is starting to dial up fiscal policy, reversing the decline in government expenditure and channeling the money into the broader economy may take time.

“It’s time to bring out all the fiscal stimulus promised in the ‘Two Sessions’ earlier this year,” said Miao Yanliang, chief economist at China International Capital Corp., in an interview with Bloomberg TV. He was referring to this year’s budget plans announced at the legislative meeting in March.

Government bonds slated to be issued during the rest of this year but still unsold were 1.5 trillion yuan ($223 billion) more than their level a year ago, according to Miao, which is equivalent to around 1.1% of China’s GDP. The government should be able to meet the growth target with spending financed by the bonds, he added.

The economy is also confronting external shocks that are widening the divergence among industries and complicating the policy outlook. Global oil prices have surged back above $100 a barrel as tensions in the Middle East intensify, squeezing downstream industries.

An overhaul of real estate policy aimed at dismantling the country’s so-called pre-sale model is likely to weigh further on property investment and local government finances in the coming months. The measure essentially delays developers’ access to mortgages to strengthen protections for homebuyers, likely curbing builders’ appetite for expansion as the industry grapples with a prolonged liquidity squeeze.
“Overall, it seems like it’s broadly stable, maybe a bit worse in August than July,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING Bank NV.
Property investment slumped 19.9% in the first eight months of this year from a year ago, deepening its decline. The urban jobless rate unexpectedly rose to 5.3% from 5.2% in July.

The historic fall in investment that began in mid-2025 shows no signs of abating, as businesses turn pessimistic. The average profit margin among manufacturers stood at 4.9% in July. While that’s an improvement from a year ago, it’s still down from as high as 6.7% in 2021.

Hopes for any rebound in investment are tied to the construction on the Six Networks, a government program covering the buildout of data centers, power grids, ultra-high-speed fiber broadband and waterways.

Projects related to the multi-trillion yuan initiative offered a rare bright spot in China’s infrastructure spending this year. Capital spending on information transmission soared 28.4% in January-August, up from 26% in the first seven months. It rose 14.7% in waterway transportation, versus 16.2% in the period through July.

The continued plunge in car sales was again the biggest drag on consumer spending, with auto sales plummeting 18.5% in August from a year ago. Excluding cars, retail sales grew 2.5% in August, the same pace as in July. The phasing out of car purchase subsidies this year weighed on consumers, who are also contending with a worsening job market and falling property values.

“Thanks to exports, China’s factory activity is holding up,” Raymond Yeung, chief economist for greater China at ANZ. “But investment is falling faster, not to mention the persistent weakness in retail sales. Domestic demand is very weak. The economic momentum is clearly uneven across sectors.”

items.title: Waymo to Start Tokyo Robotaxi Service Next Year in Asia Push
body: Alphabet Inc.’s Waymo plans to bring its robotaxis to Japan next year as the US market leader continues its global expansion.

Waymo will partner with Japanese taxi firms Go Inc. and Nihon Kotsu Co. to start a fully autonomous service in Tokyo in 2027, it said Tuesday. The companies expect to start with a small fleet and then expand gradually to 100 vehicles.
Shares of Go, which manages Japan’s top taxi-booking app, rose as much as 9.7% on Tuesday. The stock is up more than 40% since its initial public offering in June.

Waymo has been expanding rapidly in the US and is now setting its sights on overseas markets, with the manufacturer also preparing a service in London. It has been testing in Tokyo for the past year and its autonomous service would be the first on Japanese public roads.

The robotaxis would “complement Tokyo’s world-renowned transportation network, while helping Japan support an aging population and address future labor shortages,” Waymo said in a blog post. Rides will be accessible through the Go and Waymo apps.

Autonomous driving was long seen as a pipe dream in Japan, where the streets are narrow and crowded, and regulation is notoriously strict. But in the past months, companies have made efforts to get things going.

Earlier this year, US self-driving startup Nuro Inc. began testing in Tokyo, its first location abroad after partnering with Uber Technologies Inc. and Lucid Group Inc. Backed by the likes of Nvidia Corp. and Toyota Motor Corp., Nuro aims to compete with Waymo and Amazon.com Inc.’s Zoox.
Read More: US Self-Driving Startup Nuro Begins Testing on Tokyo Streets

Waymo said it still has to secure the necessary permits and licenses for its Japanese service. The country’s regulations currently require a human being in the driver’s seat, regardless of the vehicle’s level of autonomy.

items.title: China Home Price Slump Persists as Focus Turns to Support
body: China’s residential prices fell in August, with used-home values dropping at a faster pace, the latest sign of a slump that pushed policymakers to unveil fresh steps to support the market at the end of last month.

New-home prices in 70 cities declined 0.17% from July, when they slid 0.18%, figures from the National Bureau of Statistics showed on Tuesday. Resale home values, which are subject to less government intervention, slid 0.31%, accelerating from the previous month’s 0.29%.

China’s five-year property downturn has curtailed domestic demand that officials are counting on to boost the economy. That pushed Beijing to unveil sweeping policy changes on Aug. 28, including bringing an end to a once dominant pre-sale model.
The changes came too late to affect the monthly figure — and analysts think it could still take a little while longer before they have a real impact on demand.

“Given the package is a structural reform rather than a cyclical stimulus, it will lend limited direct support to near-term property sales,” Moody’s Ratings analysts led by Lillian Li said in a report this month. “Over time, these changes could help restore confidence in the housing market.”

The recent measures include a plan to push developers to offer completed properties instead of using the pre-sales model that exacerbated the housing crisis. China will also support fundraising by developers through equity and bond sales. Homebuyers will be allowed to take out 40-year mortgages, up from a maximum of 30 years previously.

The longer-term loans “won’t halt the slide in home sales, which we expect will continue into 2028,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Kristy Hung wrote in a note last week. Given age and collateral limits, the credit will only be available to a small portion of borrowers, and the policy doesn’t address the potential for equity losses if prices keep falling, Hung said.

Local governments have also taken steps to ease the crunch, although their changes have largely been marginal. Last month, Beijing further eased homebuying rules for non-residents, as the capital city joined Shanghai in lifting decade-long restrictions.

In the short run, the property sales overhaul will raise developers’ financing costs by restricting access to proceeds until projects are completed and delivered, weighing on real estate investments, according to Bloomberg Economics. The changes have already put pressure on funding for China’s local governments, which have long relied on land sales for revenue.

Home prices in China’s wealthy tier-one cities such as Beijing and Shanghai have been rising for most of this year, but the latest data shows even that small sign of recovery is losing steam. Used-home prices in the four biggest cities climbed 0.08% on average in August, slowing from a 0.23% gain in July.

items.title: Landmark NSE IPO Threatens to Hollow Out India Shadow Market
body: The landmark listing of National Stock Exchange of India Ltd. is set to deliver a major boost to the country’s primary market, but it will be a significant blow to the booming trade in unlisted shares.

The operator of the world’s busiest derivatives market accounted for roughly half of the trading volume in the shadow market, according to an estimate by trading platform UnlistedZone. Its initial public offering threatens to trigger a sharp drop in activity, forcing platforms that facilitate such transactions to find the next big draw.

As India set consecutive records in IPO proceeds the last two years, the unlisted market emerged as a venue for wealthy individuals and funds to make bet on companies in the listing pipeline. The booming interest fostered an ecosystem of online platforms and specialist brokers that specialize in connecting buyers and sellers.

NSE had been a linchpin of the growing market because of its scale, profitability, dominant position and disclosures that mirrored listed companies. The presence of smaller listed rival BSE Ltd. gave investors a valuation benchmark, while years of delays in its listing meant an unusually long trading window.
Read More: India’s 500% Boom in Unlisted Share Trades Shows Rush for Riches

That helped turn a once-niche corner of India’s financial system into a mainstream investment avenue, giving rise to intermediaries that assisted investors with the regulatory approvals, documentation and transfers needed to buy shares.
“NSE was quasi-listed,” said Sandipan Roy, chief investment officer at Motilal Oswal Private Wealth. “It spawned an entire industry.”

The exchange had 231,378 shareholders ahead of its IPO, more than several listed companies. That compares with fewer than 80 shareholders it had in 2016, according to its December 2016 draft prospectus. Until last year, NSE made monthly disclosures on share transfers. Its last such release in March 2025 showed nearly 15 billion rupees ($170 million) of shares changing hands during the month.

Staying relevant without NSE may prove more challenging for platforms that have mushroomed over the years. As no issuers currently offer the combination of size, familiarity and liquidity of NSE, they may have to persuade investors to trade smaller companies with typically less financial disclosure and thinner liquidity.

“We expect interest in the unlisted market to remain selective as companies emerge across sectors such as space technology, aerospace, defense, data centers and other new-age industries,” said Rajan Shah, Founder, 3A Capital Services, which operates a platform for dealing in unlisted shares.

Companies attracting market interest include Sterlite Electric Ltd, Indofil Industries Ltd, Krasny Defence Technologies Ltd, Berar Finance Ltd, Kineco Ltd, Indian Potash Ltd and Garuda Aerospace Ltd, he added.

Investing in unlisted shares hasn’t always proved profitable. Investors in some high-profile names, including HDB Financial Services Ltd. and Tata Capital Ltd., suffered losses, while those who bought NSE shares over the past year may also enter the IPO sitting on losses.
“There have also been instances of outsize returns in the unlisted market,” said Umesh Paliwal, co-founder, UnlistedZone. “Ultimately, entry timing and valuations are critical.”

items.title: BlackRock Raises EM Equities Back to Overweight on AI, Earnings
body: BlackRock Inc. has returned to an overweight recommendation on emerging-market equities, betting that access to the scarce resources needed for the artificial-intelligence boom and strong earnings will drive outperformance.

South Korea and Taiwan “sit at the heart” of semiconductor and memory chip supply chains, while Latin American markets offer exposure to the commodities and infrastructure needed for the AI buildout, strategists in the company’s research arm, including Wei Li, wrote in a report on Monday. BlackRock expects growing investment in the technology to increase the value of those constrained resources and support corporate profits.

The move marks a reversal from June, when the world’s largest asset manager cut emerging-market equities to neutral from overweight, warning that AI concentration and leverage, particularly in South Korea, had weakened the risk-reward profile. BlackRock said deleveraging in Korean stocks following the sharp July selloff helped support the return to overweight.

The call will now hinge on whether faster earnings growth and cheaper valuations can outweigh risks from rising borrowing costs, elevated oil prices and geopolitical tensions. BlackRock also sees a weaker dollar and improving capital flows providing support as investors reassess emerging markets after recent volatility.

“AI-related investment can support growth and profits even as the same investment boom absorbs capital, power and other scarce resources,” the strategists added. “The numbers reinforce the case for returning to EM equities.”

Consensus forecasts show earnings for the MSCI Emerging Markets Index growing more than 34% over the next 12 months, versus about 20% for the MSCI USA Index, according to the note. Emerging-market equities trade at about 10 times forward earnings, roughly half the multiple of US stocks, representing a 50% discount, the strategists said.

“The bar for taking risk is rising as rates reset higher, making the durability of earnings more important,” the note added. “EM equities now offer another place where earnings can clear that higher hurdle.”

items.title: Volatility Surges in First After-Hours Session on Korea Exchange
body: The first after-hours session on South Korea’s main stock exchange saw erratic and retail-dominated trading, in a sign of the challenges ahead as it seeks to attract more global investors.

Monday’s launch represents the first step by a major Asian exchange toward around-the-clock trading. Nasdaq Inc. and the New York Stock Exchange are among other markets looking at such moves to better tap international demand.

Korea Exchange now offers late trading between the hours of 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. In Monday’s extended session, volatility spikes in individual stocks triggered brief trading halts 1,637 times, more than four times the number during the day’s regular session, according to data from the bourse.

“Institutional traders mostly stayed on the sidelines, so there just weren’t enough buy and sell orders in the market,” said Sanghyun Park, founder of Clepsydra Capital. “Retail investors clearly want after-hours trading, but until bigger players step in and provide more liquidity, it’s likely to remain pretty risky.”
Read more: Korea Tests Global Investor Appetite With Longer Trading Hours
A total of 2,501 different stocks were traded in the evening hours, with some activating the so-called volatility interruption (VI) mechanism more than once.

Individual investors accounted for 93% of the extended session’s total turnover of 1.8 trillion won ($1.34 billion), Korea Exchange said in a statement. Foreign investors accounted for just 3.9%, with local institutions accounting for the rest.

Extended hours have been seen as a way to help level the playing field for retail traders, and allow more investors to quickly act on late-breaking news. Seasoned investors are bracing for volatility, however, as global exchanges look to keep pace with the 24-hour trading provided by electronic platforms.
“Smaller stocks were an absolute roller coaster, jumping 15% to 30% on relatively minor news before dropping just as quickly,” Clepsydra’s Park said, describing Monday’s session.

items.title: India's Art Scene Takes Over the Venice Biennale, London and New York
body: The Venice Biennale is known as the Olympics of the art world — roughly 100 countries, along with many more museums, artists and foundations, put on exhibitions throughout the Italian city. This year there was no escaping the omnipresence of India during the festival’s opening in May, with at least five major exhibitions of Indian art. The most publicized, at the official  Pavilion of India, was a group show featuring a scale reproduction of Sumakshi Singh’s (now-demolished) family home made from lacelike threads. Visitors could walk through the ethereal, two-story installation, which felt like wandering through a dream.

Several solo shows by Indian artists were also spread across the city, including  “Of Woman Born” by Nalini Malani, one of the grande dames of the country’s contemporary art scene. Malani, best known as a pioneer of video art, projected more than 60 giant animations of semi-abstracted figures onto the walls of a dimly lit warehouse and accompanied them with a 20-minute sound piece. Conceived as a work that would bring to the forefront the burden borne by women during global conflict, the piece was towering, slightly weird and surprisingly moving.

And Venice was just the teaser. In the months since, we’ve seen an unprecedented number of global exhibitions devoted to Indian art and artists. In London a presentation of mythological sculpture by Bharti Kher  is on view at the V&A Museum through Jan. 24; the Museum of Modern Art in New York will show the monumental paintings of  Nilima Sheikh. In Berlin at the Hamburger Bahnhof, a solo exhibition by multidisciplinary artist Shilpa Gupta will be  on display until early January. “On the Sweetness of the World. Contemporary Indian Art,”  a group show at the State Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, Russia, runs into early October.

This sudden omnipresence is notable, because, until recently, contemporary Indian art was nowhere near as popular. “Ten years ago, broadly, India was often viewed as an emerging market,” says Jaya Asokan, director of the annual  India Art Fair in Delhi, which will have its 18th edition in February. “Today there is much greater confidence. Indian collectors are buying more thoughtfully, galleries are more ambitious, institutions are stronger, and artists are increasingly part of international exhibitions and museum collections.”

There’s much behind this gold rush. As India’s economy has boomed and its population of newly rich citizens ballooned — in 2025 the country had more than 868,000 millionaires and 185 billionaires — a new class of collectors and patrons has supercharged the art scene. This movement is arguably led from the top down, with a small ultrarich coterie devoting vast resources to promote their art at home and abroad. “The wealthier people in India have finally accepted the fact that the best legacy they can leave behind is art and culture,” says Dinesh Vazirani, co-founder and chief executive officer of the auction house Saffronart.

The construction of two massive, privately funded cultural centers is a case in point. In Delhi the industrialist Munjal family is building an 8-acre, 1.4 million-square-foot arts compound called the Brij, which will include performance spaces, workshops, a library, restaurants and a museum. A roughly 30-minute drive away, tech billionaire Kiran Nadar is working on her new arts center, which will showcase work by modern and contemporary South Asian artists in a 1 million-square-foot complex designed by starchitect Adjaye Associates; it will include galleries, archives, a library and auditoriums. These projects will join a handful of existing, privately funded museums across the country, including philanthropist Abhishek Poddar’s Museum of Art & Photography in Bengaluru, which opened its doors in 2023.

Cities around the world have attempted to generate economic growth through cultural programming. What’s particularly remarkable about India’s experience is that the development of its art scene was initially targeted toward a national, rather than international, audience. Much like America’s robber barons a century ago, India’s business leaders see art as a tool for civic improvement. “A lot of these initiatives were actually born out of the need to step in where the government, historically over the last two to three decades, has not been as proactive,” says Shanay Jhaveri, head of visual arts at London’s Barbican Centre. “The impetus for them starts earlier than this particular moment, and it’s of course catalyzed momentum, with the economy doing better and wealth generally growing.”

Now this cultural investment has turned international. “India is a country that is one of the fastest-growing economies in the world,” says Sunil Kant Munjal, the chairman of Hero Enterprise and founder of Serendipity Arts, the umbrella organization for his family’s sprawling cultural programs. “It’s a country which wants to be seen and heard and be on the top table.”

“India is at the cultural center of the world right now,” says the architect and designer Ashiesh Shah, whose show at London’s Carpenters Workshop Gallery closed on Sept. 5. “Fashion, music, art — it’s all being appreciated at scale.”

Twenty years ago, American and European museums, foundations and collectors showed, at best, a desultory interest in 20th century and contemporary Indian art. By about 2016, spurred by the growing awareness of this bias (and others), these same institutions began to fill the notable holes in their collections. During his six years as a curator at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Barbican’s Jhaveri says he “had a focus on South Asia, and it was dedicated to collection-building, exhibitions and special projects.” He adds, “That was, for me, a very interesting exercise, because that was happening in tandem with a lot of the initiatives we’re talking about taking off within the country itself.”

Western institutions such as the Met, Jhaveri continues, quickly realized they were late to the game. “They had to acknowledge their belatedness in engaging with what had become a pretty self-sustaining ecosystem of its own,” he says. That, in turn, has resulted in an inevitable boom in the market for Indian art, both nationally and abroad. “It’s astounding to everybody, the immense pace at which [the market has] evolved in the last few years,” he says. In April, Saffronart set a record for an Indian artist when it sold a 19th century work by the figurative painter Raja Ravi Varma for almost $18 million. “The opportunity is not to replicate the US, European or Chinese market,” says Nadar, “but to build a strong Indian market that is confident enough to participate in the global one.”

India has always had an old-money, art-collecting upper class, but for decades those collectors acquired work by Indian artists without much competition. “We saw that most Indians collected Indian art, because of course it meant something to them,” says Amin Jaffer, who curated India’s popular official pavilion in Venice and previously worked at Christie’s auction house. Even then, prices were almost comically low, says Poddar, whose museum houses more than 100,000 works of art. “A pair of dress shoes would cost you what a decent canvas would cost you, by a relatively well-known artist of the day,” he says, speaking of the 1970s and ’80s.

The calculus no longer applies. That old-money collector base is now competing with the country’s rising class of newly rich. From 2021 to 2026, the number of people in India worth $30 million or more jumped 63%, from roughly 12,000 to about 20,000, according to The Wealth Report 2026 from Knight Frank LLP. “It used to be the top 1%,” says Asokan, the art fair director. “What’s changed now is there’s this whole layer underneath that.”

When Western institutions finally waded into the market, competition grew further. “We have a great relationship with the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, for example,” Asokan says. “We’ve actually seen direct acquisitions” as a result, she continues. “Auction -headlines attract attention, but underneath that you’re seeing this very strong network of institutions and galleries and sustained investment in artists.”

Those auction headlines speak to the proliferation of Indian art around the world. “There is also a significant shift in how Indian and South Asian art is being positioned globally,” Nadar says. “The interest is no longer only about market value or investment; there is a growing engagement with the artists, histories and ideas shaping the region.” The shallow market of 20 years ago has deepened, with local and international institutional participation. That means more people in the US, Europe and Asia are looking to acquire Indian art specifically. “Today if someone has a great painting, you’d have, for the first time, at least five buyers for it at top value,” says Saffronart’s Vazirani.

Dozens of Indian artists have broken their personal high prices in the past five years. Vazarini recalls a foreign buyer visiting Saffronart’s gallery a few decades ago and asking about a piece by S.H. Raza, a renowned abstract painter. It was priced at $10,000. “He said, ‘Call me when it’s $200,000,’ ” Vazirani says. “Art builds gravitas with value. That’s when people start taking it seriously.” Raza’s top auction price is now $6.3 million; his work has sold for more than $1 million 38 times, according to the Artnet price database.

Indian art, to put it mildly, has more than enough gravitas to go around today. Still, its market is minuscule compared with those of other major countries. It doesn’t figure in the most recent annual Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report, and to date there’s no reliable data on its overall size — a sign there’s not much to count in comparison to the US, China and other countries.

But India’s cultural leaders are far from finished. “The soft power of India is a wonderful instrument,” says Serendipity’s Munjal. “It is not a jackhammer, which is often used in politics, and it is a message that will outlast any trade agreement.”
